articles.title: ‘We Are Christians, Good People’: Russian Media Tycoon Urges Nuclear Strike on Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian nationalist media tycoon Konstantin Malofeyev urged President Vladimir Putin to launch a nuclear strike on Ukraine after a 72-hour evacuation warning, while insisting Russians were “good people” who did not want to kill Ukrainians.
Speaking on Piers Morgan Uncensored, the owner of the pro-Kremlin Tsargrad channel proposed an ultimatum threatening nuclear attacks on sites holding Western weapons in western Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Malofeyev argued that the warning would allow civilians to leave before the strike. He presented the proposed attack as a means of ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“We are Christians, we are good people,” he said, describing Ukrainians as fellow Slavs and insisting Russians did not want to kill them.
Morgan challenged that argument: “Good people don’t invade their neighbors.”
Asked to identify something he criticized Putin for, Malofeyev pointed to the Russian leader’s failure to use nuclear weapons.
“And I criticize him for that,” he said.
Earlier call for a tactical nuclear attack
The remarks were not Malofeyev’s first public appeal for a nuclear strike.
In April, he urged the use of tactical nuclear weapons after Ukrainian arms manufacturer Denys Shtilerman discussed developing ballistic missiles capable of reaching Moscow, The Moscow Times reported.
Writing for Tsargrad, Malofeyev expressed concern about potential strikes on the headquarters of Russia’s Federal Security Service, the military’s General Staff and defense manufacturer Almaz-Antey.
443 Drones Downed: Russian Airfield, Chemical Plant and Tax Data Center Targeted in Overnight Attacks
He proposed a nuclear strike on western Ukraine after a 72-hour warning, followed by what he called “denazification,” including public executions of Ukrainian nationalist leaders and officials working for military recruitment centers.
Kyiv Post previously examined Malofeyev’s imperial ambitions, including his relationship with former Russian intelligence officer Igor Girkin and their role in promoting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Marriage to official wanted by the ICC
Malofeyev is married to Russia’s children’s rights commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova. He publicly confirmed their marriage in September 2024.
The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova in March 2023 over their alleged responsibility for the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied territory to Russia.
The warrants concern alleged war crimes and do not constitute convictions. Kyiv Post’s examination of the deportations details the evidence and accountability efforts surrounding Russia’s removal of Ukrainian children.

articles.title: Denmark to buy cheap U.S. cruise missile built in Germany
articles.body:
- Denmark will buy Covenant’s ground-launched Anthem cruise missiles, to be built in Leipzig, Germany, alongside Kongsberg Joint Strike Missiles for its F-35s.
- Germany’s defense ministry is also in talks with Covenant as the Bundeswehr evaluates low-cost cruise missiles for its own long-range strike needs.
Denmark will buy Anthem ground-launched cruise missiles from U.S. defense company Covenant Industries, giving the Danish military its first land-based option for striking targets deep inside enemy territory, the Danish Ministry of Defense announced on Oct. 22, 2026.
The ministry said the purchase is meant to strengthen Denmark’s national and collective deterrence, describing the new missiles as long-range precision weapons that NATO has asked allies to provide. They use advanced navigation to hit targets accurately over long distances and can both deter an attack and strike back deep inside an enemy’s territory if necessary, and the acquisitions follow a recommendation from Denmark’s chief of defense.
“The acquisitions are a significant step in making Denmark better able to defend itself and carry our share of the burden in NATO, and at the same time we are sending a strong signal that we have the ability to strike back,” said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus, in remarks translated from Danish.
Officials told reporters at the announcement that the contracts have already been signed, but withheld quantities, prices and delivery dates for security reasons. They said one reason for choosing the weapon was that it can be delivered relatively quickly and at a competitive price, and the Anthem missiles for Denmark will be built in Leipzig, Germany, where Covenant is setting up its European production line.
Anthem is a jet-powered cruise missile designed from the start for low cost and mass production. Covenant says it can carry a 200 kg (440-pound) warhead for precision strikes deep in enemy territory, and the missile reportedly has a range of more than 1,000 km (620 miles), with some media reports putting it as high as 1,500 km (930 miles). The company plans to sell it for a six-figure sum, under $1 million per missile, compared with the several million dollars typically charged for comparable cruise missiles.
Anthem first flew in August 2025, and Covenant says it has since been used in more than 200 tests, including several flight tests with U.S. forces in the United States and abroad, although the missile has not yet been used in combat. Choosing it marks a departure for Denmark, which has traditionally bought proven, production-ready systems for its armed forces.
Covenant opened a 10,000-square-meter (108,000-square-foot) plant in Leipzig earlier this month to build missiles for European NATO allies. Production is set to begin in 2027, with the company planning 1,000 missiles in the first year and 5,000 in 2028, and Covenant aims to source more than 95% of the components for its European version from inside Europe, with the Leipzig facility handling assembly and warheads integrated later at customer locations.
Germany is also studying the missile, and the German defense ministry has said it is in talks with Covenant about closing its own long-range strike gap, although no German order has been publicly confirmed. Lt. Gen. Christian Freuding, the head of the German Army, has confirmed that the Bundeswehr wants to buy new low-cost cruise missiles for mass use and is evaluating two systems already on the market, though he did not name them. Anthem has been reported as one of the candidates, alongside the Flamingo cruise missile from Ukrainian company Fire Point, and Covenant has brought in Andreas Marlow, a retired lieutenant general and former deputy commander of the German Army, as an adviser.
Denmark is pairing Anthem with a second, air-launched weapon, the Joint Strike Missile, built by Norway’s Kongsberg with Raytheon. The stealthy JSM fits inside the internal weapons bays of Denmark’s F-35 fighters, weighs 416 kg (917 pounds) with a 120 kg (265-pound) warhead and has a range of more than 350 km (217 miles). It is derived from Kongsberg’s Naval Strike Missile, which Denmark already operates on its frigates and for coastal defense.
Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin responded quickly to the announcement, saying Danish policy is built on confrontation and preparation for a possible conflict with Russia, and calling it a dangerous illusion to think precision strike weapons could pose a military threat to a nuclear power.
Denmark’s military planning has traditionally focused on defending its own territory, and the new missiles give it a way to strike targets in an adversary’s rear areas for the first time. With Covenant’s Leipzig line due to start production in 2027, the first Anthem missiles for Denmark are expected to come from that plant.

articles.title: Air Defenses at Russian Drone Factory Linked to Forced Labor Rival Putin’s Residence
articles.body:
Russia’s main Shahed drone factory has become one of the country’s most heavily defended sites, alongside President Vladimir Putin’s Valdai residence, according to satellite imagery published on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
The expanding defenses surround the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, where a separate US research report describes forced labor involving North Korean workers and the exploitation of foreign women recruited largely from Africa.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Radio Svoboda identified 33 air-defense positions around the complex, including new concrete towers and raised platforms intended for Pantsir or Tor air-defense systems.
The site also has towers for heavy anti-aircraft machine guns and structures supporting anti-drone barriers over production buildings.
The concentration of defenses puts Alabuga alongside Putin’s Valdai residence, where Radio Svoboda identified 31 towers and two S-300 or S-400 missile positions. The outlet reported more than 100 new air-defense positions across Moscow and the surrounding region since the full-scale invasion. Its findings do not establish a definitive national ranking of the best-protected sites.
Towers, cables and reinforced buildings
An investigation by the Institute for Science and International Security, updated on Sept. 25, used high-resolution Vantor and Airbus imagery to document two defensive perimeters around Alabuga’s production facilities.
Shorter towers surround the main production buildings. A taller outer ring encloses a wider area, including the neighboring Alabuga-Volokno plant, which supplies carbon fiber used in drone manufacturing.
Ukraine Ends Blanket Deferments, Ties Full Exemptions to Military Service
Cables strung between the towers are intended to intercept incoming drones or cruise missiles before they reach the buildings, or force them to fly higher and become more exposed to air defenses, the institute said.
Satellite images also show new production buildings being hardened with layers of earth and reinforced concrete.
Kyiv Post previously reported on Alabuga’s expansion, including new industrial buildings and dormitories for foreign workers.
North Korean workers lose most of their wages
A report published on Oct. 14 by the Center for Strategic and International Studies and the George W. Bush Institute describes Alabuga as a site of human trafficking and serious labor abuses.
The report cites Ukrainian intelligence estimates of up to 12,000 North Korean workers assigned to the complex. Its underlying source, however, is a November 2025 intelligence announcement describing plans to bring in that number, previously covered by Kyiv Post.
The figure therefore should not be treated as an independently verified count of workers currently at the factory.
According to the report, North Korean laborers earn approximately $2.50 an hour, while their government withholds 70–90% of their wages. At that rate, a 12-hour shift would generate $30 before deductions, leaving the worker between $3 and $9.
The authors describe the arrangement as state-sponsored trafficking, with minders restricting workers’ movements and Pyongyang collecting most of their earnings.
The report also notes that the overseas labor arrangement violates UN sanctions requiring countries to repatriate North Korean workers by December 2019.
Foreign recruits promised different jobs
Alabuga also recruits Russian students as young as 15 under a “work experience” program, according to the CSIS–Bush Institute report. They reportedly face long shifts, production quotas and threats of fines if they tell their families what they build.
Foreign women recruited through the Alabuga Start program are promised hospitality jobs, educational opportunities and salaries starting above $500 a month, the report said. Some instead find themselves assigned to weapons production.
Their pay is reduced by deductions for flights, accommodation, medical care and mandatory Russian-language classes. The report also describes passport confiscation, restrictions on movement and threats against workers who discuss their jobs.
Kyiv Post previously reported on African and Asian women misled into assembling drones, drawing on interviews with recruits who said their actual work differed from what they had been promised.
These accounts distinguish between agreeing to travel to Russia for employment and consenting to the work and conditions encountered after arrival.
Expanding production despite Ukrainian strikes
Located more than 1,000 kilometers from Ukraine, Alabuga is a principal Russian production center for Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones and their Russian Geran variants.
The CSIS–Bush Institute report describes a complex capable of producing more than 5,500 drones a month, with extensive construction supporting its growing workforce and output.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the site. An April 2024 strike injured 13 students employed at the complex, according to reports at the time.
Ukraine’s General Staff also confirmed a strike on the facility in June 2025. The publicly available reporting does not establish the extent of any lasting reduction in production.
The drones manufactured at Alabuga form part of Russia’s long-range bombardment of Ukraine. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission recorded 165 civilians killed and 1,119 injured by long-range missiles and drones in September 2026. Those figures cover multiple weapon types and cannot be attributed solely to Alabuga-made drones.
Ukraine has sought US Tomahawk cruise missiles to strengthen its ability to strike military-industrial targets deep inside Russia. President Volodymyr Zelensky pressed the request during his October 2025 visit to Washington, but the meeting ended without a commitment to supply them.
Putin had warned that providing Tomahawks would damage US-Russian relations, while Trump publicly raised concerns about escalation and American stockpiles.

articles.title: Uninvited guest: How a GRU spy connected to state hackers broke into the African Union’s diplomatic residence in Ethiopia
articles.body:
After the death-by-plane crash of Wagner Group founder Yevgeny Prigozhin in August 2023, the Kremlin’s influence operations in Africa have undergone a transformation. In addition to the Africa Corps — a state-run armed formation made up mostly of former Wagner fighters — Russia’s military intelligence agency (GRU) is also active on the ground. However, fresh revelations about a GRU break-in at an African Union facility in Addis Ababa threaten to tarnish relations between the Kremlin and the continent. The news couldn’t come at a worse time for Moscow, which is set to host the third ever Russia-Africa Summit on October 28-29.
On April 28, 2025, Mahamoud Ali Youssouf, the Chairman of the African Union Commission, arrived at a house in the upscale neighborhood of Bole Atlas in Addis Ababa, where the union’s secretariat is headquartered. The property is the official residence of Selma Haddadi, the Deputy Chairperson of the Commission, which is the executive arm of the supranational body representing all 55 African countries. But on that afternoon, it was in use by Youssouf and his family, who were then still recent transplants to the Ethiopian capital after arriving days earlier from Djibouti, Youssouf’s native country, where up until the previous month he’d served as its foreign minister.
At 3:32 p.m., a vehicle with diplomatic license plates pulled into the parking area outside the main compound of Africa House. Out of it stepped a white man of medium build with short hair, dressed in a button-down shirt and tie. He waited until a car transporting Youssouf’s university-aged daughter entered the premises via an opened security gate and then snuck in on foot before the gate closed behind him. The intruder entered the residence and proceeded directly to the bedroom where Youssouf was staying, remaining inside the building for 4 minutes and 24 seconds. At some point, the unknown intruder ran into the daughter (The Insider is withholding her name) inside the house. A stationed private security detail met the man as he exited the residence at 3:37. They tried to question him, but the detail worried he might have been a VIP who’d gotten lost or entered without the proper checks. Amid the confusion, the intruder drove off at 3:38.
The exterior moments of this brief and seemingly uneventful trespass were captured on CCTV images, which The Insider has exclusively obtained. Facial recognition software confirms that the break-in artist was Major Aleksandr Dubikov, the assistant to Nikita Zayats, Russia’s military attaché in Ethiopia.
The footage of the break-in is available in our video below.
Zayats was reportedly expelled from Portugal in 2022 over alleged links to the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency. As it happens, Dubikov, a 36-year-old Moscow resident, is also a GRU officer, meaning his illicit entry into a diplomatic residence in Addis Ababa was almost certainly an intelligence operation.
The Insider is publicly revealing his identity as the break-in artist for the first time. It is unclear if the African Union or the Ethiopian government knew of Dubikov's role in this incident, or his work for the GRU.
Records show that he was registered to a well-known dormitory of the GRU Academy at 52 Narodnogo Opolcheniya Street in Moscow. On his VK profile, last updated in May 2008, Dubikov says that he is a student of the Peter the Great Military Academy of the Strategic Missile Forces, a premier defense institution now based in Balashikha, Moscow region, where he studied computer science and information technologies in control systems. “Like everyone else,” he writes, “I study — but in my own way, combining usefulness with pleasure… Just a cadet.”
He described himself as “[v]ery kind and cuddly. I’m a well-rounded person interested in many things,” and was a fan of Rihanna, Chris Brown, the Mafia and Max Payne video games.
An Insider analysis of Dubikov’s phone data found several numbers belonging to GRU officers. His second-most frequently called number belongs to 37-year-old Vladislav Popov, a known GRU hacker linked to “Sandworm,” or GRU’s Unit 74455, responsible for launching a series of destructive and costly cyberattacks — including one in 2017 shutting down operations by Danish shipping company Maersk and U.S. pharmaceutical giant Merck, and mission-critical hospital computers in Pennsylvania. NotPetya, malware developed and deployed by “Sandworm” that initially infected Ukrainian computer systems, caused more than an estimated $10 billion in damages globally.
Following the 2025 incident in Addis Ababa, a source familiar with the matter told The Insider on the condition of anonymity that the African Union’s Security Directorate had strengthened security measures around Africa House. However, the breach raises concerns that Dubikov may have tried to steal files, data, or electronic devices belonging to Youssouf, or to install surveillance equipment to gather information about the chairman. Dubikov’s closeness to Popov and Sandworm only adds to that suspicion.
The breach raises concerns that Dubikov may have tried to steal files, data, or electronic devices belonging to Youssouf
According to flight records, Dubikov is still in the country—which means that either the Ethiopian authorities failed to identify him prior to this report, or they simply chose to ignore the scandal. The latter cannot be ruled out; judging by the frequent travel of GRU operatives — as analyzed by The Insider — Ethiopia has become a key hub for Russian intelligence activity in recent years.
“Ethiopia has long been an important operating base for Russian intelligence in East Africa,” according to Philip Obaji, a Nigerian Russia expert and investigative journalist who has extensively reported on Russia’s covert operations in Africa. “Senior GRU officials Anton Papshev and Yury Mikheyev, who play key roles in coordinating Russian intelligence activities across the continent, were based there for years.”
A spokesperson for Youssouf did not respond to a request for comment.
The disclosure of a Russian spy’s break-in of a diplomatic compound in East Africa comes at an awkward moment. On October 28-29, the third Russia-Africa summit is set to take place in Moscow, with Yuri Ushakov, Vladimir Putin’s adviser, heading its organizing committee. The second summit, held in 2023, aimed to “bolster comprehensive ties between the Russian Federation and African states, while establishing fresh frameworks for bilateral and multilateral collaboration,” according to its official website.
The co-chairs for the upcoming summit will be Vladimir Putin and Évariste Ndayishimiye, the Burundi president who this year holds the African Union’s rotating chairmanship.
“While Russia continues to establish relations with many African Union member states, the GRU break-in reveals its twofold game,” a Western security official told The Insider. “While it officially engages in cooperation with African Union members, it does not hesitate to use manipulation and lies to achieve its aims.”
Russia’s role in Africa is both expansive and fraught. Much of its military presence was established by the Wagner Group, formerly headed by catering magnate-cum-mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin, who died in a plane bombing in August 2023, two months after attempting an abortive mutiny against the Russian government. From 2017 until its demise, Wagner acted as a plausibly deniable arm of the Kremlin in multiple African theatres — Mali, Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. The mercenaries have acted as bodyguards and protection squads to help coup-proof regimes (they were the praetorian guard for CAR President Faustin-Archange Touadéra for over half a decade) and as combat forces to wage war against jihadist and rebel groups.
From 2017 until its demise, Wagner acted as a plausibly deniable arm of the Kremlin in multiple African theatres — Mali, Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic
Wagner’s political technologists have also overseen information operations similar to the troll farm campaigns Prigozhin’s employees ran out of St. Petersburg to interfere in Western elections. Using the front organization AFRIC, they imported European neo-Nazis and white supremacists to act as ”election monitors” in several African countries, though their real purpose was to act as agents of influence to promote certain candidates and drum up anti-Western sentiment. (That white racists were at times pushing a pan-Africanist agenda at the expense of the bitter legacies of British and French colonialism was an irony Prigozhin may have relished privately.) Quite often, in fact, Wagner armed and funded opposing sides or a multiplicity of political actors vying for control of the same government — especially in Libya, where it worked on behalf of Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, the son of slain dictator Col. Muammar Gaddafi, and also of Gen. Khalifa Haftar, a Libyan warlord once beholden to the CIA.
“Russia’s broader approach in Africa is highly opportunistic,” Obaji told The Insider. “It deals with sitting governments while quietly maintaining relationships with opposition figures working against them. Rather than showing consistent loyalty to any one side, Moscow runs a dual-track strategy designed to protect and advance its own interests no matter which way the political winds blow.”
Wagner has enriched itself by extracting natural resources where it operated, running gold and diamond mines. In late 2021, Wagner usurped the French military in Mali at the invitation of the country’s ruling junta to defend the Bamako regime against Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, the al-Qaeda affiliate, and Tuareg rebels. Both groups routed Wagner in Tinzaouatène, Mali, in 2024, precipitating the group’s withdrawal in 2025.
The UN Panel of Experts for Mali stated in an August 2023 report that Wagner, which was credibly accused of gross human rights abuses such as torture, beheadings, and summary executions, has hardly been a successful counterterrorist force in the country, allowing the ISIS franchise in Mali to nearly double its territorial control in under a year. Wagner has, however, tried to pass off its atrocities as the work of the French military, including the on-camera burial of bodies in a mass grave near a Malian military base Wagner was using in April 2022.
Wagner has hardly been a successful counterterrorist force in Mali, allowing the ISIS franchise to nearly double its territorial control in under a year
Since Prigozhin’s death, Wagner’s operations have largely been incorporated into Africa Corps, a Russian state-run expeditionary force headed by Gen. Andrey Averyanov, now the deputy director of the GRU but formerly the founding commander of Unit 29155, the service’s black ops team responsible for poisoning the Skripals in Salisbury, staging a failed coup in Montenegro, and blowing up a series of weapons and ammunition storage facilities across NATO territory, where materiel destined for Georgia, Ukraine and Syrian rebels were being stockpiled. Averyanov, in fact, took Prigozhin’s place at a roundtable discussion on the last day of the second Russia-Africa summit in St. Petersburg in July 2023. Seventy to eighty percent of Africa Corps’ forces are ex-Wagner mercenaries, according to an investigation by Reuters.
Moscow’s hard power projection in Africa, meanwhile, competes with soft power initiatives that are often masquerades for intelligence operations. Rossotrudnichestvo, the Foreign Ministry’s cultural arm, which doubles as a conspicuous clearinghouse for the SVR, has plans to open new “Russian Houses,” or educational and cultural centers, in Egypt , Zambia, Tanzania, South Africa, and Ethiopia. In 2025, Russia granted 5,000 state-funded places at Russian universities to African students, mainly from Sudan, Guinea, Ghana, and Chad.

articles.title: France to field twelve SAMP/T NG air defence units
articles.body:
France has ordered four additional SAMP/T NG firing units, taking its total order for the ground-based air and missile defence system to twelve, according to eurosam.
The Organisation for Joint Armament Cooperation, known as OCCAR, placed the contract on behalf of France with eurosam, the Franco-Italian grouping formed by MBDA France, MBDA Italy and Thales. The units will be delivered to the French Air and Space Force in a multi-layer configuration combining Aster and MICA VL missiles.
The company said: “This order is an additional step towards the renewal of the European Long-Range Air and Missile Defence ground capabilities, following the SAMP/T NG development launched in 2021.”
It added: “OCCAR-EA, eurosam and its members, MBDA and Thales will continue to lead the way in state of the art and sovereign air and Missile defence systems for the benefit of European defence. These advanced air defence systems are crucial in the current global context to respond to increasingly challenging threats.”
A SAMP/T NG firing unit holds up to forty-eight Aster missiles ready to fire, carried across up to six launcher modules of eight rounds each, alongside a multi-function radar and identification module able to detect and identify targets beyond 350km, and an engagement module. The whole system is mobile and eurosam says it can be operational in under thirty minutes, offering 360-degree coverage and engaging targets beyond 150km.
The system is designed around the Aster 30 B1 and the newer Aster B1NT. The B1NT uses a Ka-band seeker and new interception algorithms to give what the company describes as a hit-to-kill capability against short and medium range ballistic missiles, low manoeuvring targets and hypersonic missiles.
Britain has a stake in the wider programme, since the United Kingdom is a participant in the FSAF-PAAMS arrangement that OCCAR manages, and the fourteenth amendment to that contract, signed in Paris in January 2024, covered supplementary procurement of equipment allowing Britain to carry out mid-life upgrades to its own Aster missiles. Aster is the weapon carried by the Royal Navy’s Type 45 destroyers as part of the Sea Viper system, which HMS Diamond used against Houthi missiles and drones in the Red Sea.
France and Italy have supplied SAMP/T systems to Ukraine, where the type has engaged Russian ballistic missiles.
The order lands while Britain has no ground-based long-range air defence system assigned to the defence of the United Kingdom. Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, confirmed this week that a further £790 million will be invested in homeland integrated air and missile defence, covering enhanced command and control, improved sensing and radar systems, counter-drone capabilities and more effective layered defences.
The Defence Committee reported yesterday that anti-strike capabilities for shooting down ballistic, hypersonic and cruise missiles and drones are among the capabilities European NATO members lack in sufficient numbers, and that replacing American military capabilities with European weapons has been costed by the Kiel Institute at an extra €50 billion each year over the next decade.
Sky Sabre gives the British Army a medium range ground-based system, currently deployed in Poland and the Falkland Islands. This publication has reported on continuing work on the potential of British destroyers in the ballistic missile defence role and on when those destroyers will receive their missile upgrades.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Ukraine, Russia agree to local ceasefire for Russian-occupied Oleshky, mediated by Melania Trump
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Ukraine, Russia agree to local ceasefire for Russian-occupied Oleshky, mediated by Melania Trump
Key developments on Oct. 23:
- Ukraine, Russia agree on local ceasefire for Russian-occupied Oleshky, mediated by Melania Trump
- Civilian cargo ship sinks off coast of Romania after Russian drone strike, authorities say
- Ukraine to end automatic 100% mobilization exemptions for critical industries, Prime Minister says
- Ukrainian drone attack triggers shut down of Moscow airports, missile reportedly strikes Oryol semiconductor plant
- 270 Ukrainian POWs return home in latest swap with Russia
U.S. First Lady Melania Trump has mediated a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in and around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and delivery of humanitarian aid, Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on Oct. 23.
The move comes amid increased attention to the worsening humanitarian crisis in the city, which over the past weeks has gained international attention, including from Pope Leo XIV.
According to the press release from the White House press service, the First Lady "initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement's objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary."
The ceasefire is scheduled to begin on Oct. 29, the press release added.
Lubinets, confirmed the agreement in a video statement on Telegram later on Oct. 23.
"I personally thank Melania Trump and her team for their efforts, leadership, and coordination between the two negotiating groups of Ukraine and the Russian Federation in reaching agreements," Lubinets said.
Under the agreement, a ceasefire will be put in place, humanitarian cargo will be delivered to Oleshky, and civilians will be allowed to leave the city freely, according to Lubinets.
"The operation will take place gradually. It is extremely difficult to implement," he said. He will keep the Ukrainian public informed and show the results of the operation, he said. He also asked the public to be careful about spreading information on the mission.
Lubinets added that he had led the negotiations on the Ukrainian side and that Russia's human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, had led them on the Russian side.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also welcomed Melania Trump's role, saying she had "made a significant contribution to agreeing on the humanitarian operation" in Oleshky, Russian pro-Kremlin media outlet Ura.ru reported. Peskov said the sides are working to agree on a ceasefire in the area so that residents can be evacuated.
State-aligned Russian media RBK reported Russia's General Staff had announced a ceasefire from 04:00 a.m. local time on Oct. 27, citing Valeriy Gerasimov, Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces.
Gerasimov added that to ensure the safety of people and the delivery of vital supplies, engineering reconnaissance will be conducted.
Oleshky, located just across the Dnipro River from Kherson, has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces in the area, who prevent humanitarian aid from entering. Civilians attempting to flee via the only roads in and out of the city are frequently targeted by drones.
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," Melania Trump was quoted as saying in the press release.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."
According to the document, an "impartial American media organization" will visit the area to document the work of both sides in the area.

Civilian cargo ship sinks off coast of Romania after Russian drone strike, authorities say
A civilian cargo ship sank after being struck by a Russian drone near Romania's Black Sea coast on Oct. 23, Romanian authorities reported.
The attack is the latest in a series of brazen Russian strikes on civilian shipping in the Black Sea, part of a broader escalation in Russia's economic warfare against Ukraine this year.
The ship, Khoryv, was sailing from Turkey under the flag of the Comoros and was crewed by Ukrainian and Azerbaijani nationals.
According to Romanian President Nicusor Dan, one person was confirmed dead and three others were missing from the 14-member crew.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry later confirmed that a Ukrainian crew member on board the Khoryv was killed. Four other Ukrainian nationals, including the ship's captain, were hospitalized, while two Ukrainian crew members did not require medical assistance.
The ministry said the vessel had sunk near the Romanian city of Constanta with 14 crew members on board. According to preliminary information, a drone strike may have caused the sinking.
Ukraine's Embassy in Romania is working to establish the circumstances of the incident, as well as the whereabouts and condition of the rescued Ukrainian nationals, while remaining in contact with Romanian authorities, the ministry said.
"This attack is a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine," Dan wrote on social media.
"It is time for Russia to take the peace initiatives proposed by the United States and Europe seriously, accept the ceasefire proposals and end the war."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attack, describing it as another Russian escalation in the Black Sea.
"These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law," von der Leyen wrote on X.
Romania's Interior Ministry later confirmed that nine crew members had been rescued, publishing a video showing the keel of the overturned ship barely protruding above the water's surface.
In response to a series of attacks on civilian shipping, NATO plans to increase its military presence in the Black Sea by deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones.
The announcement came after NATO's main decision-making body, the North Atlantic Council, met at the alliance's headquarters in Brussels on Oct. 20 to discuss security in the Black Sea.

Ukraine to end automatic 100% mobilization exemptions for critical industries, Prime Minister says
Ukraine's government finalized changes to its military exemption system that will end automatic 100% exemptions for employees in critical industries, including defense manufacturing and energy, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced on Oct. 23.
Koretskyi said the changes seek to make the exemption system fairer and prevent abuses.
"The number of workers exempted from mobilization is growing by tens of thousands every month. Meanwhile, those who have been defending the country for five years must have the opportunity to return home from military service. That is why we are making difficult but necessary decisions," Koretskyi said.
Companies working in critical sectors, including defense manufacturing, energy, telecommunications, logistics, and utilities, will retain their critical status. However, the government will review the criteria used to determine which businesses qualify as critical.
Companies will still be able to request higher exemption quotas if needed to maintain operations, while the government is also developing a mechanism that would allow companies to exempt all their employees if they regularly arrange for some of their workers to voluntarily join the military, Koretskyi said.
Those joining the military would know where they would serve and for how long, while keeping their jobs and salaries, Koretskyi said.
"This will give those on the front line confidence that rotations are possible and that others will take their place. Those joining the military will also know that they are serving for a clearly defined period," he said.
Under the new rules, defense industry companies will be able to exempt up to 95% of their eligible employees from mobilization, the Defense Ministry said.
The ministry stressed that exemptions should remain available to employees directly involved in producing weapons and other equipment for Ukraine's military.
"Companies must be able to plan their operations, retain specialists, and increase production," Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said.
The Defense and Economy ministries will work out the conditions for the mechanism with businesses, with the government aiming to approve it by Dec. 1., Korestkyi said.

Ukrainian drone attack triggers shut down of Moscow airports, missile reportedly strikes Oryol semiconductor plant
Civilian flights at all four of Moscow's main airports were suspended on the afternoon of Oct. 23 amid a Ukrainian drone raid on the Russian capital, local authorities reported.
Restrictions on arriving and departing flights at Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports were announced by Russian civil aviation authority Rosaviatsiya at 2:05 p.m. local time.
At Sheremetyevo, Moscow's largest airport, an air alert was sounded, and waiting passengers were advised to take shelter.
Photos later emerged on social media that allegedly showed debris from a downed drone on the tarmac at Sheremetyevo.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the photos.
Open-source flight tracker FlightRadar24 reported 85 cancelled flights and a further 229 delayed at Sheremetyevo over the day.
According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, 17 drones were shot down while heading toward the city on the afternoon of Oct. 23.
Ukraine had not commented on the reported attack as of the time of publication.
The all-clear was later sounded at Sheremetyevo Airport, Russian state news agency TASS reported at 5 p.m. local time.
An evacuation was also reported at the IQ-quarter skyscraper in the Moscow City business district, which houses offices of several Russian government ministries, including the Digital Development Ministry, Economic Development Ministry, and Industry and Trade Ministry.
Russian state news agency TASS later reported, citing emergency services, that the alarm had been false.
Meanwhile, explosions were reported in the Russian city of Oryol, approximately 350 kilometers (217 miles) southwest of Moscow, where a local industrial facility was reportedly targeted in a missile strike.
Oryol Oblast Governor Andrey Klychkov confirmed that an enterprise had been targeted, while independent Russian media outlet ASTRA, citing its open-source intelligence analysis, identified the facility as the Proton plant.
The plant manufactures semiconductor devices, LEDs, and electronic components for industrial and specialized equipment that could be used in Russian weapons systems.
Local residents reported hearing at least four explosions, ASTRA said.
As Ukrainian long-range drones have reached deeper into Russian territory, temporary airport closures across Russia have become increasingly common during Moscow's full-scale war against Ukraine.

270 Ukrainian POWs return home in latest swap with Russia
Ukraine and Russia exchanged prisoners of war on Oct. 23, with 270 Ukrainian service members returning home, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced.
The exchange, the first in two months, also saw 270 Russian prisoners of war returned to Russia from Ukrainian captivity.
According to Zelensky, most of the Ukrainians returning home had been captured during the Siege of Mariupol in spring 2022. They included service members from the Ground Forces, Navy, and Air Assault Forces, as well as border guards and fighters from the Azov regiment, which led the city's defense.
Five of the released POWs survived the Olenivka prison massacre in July 2022, when a thermobaric munition was detonated inside a prison barracks housing Ukrainian prisoners of war.
According to Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, a "significant portion" of the released prisoners had been found guilty on sham criminal charges while in Russian captivity.
Seven Ukrainian civilians were also brought back from Russia with the help of Ukrainian authorities on Oct. 23, Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said in a Facebook post. Lubinets added that another seven civilians had traveled to Russia as part of family reunification efforts supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
Zelensky, as well as the Coordination Headquarters later said that nine civilians had been released.
Lubinets called the prisoner exchange "historic," saying it brought home the largest number of convicted Ukrainian service members since 2022: 86 convicted soldiers and one person who had been facing criminal prosecution.
Ukraine, international human rights organizations, and the U.N. have described such trials in Russia as war crimes. The Third Geneva Convention grants POWs protected status under international humanitarian law and prohibits prosecuting them solely for their participation in hostilities, subject to the rules governing lawful combatant conduct.
Lubinets added that the exchange marked the return of Azov Regiment service members for the first time "in a long while."
Two of those released had been held in Russian captivity since 2018 and 2020, spending eight and six years in captivity, respectively, Lubinets said.
The youngest released POW was 24, while the oldest was 63, he added.
While intermittent U.S.-mediated "peace talks" between Russia and Ukraine have failed to secure even a partial ceasefire, prisoner exchanges remain one of the few channels of regular cooperation between Moscow and Kyiv.
The latest swap was the 11th reported prisoner exchange of 2026. The previous two exchanges took place in August.

articles.title: Turkey says renewed attack on Iran would expand conflict, diplomacy only way
articles.body:
Turkey says renewed attack on Iran would expand conflict, diplomacy only way
ISTANBUL, Oct 23 - Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan cautioned on Friday against any renewed attack on Iran, saying such a move would exacerbate tensions and further expand the conflict there, adding that diplomacy and dialogue were the only way to end the war.
Fidan met his counterparts from Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Germany, France, Britain and Italy in Istanbul to discuss developments in the Iran war, attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi militants, and Russia's war in Ukraine.
It was the first collective meeting between the countries, comprising the Regional Four (R4) and EU 3 (E3), alongside Italy.
"We are all in agreement that a new attack on Iran would expand the war in the region," Fidan told a press conference after the meeting. "A military intervention on Iran is not in any way a solution. Nobody approves this at the moment," he added.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said after Friday's meetings that renewed escalation between Iran and the United States would only have losers and raise oil prices.
The comments followed a New York Times report on Wednesday that the US and Israeli militaries had drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm congressional election next month. Citing US officials, it said likely targets would include Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and its missile and drone arsenal.
US President Donald Trump said earlier this month that the US would not launch an attack on Iran before the midterms, as Washington and Tehran were having "productive" talks about ending their six-month-old war. On Friday, he said the US could end the war quickly but questioned whether Washington should seek a swift conclusion or allow the conflict to gradually wind down.
NATO member Turkey has been in close contact with Washington, Tehran and regional mediators to seek an end to the war. It has repeatedly called for attacks to stop and warned against the regional expansion of the conflict.
Fidan also said the countries meeting on Friday had discussed possible parameters to ensure the war in Iran does not expand further, but did not elaborate.
Following Friday's meetings, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany, France, and Britain were ready to negotiate with Iran to rule out its acquisition of nuclear weapons, while calling for support for Saudi Arabia and Yemen. REUTERS

articles.title: Saudi missile plant expansion may produce more powerful missiles, study says
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia expanding missile plant to build bigger weapons, satellite image researchers believe
- Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its al-Duwadimi missile plant, with satellite images showing new casting pits and storage buildings for larger solid-fuel missiles.
- US researchers said the work could help Riyadh build longer-range or heavier weapons, boost defence against Iran, and widen its role in the Yemen conflict.
- The move may deepen fears of missile proliferation and increase US political opposition to a Saudi nuclear deal, while the plant could be ready by year-end.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its ballistic missile factory to build larger solid-fuel missiles that could fly farther or carry heavier payloads, according to two US researchers who analysed more than a year of commercial satellite images.
More capable missiles could help Saudi Arabia to deter attacks by Iran and make its military more self-reliant, while possibly strengthening its position in a deadly conflict with Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthi fighters.
But they risk fuelling a regional missile race and could deepen opposition in the US Congress to a US-Saudi civilian nuclear agreement that has already raised concerns about proliferation.
Satellite company Planet Labs, based in the US, took images of the al-Duwadimi complex about 200km west of Riyadh between April 2025 and September 2026.
The two researchers, Sam Lair and Michael Duitsman of the Foreign Policy Research Institute, assessed that those images show a new building that houses casting pits - wells in which a mixture of fuel ingredients is poured into missile motor casings and allowed to harden.
The Saudi embassy and Information Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
The building, flanked by what appear to be walls to protect nearby structures from accidental explosions, is at least twice as large as the one believed to house the plant’s existing casting pits, Lair and Duitsman said in their assessment.
The Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI) is a non-partisan research organisation in Philadelphia.
A second new building could be used to store fuel ingredients or finished missile components, they said.
The imagery “suggests that Saudi Arabia is expanding the infrastructure at the missile production complex, likely to produce larger missiles which could deliver larger payloads or reach longer ranges,” they wrote.
Militaries favour solid-fuel missiles because they can be stored for long periods and launched more quickly than liquid-fuel systems.
Lair and Duitsman and experts from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) and the CNA research and analysis organisation told Reuters that the makeup of Saudi Arabia’s missile force suggests that the al-Duwadimi complex relies on Chinese technology.
Lair and Duitsman said that its characteristics also are similar to Chinese missile plants.
Saudi Arabia secretly acquired about 40 liquid-fuel DF-3 ballistic missiles from China in 1987, according to a 1991 declassified CIA estimate. It displayed two of them for the first time in an April 2014 military parade, according to a Youtube video and photographs of the event.
The FPRI team also recently identified from social media videos and photos what they assessed was the wreckage in Yemen of a Saudi-fired Chinese-designed DF-15 missile.
Lair said the kingdom may now be producing the solid-fuel DF-15, and that the expansion of a1-Dumadimi is likely for the production of the longer-range DF-21 or a similar missile.
Riyadh is believed to have turned to Beijing because Washington has long restricted exports of longer-range missile systems.
The Chinese embassy and defence ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
The CIA declined to comment.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Missiles would alter balance of power
Sascha Bruchmann, a research fellow at IISS, said longer-range missiles would allow Saudi Arabia to strike Iran without risking its US-supplied F-15 jet fighters against Iranian air defences.
“You’d want a system to threaten whatever is holy to Tehran... if you don’t have the political will to send an F-15 with JDAMs over Tehran,” said Bruchmann, referring to US-made satellite-guided bombs.
“Iran has a lead because its missiles and drones can strike Saudi wherever it wants. The Saudis could close that capability gap a bit.”
Bruchmann, who reviewed the FPRI analysis at Reuters request, concurred that the expansion of al-Duwadimi could be for producing more powerful solid-fuel missiles.
Janes, the defence intelligence company, also reviewed it and said the buildings “may suggest an effort to expand production capability or support the development of longer-range missiles.”
Saudi Arabia’s apparent pursuit of more powerful missiles comes as other Gulf powers are also seeking to expand their offensive and defensive arsenals, said Decker Eveleth, a CNA analyst who has been tracking the al-Duwadimi construction with commercial satellite imagery and concurred with the FPRI assessment.
“This is being replicated across the Middle East,” he said.
“You see exactly the same thing happening in the UAE. You see the exact same thing happening in Turkey. Everybody is doing this now.”
The expansion of al-Duwadimi could have political consequences in the US by stiffening bipartisan congressional opposition to a US-Saudi agreement under which the US would help Riyadh establish uranium enrichment for power generation.
Opponents say that the deal lacks sufficient safeguards to prevent Riyadh from secretly building a nuclear weapon. The kingdom has denied any such plan.
Work on the plant began in 2025
The FPRI assessment said the Planet Labs imagery showed that the expansion at al-Duwadimi began in April 2025 with ground-clearing and digging for the suspected storage building. Work on the suspected casting-pit building began later that month or in early May, it said.
A Dec 12, 2025, photo showed what researchers assessed were two deep pits inside the building that had no roof yet.
A Sept 18, 2026, photo shows the roof still partly missing and “heavy duty blast diverting walls” on either side to prevent accidental explosions from damaging adjacent structures.
The walls, the researchers said, are somewhat similar to those depicted in imagery of US and Iranian missile plants and “further evidence the building is for casting solid propellant motors.”
Finishing the roofs would not take long, the FPRI said, but installing casting equipment may take several months. The facility could be ready to start producing missiles as early as the end of the year. REUTERS

articles.title: Denmark to purchase long-range air and ground precision missiles
articles.body:
Denmark has announced that it will be purchasing its first long-range precision missiles as Russia continues to carry out hostile actions against Europe.
The missiles are air-launched Joint Strike Missiles (JSM) made by Norway’s Kongsberg for the Nordic country’s F-35 stealth fighter jets and the ground-launched Anthem missile made by Covenant.
“The purpose of the acquisitions is to strengthen national and collective deterrence. These are weapons that are in demand by NATO and that contribute to Denmark's security,” Denmark’s Defense Ministry said in a statement on Thursday, adding that “they can both deter attacks from outside and strike back deep inside enemy territory if necessary.”
The JSM is a fifth-generation air-to-surface missile that fits in the internal weapons bays of the F-35A, allowing the aircraft to retain its stealth profile. The high-subsonic missile has a range of 350 kilometers and autonomous target recognition capabilities. It is in use by 15 other countries, including the United States, Germany, Norway, Romania, and Poland.
Covenant, which has operations in the US, Germany, and Israel, emerged from stealth last month. Covenant’s flagship system, Anthem, is built to deliver heavy payloads at extended ranges while remaining affordable enough to produce in large quantities. The company has disclosed relatively little about Anthem’s specific performance characteristics, including its precise range, payload, and unit cost.
According to the company, most of Anthem’s components are commercial‑off‑the‑shelf (COTS) parts, supported by long‑term agreements for critical parts. Covenant says this approach allows the missile to be produced quickly and reliably, even during wartime, by drawing on supply chains across allied nations.
“Covenant Industries is proud to partner with Denmark as it moves with urgency to strengthen European defense and NATO’s collective security. As a global defense company with a growing European industrial footprint, Covenant is committed to delivering affordable, long-range precision strike capabilities at scale. This agreement, signed through our German company, represents an important step in our commitment to producing Anthem in Europe, for Europe, supported by a sovereign European supply chain,” Abby Denburg, its president and CGO told Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post.
Denmark’s Minister Defense Jeppe Bruus said that “the acquisitions are a significant step toward making Denmark better able to defend itself, strengthening NATO, and increasing our ability to strike back.”
Last year, Denmark said that it would be spending 58 billion Danish crowns ($9.20 billion) on European-made air defense systems, its largest arms purchase ever. A week later, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen made the announcement that it would be purchasing long-range precision missiles because the country “must be able to credibly deter attacks on Denmark and NATO, and it is not enough to just have strong air defenses.”
Reuters reported that the Russian embassy in Copenhagen said that Denmark's missile policy aims at confrontation with Moscow and warned of "inevitable disastrous consequences.”
"Copenhagen is enthralled by the dangerous illusions that purchasing offensive high-precision long-range weapons to pose a military threat to a nuclear power will help strengthen Denmark's security and defense," the embassy said.

articles.title: Regional powers, European heavyweights meet in Istanbul for 1st joint talks
articles.body:
The R4 meeting was attended by Pakistani Foreign Minister Muhammad Ishaq Dar (2nd L), Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty (L), and Saudi Arabian Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan (R). (AA Photo)
Istanbul hosted high-level diplomatic talks on Oct. 23, bringing together foreign ministers from regional and European powers to discuss the Iran conflict, maritime security, the Palestinian issue and the Russia-Ukraine war. 
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan chaired the inaugural joint meeting of the R4 and E3 diplomatic groups, bringing together Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia under the R4 framework, alongside Britain, France and Germany, which constitute the E3.
The Oct. 23 meeting marked the first joint gathering of the two mechanisms, reflecting efforts to expand cooperation between European powers and key regional actors amid mounting geopolitical tensions.
Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani was also expected to attend the talks, bringing the number of participating countries to eight.
Fidan held separate meetings in Istanbul with British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Pakistani Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar.
The discussions were scheduled to begin in the R4 format before being expanded to include top diplomats from the E3 group and Italy.
According to Turkish diplomatic sources, Fidan was expected to emphasize that regional security requires countries in the region to assume primary responsibility for addressing their own challenges.
Within this framework, he was expected to highlight Türkiye's commitment to strengthening cooperation mechanisms founded on regional ownership.
Fidan was also expected to stress that existing disputes must not exacerbate one another, conflicts must not spread to new fronts, and regional tensions must not escalate into wider instability.
The Turkish foreign minister was expected to identify Israel's policies toward the Palestinian territories, which he considers an obstacle to peace efforts, and its expanding military actions across the region as major drivers of instability in the Middle East.
Fidan was also expected to underline that tensions between the United States and Iran could be resolved only through diplomacy and dialogue, warning that military approaches fail to deliver lasting solutions and instead deepen regional vulnerabilities.
Ensuring freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on a lasting basis was another key priority on the agenda, given the waterways' significance for regional and global stability.
The discussions were also expected to cover Houthi attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. Fidan was expected to reaffirm Türkiye's support for Saudi Arabia's security and highlight the principle of collective security and solidarity underpinning the Mecca Defense Agreement.
Ahead of the talks, Miliband's office said the discussions would focus particularly on the Strait of Hormuz and the security situation in Saudi Arabia.
He was also set to warn that Iranian tactics were being replicated elsewhere in the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilizing the Middle East and placing additional pressure on strategic maritime routes, including Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal.
The meeting was also expected to address the security implications of the Russia-Ukraine war, particularly the risk of the conflict spreading into the Black Sea.
Fidan was expected to reiterate that Türkiye, as a Black Sea littoral state, would continue presenting proposals to the parties to prevent further escalation and contain the conflict's impact on regional security.
Attacks on commercial vessels, frequently involving drones, have increased in recent months as the conflict has extended its reach across the Black Sea, placing Turkish shipping at growing risk.
Türkiye submitted a proposal to Russia and Ukraine last month aimed at halting attacks on maritime targets. However, strikes have continued in recent weeks, particularly in waters near Romania and Bulgaria.
NATO announced on Oct. 20 that it was deploying additional aircraft, drones and radar systems to the Black Sea to improve regional surveillance and situational awareness through enhanced sensor coverage and greater information-sharing.
The R4 mechanism, established this year by Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, is intended to promote lasting regional stability and strengthen dialogue on shared challenges through an approach based on regional ownership.
The four countries have held six foreign ministers' meetings, beginning in Riyadh on March 18, with the most recent taking place in New York on Sept. 21 on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly's high-level week.
The E3, comprising Britain, France and Germany, emerged from diplomatic coordination on Iran's nuclear program launched in 2003. Initially focused on the nuclear issue, the grouping has gradually developed into a platform for joint diplomatic initiatives on a broader range of regional and international matters.

articles.title: Pentagon Bets Big on Drone-Killing APKWS Laser-Guided Rockets
articles.body:
The Pentagon has concluded a new agreement to buy laser-guidance kits that turn rockets into drone-killing weapons.
BAE Systems and the Defense Department announced a framework deal of up to seven years for 25,000 Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System guidance kits annually for the U.S. military.
Another 10,000 kits could be produced each year for international customers, who are increasingly interested in the system.
APKWS is a laser-guidance kit that converts 2.75-inch unguided rockets into precision munitions. It is currently fielded by the U.S. Air Force, Army, Marine Corps, and Navy, as well as U.S. allies.
APKWS has become the preferred method for U.S. warplanes to down drones fired by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in the Middle East over the past few years. But it is not just an air-to-air weapon. APKWS munitions can also be fitted to various platforms for air-to-surface, surface-to-surface, and surface-to-air use.
APKWS is an attractive capability for the Pentagon because of its low cost—roughly $35,000, according to officials. That gives the Air Force a way to shoot down drones without expending costly air-to-air missiles.
For compraison, Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles cost roughly $1 million each, and AIM-9s cost hundreds of thousands of dollars depending on the variant. The most capable model is the AIM-9X, which costs around $500,000. APKWS was first tested in an air-to-air role in 2019. The Air Force did not pursue the idea heavily until a few years later, before fielding it in combat in 2024.
“We were on the wrong side of the cost curve in our munitions employment,” former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin said in an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“The great thing about it is that there wasn’t a formal requirement set out for this. This was sort of organic. People started figuring it out without it being a big program of record,” Allvin added. “Good thing they did.”
Now, just a few years later, the Pentagon is betting big on APKWS’ future.
APKWS scored its first combat air-to-air kill in the fall of 2024 in the Middle East by F-16 from the 510th Fighter Squadron at Aviano Air Base, Italy, current and former officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
When the 480th Fighter Squadron from Spangdahlem Air Base, Germany, deployed to the Middle East soon after, they scored dozens more aerial kills—108 in total using all weapons during their deployment.
By the spring of 2025, the Air Force began flight testing APKWS on F-15E Strike Eagles, and fielded the capability in the Middle East within roughly a week. Around the same time, U.S. Air Forces in Europe also fielded APKWS for its air-to-air training. The system has also been on A-10s to shoot down drones.
The APKWS has its origins in the decades-old Hydra rocket system and was first used as precision air-to-ground weapon during the Global War on Terror, deploying in 2012.
It was adapted to serve in an air-to-air role when Air Forces Central, commanded by then-Lt. Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich from 2022-2024, began looking for an alternative to using costly air-to-air missiles against drones. CENTCOM and the Air Force supported the effort.
The framework agreement is intended as a signal of what the Pentagon plans to buy, subject to specific contracts and the congressional funding needs for those deals.
BAE says the new agreement will help expand production at its facilities in Hudson, N.H., and Austin, Texas.
“This agreement highlights the importance of sustained investment in critical munitions to strengthen readiness and equip forces for evolving operational needs,” BAE Systems president and CEO Tom Arseneault said in a statement.
“By securing multiyear demand, this agreement keeps production lines running at capacity, provides our forces with interceptor inventory, and flips the cost calculus in the taxpayer’s favor,” Michael Duffey, undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, added.
APKWS can also be used in a ground-to-air role, as the modifications needed to hit aerial targets are largery limited to software and the use of a proximity fuse. It can be fitted to anti-air systems such as Sierra Nevada Corporation’s BRAWLR, which is deployed overseas by the U.S. military, and L3Harris’ VAMPIRE, which is used by Ukraine and is being supplied to the U.S. It has been fitted to other nations’ fighter platforms and has been tested on the MQ-9 Reaper as well.
“This drone problem is not going away,” retired Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, who led Air Forces Central from April 2024-August 2026, said in a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “It’s accelerating in tactics, speed, advancements, and the numbers. That’s the direction that we’re going.”

articles.title: Russia may stage sabotage in Eastern Europe, but wants Kyiv blamed, Ukraine’s Intelligence warns
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) warned that Russia may stage sabotage in Central and Eastern Europe, including the Baltic states, and blame Ukraine for the attacks, in a Telegram post on 23 October.
The warning comes three days after The Wall Street Journal reported that US intelligence traces Europe’s sabotage wave to Putin’s personal order. If Russia stages new attacks and pins them on Ukraine, as HUR warns, European anger could turn on Kyiv rather than the Kremlin. This goes further than HUR’s statement on 2 October, which named potential Russian targets in Europe but did not mention a plan to blame Ukraine for attacks.
HUR says Moscow wants to discredit Ukraine’s army
Russia is stepping up its hybrid strategy to destabilize the European Union, according to HUR. The agency identified two aims: reducing foreign support for Ukraine by discrediting its Defense Forces, and intimidating European governments and societies.
The accusations would be spread through Russian propaganda channels and international platforms accessible to the Kremlin.
Potential targets include infrastructure and Russian Orthodox Church sites
HUR listed several potential targets for Russian provocations:
- critical infrastructure and areas bordering Russia;
- the Kaliningrad exclave;
- areas of EU countries with Russian-speaking populations;
- Kremlin-controlled sites, including properties belonging to the Russian Orthodox Church network;
- historical sites associated with Russia.
The list reflects HUR’s assessment of potential targets, not confirmation that attacks at these locations are planned.
Earlier warnings and reported sabotage
On 2 October, HUR said Russian intelligence services had been ordered to increase activity in EU and NATO countries. It named military facilities, critical infrastructure, communications systems, and Starlink ground stations as potential targets and said it had alerted partners.
Warnings of Russian false flags on NATO’s eastern flank predate HUR’s. In August, Bloomberg reported, citing an unnamed European intelligence official, that Russia might expand hybrid attacks against Poland and the Baltic states, including false-flag attacks. A European government official separately told the agency that the CIA had warned countries in the region of a possible Russian attack. Lithuania’s military intelligence had warned earlier in August that Moscow might reassemble captured Ukrainian drones for false-flag strikes on critical infrastructure in the Baltic region.
Meanwhile, The Wall Street Journal reported on 20 October that US intelligence agencies believe the attempted drone attack on Leipzig-Halle Airport in Germany in early August was among the opening shots of a sabotage campaign ordered by Russian President Vladimir Putin. The Journal cited European officials briefed on the intelligence findings.
According to the newspaper, at least three drones carrying military-grade Semtex explosives were involved. One struck an Antonov cargo plane used to transport military aid to Ukraine but failed to explode. Another collided with a different aircraft, while a third detonated near the airport perimeter. German newspaper Welt am Sonntag has since named two suspects, citing German investigation files. Earlier German media reports described the sequence differently.
The Journal also reported sabotage attacks on Starlink stations in Poland, Lithuania, and Bulgaria in recent weeks. In August, Slovak authorities said they had foiled a planned arson attack on a Ukrainian drone factory, the Journal reported.
Russia denies involvement in sabotage in Europe. Responding to Berlin’s accusations over the Leipzig incident in early September, Putin asked where the evidence was.
