articles.title: Ukraine receives 50,000 rounds of ammunition for F-16s from Denmark
articles.body:
Denmark has delivered 50,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition for the autocannons on Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Oct. 23.
First delivered to Ukraine in 2024, the U.S.-made jets have become a key part of the country's defenses against Russian attacks on its rear areas, particularly jet-powered drones.
"Ukrainian pilots are already using them to intercept jet-powered attack drones," the ministry said on social media.
"We are grateful to Denmark for its quick and efficient response to our request for additional ammunition."
In addition to mounting points for various air-to-air and air-to-ground missiles,F-16 fighter jets are equipped with 20 mm M61 Vulcan rotary cannons designed for close-range engagements.
While missiles are often used to shoot down Russian cruise missiles during mass attacks, the cheaper autocannon ammunition is frequently used against Russian jet-powered drones, which are too fast for most Ukrainian interceptor drones to intercept.
On Sept. 30, Bloomberg reported that Kyiv was seeking to procure additional 20 mm rounds for its F-16s, with sources saying an average of 150 rounds was required per interception.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 5 that Ukraine was "scouring munitions for F-16s virtually all over the world." Zelensky also praised the jets as one of the most effective means of countering jet-powered drones.
Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Norway have collectively supplied Ukraine with around 50 F-16 fighter jets.
Intensive use in defending Ukrainian airspace means the jets require frequent maintenance, which can currently be carried out only by Kyiv's partners.

articles.title: In Syria, Israel’s female field intelligence soldiers power the IDF's covert operations
articles.body:
The Jerusalem Post recently interviewed female field intelligence soldiers on the Syrian border, overlooking areas where they routinely conduct surveillance and penetration operations.
Meeting at the former Syrian intelligence building, captured during the 1967 Six Day War, near Merom Golan in the Golan Heights, and traveling along the border to the Quneitra lookout, the Post interviewed IDF Capt. ‘O.’ and female intelligence collection soldiers ‘N.’ and ‘R.’ of Battalion 595.
They discussed what it means to be part of a new generation of women who operate inside Syria, monitor increased Iranian activity in the area, and navigate growing tensions with local Syrian residents who were once grateful for the IDF’s presence. They also discussed breaking the glass ceiling for women in combat roles in the IDF. Women now make up more than 50% of their unit.
‘N.’ and ‘R.’ specialize in a combination of direct visual surveillance and drone-based field intelligence collection.
The Post visited Battalion 595 about a year ago in a more southerly part of Israel’s buffer zone in Syria. During both visits, female intelligence soldiers described their efforts to locate and track a range of hostile groups, from Iranian operatives to Hamas members and regime-linked HTS jihadists.
In late 2025, a different group of female soldiers revealed that they had penetrated as far as 18 kilometers beyond the buffer zone into Syria. The operation included providing field guidance for the 890th Paratroopers Battalion.
During one operation, the soldiers studied four individuals who were working for, or associated with, Iran or Iranian agents. Each individual had to be analyzed separately, including their movements, schedules, and habits, one soldier, identified as ‘S.’, said at the time.
By October of this year, however, the soldiers could no longer disclose how far they were penetrating into Syria.
This came amid repeated public pressure from the Trump administration for Israel to scale back its activities in Syria and begin partial withdrawals from its buffer zone.
Nevertheless, all three interviewees, ‘N.’, ‘R.’, and ‘O.’, emphasized that they continued to carry out missions throughout southern Syria, quietly but aggressively.
The IDF has also issued several updates in recent weeks, including an announcement that it killed Iranian-linked Syrian terrorist Yusef Ali al-Hasan on October 9.
According to the IDF, al-Hasan was killed because of his involvement in a series of terrorist activities against Israeli forces, including drone operations and previous rocket fire from southern Syria.
In two separate incidents on October 4 and 5, the IDF also opened fire on three other suspects in Syria.
In the first incident, an IDF reservist from the Carmeli Brigade spotted a suspect attempting to infiltrate an IDF position and shot him dead. The suspect was found to be unarmed, and the incident is under review.
In the second incident, two suspects approached an IDF position in Syria on a motorcycle. IDF soldiers opened fire, wounding one of them, and arrested both for questioning.
These announcements followed a period in which the IDF had been relatively quiet about its activities in Syria, apart from an August 18 attack on a Turkish position. The relative silence came amid pressure from the Trump administration and growing reports of tensions with local Syrian civilians, some of whom have become increasingly frustrated with the IDF’s presence as it approaches its second anniversary.
What do these developments mean for future Israeli-Syrian security relations and intelligence collection along the border?
How female intelligence soldiers track threats in Syria
According to ‘N.’, who has served for two years and eight months, “our job is to guard the civilians, to secure this front, and to collect as much intelligence as possible.”
Asked how she and her unit determine where to focus their intelligence collection efforts within Israel’s extensive security zone in Syria and beyond, she said: “We have technological tools, and we do not work alone. We work with other intelligence partners, there are other IDF forces, and we get intelligence also from higher-ranking headquarters officers.”
Asked how long she had spent in the field on a single deployment, ‘N.’ explained that it varied according to the situation.
“It changes all the time, according to the [character of a specific] period. It could be a few days, or it could be a few hours. The longest was probably around a week, or a bit longer,” she said.
‘N.’ said she had spent longer periods in the field during the June 2025 war with Iran.
“The whole environment was hotter and more unstable, and there was a need for higher readiness, so we did what was required of us,” she said.
While international attention was focused on Israeli airstrikes against Iran and Iranian missiles launched at Israel, activity in Syria also increased.
“Whenever the situation is more tense, there are more incidents, so you need to be more ready in the field,” ‘N.’ said.
She also described an operation in which the unit gathered intelligence on several hostile individuals over a period of days.
“We collected intelligence on multiple hostiles over a period of days. We returned to the same area multiple times – and then an operation was carried out,” she said.
The process involves determining who a target is, whom they meet, and when and how those meetings take place.
“You try to find out who this is, who he meets with, when, and how,” she said, explaining that the soldiers also monitor the times of day or night when a target carries out activities or holds meetings.
‘N.’ emphasized that her unit’s role is to gather the information needed to help other forces carry out operations safely and effectively.
“[Our role is] to collect as much relevant intelligence as possible, so that the [IDF] forces which carry out the operation afterward will be able to do so in the most secure and optimal manner possible,” she said.
The soldiers collect intelligence both during the day and at night, ‘N.’ added, noting that “a lot of activities happen at night,” when people are harder to observe.
Combining drones, surveillance, and field intelligence
‘R.’, who has served for more than two years, described her experience leading teams and managing the unit’s operational readiness.
“I have commanded a few different units, including responsibilities for equipment and technology. I was a team leader [for a small unit] for running the operational activities regarding intelligence and regarding the readiness of the unit, working on their professionalism and their combat knowledge,” she said.
“We carried out many operations to get as much information as the brigade needed. We kept our eyes peeled for [collecting intelligence for] them. Sometimes they also ask for very specific intelligence, and we get as much as we can for them,” she added.
‘R.’ said soldiers must look beyond the immediate target during an operation to understand the broader context.
“Sometimes when you go out to perform an operation, it is easy to just focus on the main mission-target itself, but you can miss some of the important [secondary] things going on around the mission-focus,” she said.
She stressed the importance of connecting the unit’s observations to the overall situation in the area being monitored.
‘R.’ explained that the soldiers do not always know how an operation ultimately unfolds. They therefore try to learn what happened afterward, allowing them to understand how their work contributed to the mission.
The feedback is also important for morale, she said, helping soldiers feel that their work has made a difference even when they do not see the final outcome.
Regarding the choice between direct visual surveillance and drones, ‘R.’ said the decision depends on the mission and the target’s location.
“It depends on the mission. Where is the target? What do you need to do to get [close enough to observe the target] there?” she said.
“We have lots of different tools, and our job is to be skilled enough to choose each time what is the right tool to accomplish the mission in the best way possible,” she added.
Asked whether direct observation was preferable, with drones used when approaching a target would risk exposing the soldiers, ‘R.’ said the priority was to get as close as possible without compromising their safety.
“We want to be as close to the target as possible, without endangering ourselves. We are a clandestine unit. So we do need to keep our distance sometimes, but each time is different,” she said.
Asked about situations in which she and her fellow soldiers had faced danger, ‘R.’ said they could sense when a front was becoming more volatile, whether because of Iranian activity or threats from other groups.
Part of what helped them cope, she said, was the close-knit nature of the unit.
“We are always together, and each of us is there for the next-door soldier. So even if there is a bit more fear or official threat warnings, we have each other's backs, and this is one of the best things [about the unit],” she said.
‘R.’ added that the soldiers supported one another through conversations, body language, and eye signals, particularly when operations required them to remain silent.
“There is a dynamic between the [female] soldiers [in the unit] that they can do this [communicate] even without speaking – this is awesome, and it shows true sisterhood between the women. It is inspiring to see this, and even fun,” she said. “But sometimes with these matters which can cause stress, we need to focus and perform our operations. Then later we get to celebrate it.”
Asked how the unit determines whether a target is linked to Iran, Hamas, HTS, the Syrian regime, or another group, ‘R.’ said the process relies on cooperation with intelligence headquarters.
“These are matters that come to us from intelligence [headquarters]. We also help each other in both directions. They give me guidance in a direction about what I need to search for and look for, and I can help them in another direction, including signs relating to HTS or another group,” she said.
She added that surveillance operations are often repeated to build a more complete intelligence picture of a potential threat.
‘R.’ agreed that activity in Syria had intensified recently, saying that the soldiers could feel the change through sudden mission call-ups and other indications.
“It is felt. It is felt. Whether due to sudden mission call-ups of the unit [or other signs], but we are always ready, whether it [a threat] plays out or not, we are ready to stay here and we are not afraid,” she said.
IDF commander says threats persist despite US pressure
Capt. ‘O.’ commands the larger company to which ‘N.’ and ‘R.’ belong.
He has spent his entire five-and-a-half-year military service in the Golan Heights, including operating in Syria since December 2024, when the IDF established its buffer zone following the fall of the Assad regime.
“Once we understood what was happening with the revolution [against the Assad regime], we saw this was an amazing opportunity,” he said.
‘O.’ said the decision to establish the buffer zone was driven by the opportunity to strengthen Israel’s security by moving its defensive position forward.
“We were ready. It was not a question of whether to go in [to set up a Syrian buffer zone]. It was [only a question of] when do we go in so we can defend from a forward position. Our job is to prevent enemies from getting into Jewish towns which are right next to us here,” he said, gesturing toward nearby residential areas.
Asked about the elevated threat from Iran, including the recent incidents publicized by the IDF, ‘O.’ said the situation involved increased friction.
“There is more friction. There is more ongoing friction. We have no problem with some friction. It is a good thing as it makes us readier for anything and everything [appearing] at any place,” he said.
The Post noted that the IDF spokesperson had issued more updates about Iranian activity and other threats after a period in which IDF sources said Iranian associates had largely left Syria.
‘O.’ responded that attempts to establish terrorist infrastructure in Syria continued.
“There is always an attempt to establish [a terror] apparatus. And they will always remain [at some level]. They want to destroy us, and they will [try to] do this however they can,” he said.
He added that hostile groups would continue to look for different ways to threaten Israel, but said the IDF was prepared to defend residents and visitors to the Golan Heights.
“So sometimes they will try one way, and sometimes they will try another way, but we are ready for everything, ready to defend the civilians and tourists who live in and tour the Golan,” he said.
During the summer, he added, the area attracted many tourists, requiring the soldiers to work harder to protect them. With winter approaching, visitors would again come to see the snow on Mount Hermon, and the IDF would need to protect them as well.
Asked about diplomatic pressure to reduce Israeli operations in Syria and eventually withdraw partially from the buffer zone, ‘O.’ said those decisions were outside his remit.
“I am not part of the political echelon. I am at the tactical level…I receive orders, and I carry them out,” he said.
“What they order me to do, I do. Where they tell me to be, I will be there. If there is an operation which is approved or not, [when it is approved] we will do it as best as possible,” he added. “Whoever decides what the missions will be, that is way over my head. I am not part of these debates…I deal with the here and now.”
Asked whether he had noticed a freeze in operations following US demands, ‘O.’ said such decisions were made at higher levels and that he had not necessarily observed a change in his daily work.
“This is a decision made at the higher levels. I don’t know if I feel this [change]. We have lots of missions every day. I don’t necessarily feel there are more or fewer missions,” he said.
‘O.’ also described the difficulty of distinguishing between hostile operatives and civilians in Syria.
“The people who want to harm us are not fools. They know where to be, when to be there, how to present themselves,” he said, explaining that they also know how to observe others without attracting attention.
He added that hostile operatives can conceal themselves within the civilian population, making it difficult to distinguish between terrorists and civilians.
‘O.’ said the IDF draws on a wide range of capabilities to identify and neutralize threats, with his unit contributing intelligence gathered through clandestine observation and drones.
“The IDF is a very powerful military in all of its sections and on all of the platforms that one can use. We all do this together. In the end, I provide another perspective to complement the broader IDF picture,” he said.
He added that he was part of a larger intelligence apparatus that combines different sources and methods to address specific threats.
“In the end, there is an integration of various kinds of intelligence which collectively provide an answer to more specific issues,” he said.
Syrian civilians grow less patient with the IDF presence
The Post received independent confirmation of increased rock-throwing incidents and tensions between some Syrian civilians and IDF soldiers.
However, neither ‘N.’ nor ‘R.’ believed the situation had deteriorated dramatically. They said the soldiers were still generally received warmly.
“We receive more cherries than rocks,” ‘R.’ said, although she acknowledged that tense encounters sometimes occurred and that the soldiers had to remain prepared for any eventuality.
Field intelligence lessons from Lebanon and Jordan
‘N.’ has also been involved in field intelligence operations relating to Lebanon and Jordan.
‘R.’ described the challenges of gathering intelligence on Hezbollah in Lebanon, noting that the group operates differently from other adversaries.
“Hezbollah is a different organization and it uses different tools and methods. We use different tools and methods [against them],” she said.
‘R.’ added that her unit had been heavily involved in Lebanon during the IDF’s early 2026 invasion, describing the work as more intense in some respects than intelligence collection along a relatively quiet border.
Female combat soldiers still face resistance in the IDF
Asked about serving as a woman in a combat role, ‘N.’ said she had wanted to become a combat soldier since childhood.
“Even as a child, I always wanted to be a combat fighter, so no one was surprised that I went into combat,” she said. “Now I think that the biggest contribution female combat fighters can make is in intelligence collection. I really believe in what I and we are doing.”
‘N.’ said that while her own company was supportive, she had encountered resistance outside the unit.
“My company knows how to deal with this, but I had experiences outside my unit which were not the nicest,” she said.
“There are still both men and women who do not accept this, especially reservists who do not love it. I explained it to them, but we still have a long way to go,” she added.
In some cases, she said, she had managed to reach a “tie” with people who were initially opposed to women serving in combat roles, even if they had not fully changed their views.
‘N.’ said she had generally been admitted to the IDF bases she visited, but there had been occasions when soldiers refused to let her and her fellow soldiers stay overnight because the bases lacked separate sleeping quarters or bathrooms for women.
“It depends on who is the commander and what kind of unit is there at the time,” she said.
‘R.’ said women could perform some tasks as well as men, and in some cases better, pointing to their attention to detail and patience.
“Some things are the same and some things we can do better [than men]. The day-to-day work is less physical,” she said.
Like ‘N.’, ‘R.’ said she generally received cooperation from other IDF bases, although acceptance from male counterparts sometimes depended on the commander in charge.
At higher levels, including the battalion and brigade commands, she said, the unit enjoyed full support because senior officers understood its contribution.
“They understand what we bring to the table,” she said.
‘R.’ recalled an instance in which someone who had initially been skeptical of her role later recognized its value when he needed her help.
“Hopefully, once someone was not excited about me [being a female soldier], but then a week later, he needed me to find something,” she said, describing how their relationship improved.
Such experiences, she added, motivated the soldiers to work harder and demonstrate their capabilities.
“It just motivates us to work harder and in the end we get results,” she said.
The two female soldiers were divided on whether they were ready to see a woman become IDF chief of staff.
‘O.’, meanwhile, said he judged soldiers by their ability to carry out their missions, regardless of gender.
“I expect the same thing from female and male combat soldiers. I do not say a mission is for men or for women. It can be either one for any given mission,” he said.
“We need to remember we are all working toward the same goal: to defend the citizenry – whether a man or a woman doesn’t matter,” he concluded.

articles.title: Finland May Have Quietly Handed Ukraine Its Rare ItO 90M Air Defense Fleet
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Finland May Have Quietly Handed Ukraine Its Rare ItO 90M Air Defense Fleet
A previously undisclosed Finnish air-defense system has appeared in Ukrainian service, revealing that Helsinki quietly transferred rare ItO 90M launchers. These are now being used to defend the country from cruise missiles, aircraft, and Russia’s increasingly fast jet-powered drones.
Ukraine has now publicly confirmed the presence of Finland’s rare ItO 90M systems, showing that the launchers had been transferred without prior announcement and are already integrated into the country’s air-defense network against cruise missiles, aircraft, and jet-powered drones.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Finnish ItO 90M short-range surface-to-air missile system appeared for the first time in footage released by Ukraine’s 1039th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment, according to Defense Express on October 23.
Until now, there had been no public indication that Ukraine had received the system. Finland never announced a transfer, and it remains unclear when the launchers arrived or how many were supplied.
The footage nevertheless indicates that the systems are already operational and being used in Ukraine’s air-defense network.
Finland’s Crotale on wheels
The ItO 90M is essentially Finland’s version of the French Crotale NG air-defense system, mounted on the Sisu XA-181 armored personnel carrier chassis.
Ukraine has already operated French Crotale NG systems since 2022, but the French military uses them primarily in a towed configuration. Finland’s version gives the system significantly greater mobility by integrating it onto an armored vehicle.
Both versions fire the VT-1 interceptor missile.
The missile can engage targets at ranges of up to 15 kilometers and altitudes of around 9 kilometers. It can accelerate to approximately 1,250 meters per second—about Mach 3.6, or roughly 2,800 mph—and carries a 13-kilogram warhead.
Those characteristics make the system suitable for engaging aircraft and helicopters, but Defense Express notes that its capabilities are particularly relevant for Ukraine because it can also intercept cruise missiles and high-speed UAVs, including Russia’s newer jet-powered drones.
Secret transfer of a rare system
The biggest unanswered question is how many ItO 90Ms Finland may have supplied.
Finland acquired just one prototype and 20 production systems during the 1990s, meaning its entire original inventory amounted to only 21 launchers.
Even if all the systems survived and remained serviceable, the fleet was tiny from the outset.
Defense Express therefore raises the possibility that Finland may have chosen to transfer a significant portion—or potentially even its entire remaining ItO 90M inventory—to Ukraine rather than retain a handful of systems requiring their own maintenance, training, and logistical support.
There is currently no confirmation that all 21 were transferred, however, and neither Helsinki nor Kyiv has disclosed the number delivered.
Already defending Ukrainian skies
Whatever the size of the transfer, the first public footage confirms that at least some Finnish ItO 90Ms are no longer sitting in storage or training units—they are already being used by Ukrainian air-defense troops.
Their appearance comes as Ukraine faces a rapidly evolving Russian aerial threat, including faster jet-powered drones that place greater demands on short-range air defenses.
With VT-1 missiles capable of speeds well above Mach 3, the Finnish systems provide another layer between Ukraine’s cheaper interceptor drones and its more expensive long-range air-defense systems.
Previously, reports emerged that Finland is already preparing its 36th military aid package for Ukraine, with a decision on its approval expected before the end of 2026.

articles.title: Russia bombs Ukrainian cities despite Putin's openness to peace talks
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday that future talks on a settlement of the war in Ukraine should focus on security guarantees for both countries and an overall framework for security throughout Europe.
Putin, interviewed on Russian television a day after meeting US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff, confirmed that Russia was ready to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month.
He restated longstanding Kremlin policy that Russia never wanted to launch a war, but had run into hostile reactions from Ukraine on key issues of concern to Moscow.
Talks on a variety of matters could lead to a positive outcome, he said, but Russia remained intent on a solution ending the conflict rather than a short-lived ceasefire.
"The goal of these talks will be to ensure the security of Ukraine and Russia after reaching peace agreements, in their final form, not as a result of a temporary ceasefire for some short period of time. We are ready to resume these contacts to achieve this goal," Putin said.
Witkoff says Ukraine supports 'any proposals for a ceasefire'
The Russian president said Witkoff also stressed that discussions had to extend to "the architecture of European security as a whole. And I agree with that too. Well, let's see how things develop in the coming days."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who met Witkoff in Norway on Tuesday, said Ukraine was ready for talks likely to take place by early next month. Ukraine, he said, supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives."
Efforts headed by the United States to pursue talks stalled in February with the outbreak of the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
Many of the Ukraine war issues focus on territory, with Russia demanding Ukraine cede all of eastern Ukraine's Donbas region. Kyiv rejects any notion of giving up land it currently holds.
In his comments, Putin said any discussion on territory in eastern Ukraine had to consider what he said was the fact that the area was "historically Russian land."
And residents there, he said, had voted to be a part of Russia in referendums staged seven months after Moscow launched its invasion.
"Firstly, my attitude on this matter is that this is not their territory. It’s the territory of historical Russia," he said.
Russia strikes Ukraine despite openness to peace talks
Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles, and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow on Thursday, as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US push to end the conflict.
US President Donald Trump said SpaceX SPCX.O CEO Elon Musk had restored Ukraine's Starlink access, one of the issues linked to a rift between Washington and Kyiv that has cast doubt on US support for Ukraine.
Ukraine said Russia fired at least 21 ballistic missiles in three waves. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said three carried cluster munitions — "bomblets" that disperse over a wide area and are banned by many countries because of the danger to civilians. Russia's defense ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Russia said Ukraine launched 630 drones towards Moscow during the night.
The two sides held an exchange of war dead, with Moscow handing over 252 bodies and Ukraine handing over 25, according to the Belta state news agency in neighboring Belarus. Such exchanges have accompanied moves towards talks in the past.

articles.title: Europe faces threat of organised sabotage, terrorist attacks: Estonian FM Tsahkna
articles.body:
Europe faces threat of organised sabotage, terrorist attacks: Estonian FM Tsahkna

Estonia's counterintelligence service has recently warned that sabotage operations orchestrated by Russian special services have reached a new and dangerous phase in Europe, with targets no longer being purely symbolic. Talking Europe sits down with the country's foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, to discuss the security situation in Estonia and the European Union in general.
Speaking of undercover operations against Estonia attributed to Russian special services, Tsahkna says: "We have witnessed terrorist attacks, sabotage attacks, against the defence industry companies. We just attributed, three weeks ago, one serious attack against our defence industry company organised by the Russian secret services. We caught these three guys. They are in prison now. We see an increase in the number of these attacks. But we also see that they are not against the Baltic States as much as against Europe as a whole. We (in the Baltics) are not at the top of this list. Russia is increasing the pressure on Europe. This is about terror attacks, sabotage attacks, cyberattacks, and any kind of disinformation to divide our unity and to divide our societies as well."
Tsahkna distinguishes between this hybrid war and Russia’s actual military capabilities, which he implies have been degraded by its involvement in Ukraine.
"When I served as a defence minister in 2016-2017, we had permanently 120,000 Russian troops on the other side of our borders, very close, ready to go within 48 hours. These troops were literally sent to Ukraine; they are not existing anymore. They are dead," he says.
Tsahkna goes on: "We know exactly what to do on the military level. We have NATO troops. Actually, French troops are located in Estonia. They are 100 percent integrated with our troops. We have very solid NATO regional defence plans. So this is not the main concern. The main concern now is to keep all of us in Europe united. And we need to understand that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is testing all of us. He's very carefully watching how we are acting, how united we are, how we are responding."
On diplomatic moves to try to reach a ceasefire in Ukraine, Tsahkna warns that Europe cannot, and should not, become a kind of neutral arbiter.
"Europe is taking part in initiatives, and we just had a meeting in Oslo, together with the US representative and President Zelensky and also the Nordic presidents, prime ministers and the Norwegian prime minister, " Tsahkna says. "So it's not about whether Europe is connected. Of course, we must be there. But we must also understand the position. We cannot let ourselves be dragged into the mediating position that Putin really wants: appointing a special envoy and then trying to mediate between Ukraine and Russia. So we are part of the process, of course, but we are not in the mediating position, a so-called neutral position, in which we would somehow stop our sanctions or give the frozen assets back to Russia. So this is important to understand. "
Tsahkna also has a few observations about the recent protests, violence and unrest in France.
"Elections are coming next year in France that are so important for Europe," he notes. "Of course, using violence is not a solution. And in Estonia we have been paying a lot of attention to keeping our society united, not divided. How to not go to the way of radicalisation. Because divisions in society are making you weaker as a country and as a nation. But of course, it's a matter for France and for the French how to have this dialogue about the future. You know, I'm coming from [the] north. We are very calm people!"

articles.title: Ukraine frees 270 from Russian captivity in “historic” prisoner swap, including 5 Olenivka survivors and American teacher Stephen Hubbard
articles.body:
Ukraine has brought home 270 people from Russian captivity, including 261 military personnel and nine civilians, in the third stage of a prisoner exchange process that began on 19 August, Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said on 23 October.
Amid Russia’s full-scale invasion, prisoner exchanges remain one of the few channels of communication between Kyiv and Moscow. But with thousands of Ukrainian military personnel and civilians still held in Russian captivity, each swap brings home only a fraction of those awaiting release, while negotiations remain tied to the difficult process of securing the return of captives on both sides.
Most of those released today had been held since 2022, including many defenders of Mariupol. Five survivors of the July 2022 Russian attack on the Olenivka prison barracks are also among those returning home.
The exchange also included American Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old English teacher from Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, who was illegally captured in 2022, then sentenced and tortured by Russia, according to the Coordination Headquarters.
Exchange includes soldiers held for up to eight years
The exchange included members of Ukraine’s Armed Forces, National Guard, State Border Guard Service, and other security and defense units, as well as a State Emergency Service rescuer. Thirty-eight of the released military personnel are officers.
According to Ukraine’s Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, the exchange was “historic” because it brought home the largest number of Ukrainian military personnel sentenced by Russia: 86 who had been sentenced and one who had faced criminal prosecution.
Two of those released had been held since 2018 and 2020, spending eight and six years in captivity, respectively.
“The priorities remain unchanged: we bring home those who have been in captivity the longest, the seriously ill, and the seriously wounded,” Lubinets said, adding that efforts to return civilians and people held since 2014 also remain a priority.
Nine seriously ill prisoners among those released
Nine of the returning service members are seriously ill, and some are in critical condition, the Coordination Headquarters said. The youngest person released is 24, while the oldest is 63.
Many of those released had faced criminal prosecution in Russia and been sentenced on what Ukraine describes as fabricated charges, including life imprisonment.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said most of those returning had been captured in 2022, and many had defended Mariupol.
The released also include service members who fought in the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, and Chernihiv directions, as well as defenders of the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant.
“We remember every man and woman and continue searching for everyone,” Zelenskyy said.
Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution
US and UAE thanked for assistance
Ukraine thanked the United States and the United Arab Emirates for helping secure the releases.
All those released will undergo medical examinations, receive treatment and financial support, and take part in rehabilitation and reintegration programs after prolonged captivity.
Ukraine’s military intelligence chief and head of the Coordination Headquarters, Oleh Ivashchenko, said the return followed months of negotiations. He stressed that efforts to establish the fate of missing Ukrainians and bring everyone home would continue.
The 23 October exchange follows the previous stage on 19 August, when Ukraine brought home 103 servicemembers from Russian captivity.

articles.title: Russian Iskander parts plant likely hit by cruise missiles
articles.body:
A missile strike likely hit the Proton plant in the Russian city of Orel, a manufacturer of optoelectronic equipment whose components are used in Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missiles, Pantsir-S1 air defense systems and Kh-71 cruise missiles, according to the monitoring channel Exilenova+.
Local authorities declared an aviation and missile danger alert in Orel during the attack. Information on the extent of the damage at the plant is still being clarified, and the type of weapon used and the exact time of the strike have not yet been confirmed.
The joint-stock company Proton is part of Russia’s defense industry supply chain and produces optoelectronic equipment and components for military use. Its products include diode modules, switch-inverters and electronic components for onboard weapon systems, which are supplied for the production of the 9M723 missiles of the Iskander-M short-range ballistic missile system, the S-71 Kover air-launched cruise missile and the Pantsir-S1, a truck-mounted system that combines anti-aircraft missiles and rapid-fire cannons to shoot down aircraft, drones and cruise missiles.
The Iskander-M is one of Russia’s main weapons for long-range strikes against Ukraine, firing ballistic missiles with a range of up to 500 km (310 miles). The S-71 Kover belongs to a family of newer Russian air-launched cruise missiles, and Ukrainian military intelligence has previously identified the same R500 turbojet engine in the S-71K Kover and the new Filin ground-launched cruise missile, which Russia began using against Ukraine in late summer 2026.
Orel, the capital of Russia’s Orel region about 160 km (100 miles) from the Ukrainian border, has been the target of repeated long-range strikes. On Oct. 31, 2025, the Ukrainian Navy said it hit the city’s thermal power plant with Neptune cruise missiles, and in May 2025 drones struck the Bolkhov semiconductor plant in the same region, which produces components used by Russia’s defense industry.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian plants that build missiles and their components. In August 2026, Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missiles hit the Progress Rocket and Space Center in Samara, and earlier this month the Ukrainian General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant in Tver region, which produces components for cruise missile fuel.

articles.title: Denmark rushes 50,000 cannon rounds to Ukraine to help F-16s hunt Russia’s advanced jet drones
articles.body:
Ukraine has received more than 50,000 rounds of 20-mm ammunition from Denmark for the onboard cannons of its F-16 fighter jets, with Ukrainian pilots already using the rounds to intercept Russian jet-powered Geran attack drones, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said.
The accelerated delivery addresses a key need in Ukraine’s air defense as Russia increasingly deploys faster jet-powered drones that challenge conventional interceptors. Ukraine has also relied on F-16 cannons when stocks of air-to-air missiles are limited, making ammunition supplies important to keeping the aircraft effective against incoming aerial threats.
Denmark responds to ammunition request
The Defense Ministry thanked Denmark for responding quickly to Ukraine’s request for additional ammunition, saying the delivery directly strengthens the country’s air defenses and helps protect civilians from Russian aerial attacks.
The delivery follows a broader effort by Ukraine’s European partners to replenish F-16 cannon ammunition. On October 2, it was reported that Spain, Belgium, and Poland were also sending 20-mm rounds for Ukrainian F-16s to counter Russia’s jet-powered drones.
Belgium is also expanding its support for Ukraine’s F-16 fleet. On 16 October, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever pledged to deliver 10 F-16s by the end of 2026, up from three previously planned, and discussed supplying additional ammunition, including 20-mm rounds produced by Belgian defense company FN Herstal.
Jet-powered drones pose a growing challenge
Russia’s faster attack drones are harder to intercept than older, propeller-driven Shahed-type models. Their speed gives air defenders less time to respond and makes them more difficult for many interceptor drones and conventional short-range weapons to catch.
Ukraine’s air-to-air missile shortages have also increased the importance of F-16 cannon ammunition. Ukrainian pilots have sometimes relied on their aircraft’s built-in 20-mm cannon when air-to-air missiles are scarce.
Ukraine’s F-16s are so short of Western missiles that pilots fall back on jet’s built-in M61A1 Vulcan cannon, which risks killing civilians below
The threat from jet-powered drones is growing. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in late September that Ukraine was intercepting about 55% of Russia’s jet-powered drones, compared with more than 90% of older models.
Denmark’s ammunition delivery gives Ukrainian F-16 pilots more rounds to engage these faster targets, as Ukraine works to strengthen its defenses against Russia’s expanding drone campaign.

articles.title: Trump hints of new strikes on Iran, ministers gather in Istanbul
articles.body:
This live blog has now ended. Make sure to follow us for the latest news on Facebook, X, and Instagram.
Here were the key updates:
US President Donald Trump suggested possible further military action against Iran, claiming that the US has knocked the "hell out" of it
European and Middle Eastern foreign ministers gather in Turkey's Istanbul for security talks on the Strait of Hormuz and various conflicts in the region
Yemen's Taiz faces severe food and water shortages, with the UN warning that aid delivery has halted for about 800,000 residents. Meanwhile, fighting rages between the Iran-backed Houthis and the internationally recognised Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon, and southern Syria despite any claims of a ceasefire
France shooting 'racist, probably Islamophobic' attack
A deadly shooting in a town outside Paris on Friday was "a racist, probably Islamophobic attack," the mayor of Trappes said, as authorities moved to investigate the case as a "terrorist" incident.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, visiting the area where at least two victims were of foreign origin, said the gunman, who killed one person and wounded five others, "clearly" committed "a terrorist crime."
Six killed, 28 injured in attack at Jordan funeral
Six people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack by unidentified assailants during a funeral in Jordan's Karak governorate, the Public Security Directorate said on Friday, after state-owned media had earlier reported that seven people were killed.
Authorities said an investigation was under way and that they would announce its findings as they became available.
US authorises emergency release of up to 400,000 oil barrels
The US Department of Energy said on Friday it had authorised an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil from the nation's Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address a supply disruption affecting Phillips 66's Lake Charles refinery in Louisiana.
France's foreign minister said on Friday that any renewed escalation between Iran and the United States would only have losers and raise oil prices.
"A further escalation between Iran and the United States would leave no winners and would likely have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices," Jean-Noel Barrot told reporters in Istanbul after a meeting with counterparts from Britain, Germany, Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
UAE closes beach in Sharjah as precaution over oil spill
The United Arab Emirates has temporarily closed Al Hamriyah beach in Sharjah as a precaution against marine pollution from an oil spill involving a tanker, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said on Friday.
Authorities were taking measures to protect beaches and prevent pollution from reaching the shore and urged fishermen and sea-goers to follow official safety instructions.
The United Arab Emirates has temporarily closed Al Hamriyah beach in Sharjah. [Getty]
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday Israel would lock down Hebron in the occupied West Bank, go house to house and demolish homes after the Israeli military said Palestinian attackers killed two soldiers at a military checkpoint near the city.
The Israeli military said it had killed two Palestinians, and another three soldiers had been lightly wounded in the attack.
"We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely," Netanyahu said in a statement after the attack.
Inside Israel's ties with Bosnia's Serb separatists
This statement was hardly surprising. In recent years, Dodik has been outspoken in his support for Israel and its genocidal war on Gaza at a time in which relations between Republika Srpska and Israel are growing.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has invited his Indian counterpart, Narendra Modi, to light a torch alongside Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar at Israel's so-called 'Independence Day' celebrations next year.
The occasion marks what Palestinians call the Nakba, or "Catastrophe", when Zionist militias carried out mass expulsions of Palestinians to create the state of Israel.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday warned of an imminent large-scale military operation in the occupied West Bank and vowed to displace some residents of Hebron after Palestinian gunmen wounded five Israelis.
Israeli forces "will enter the neighbourhood from which the terrorists came, evacuate the residents, go from house to house, and destroy the terrorist infrastructure", Netanyahu said during a visit to Hebron, according to his office.
"The defence minister and I are considering a very extensive IDF (army) operation in [the West Bank], such as has not been carried out since the Six Day War," he added, referring to the 1967 Arab-Israeli war. "The IDF is ready to execute it and we will set the timing, but it is on the way."
Oil prices traded at five-month highs Friday, with benchmark crude contract Brent North Sea near $115 a barrel, as the Middle East conflict raged on.
Global markets were contending "with concerns around surging oil prices and the sustainability of AI spending", noted AJ Bell head of financial analysis Danni Hewson.
"Oil is at five-month highs amid speculation there may be renewed US-Israeli strikes after next month's US midterm elections.
"Escalating tensions in Ukraine and the prospect of increased energy demand as the northern hemisphere heads into the winter months are only adding to the upwards pressure on oil and gas prices," Hewson added.
UK stocks set for weekly declines as oil prices soar
UK stocks were set for weekly declines on Friday, as oil prices hit over five-month highs this week, weighing heavily on risk appetite, while investors parsed a slew of corporate earnings and economic data through the week.
The blue-chip FTSE 100 index fell 0.5% to 10,670 points by 1020 GMT. The midcap FTSE 250 was up 0.1%, but was set for its sharpest weekly fall in nearly six weeks.
Oil prices hit their highest levels in over five months, with Brent crude trading close to $114 a barrel. This lifted energy shares 2%
US midterms: Where do candidates stand on Gaza and Iran?
The midterm elections in the United States are in full swing, with early voting starting in most states.
The results will set the tone of US foreign and domestic policy for the rest of President Donald Trump's term. Control of both chambers of Congress—the Senate and the House of Representatives—is at stake.
Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called on Friday for a military campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza" following a shooting attack that wounded at least five people in the occupied Palestinian territory.
"There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists. Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon," said Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry. "In the next government this will be one of the first measures that we must demand and apply."
UNICEF calls on Israel's military to stop killing children
UNICEF called on Israel's military to take immediate steps to stop the killing of children in Gaza, more than a year into a ceasefire.
On Thursday the group said that the total number of children killed has surpassed 350 since Israel and Hamas reached the agreement last October.
“This level of violence against children is unacceptable,” Edouard Beigbeder, UNICEF’s regional director for the Middle East and North Africa, said in a statement. He called on Israeli authorities to take immediate and decisive action to protect children.
Children make up roughly half of Gaza's population. [Getty]
Strikes by Israel's army killed at least one person in southern Gaza Friday morning, according to Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.
More than 1,500 Palestinians there have been killed by Israel since an alleged ceasefire began in October 2025, according to the Gaza's health ministry.
All 14 Indians in yacht incident off Yemen coast safe
All 14 Indian nationals on a yacht involved in an incident off Yemen's coast are reported safe, the Indian embassy in Yemen said on Friday.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Thursday they were rescuing a boat carrying 14 Indians that was attacked off Jabal Zuqar island near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, and blamed Saudi Arabia for the attack.
Saudi authorities did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on Thursday.
"Reports suggest that all 14 Indian nationals are safe and located around Hodeidah in Yemen. We will continue to work for ensuring their well being," the Indian embassy in Yemen said in a post on X, without elaborating.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the closure of the occupied West Bank days before Israeli elections after two Palestinian men wounded six Israeli soldiers on Friday before they were killed in a prolonged shootout.
Netanyahu, facing a tight race for a new term in Tuesday's election, claimed that Israeli troops prevented what could have been a "major attack", with the assailants allegedly carrying a large quantity of ammunition in their vehicle.
UAE reports oil spill from tanker as ships attacked
The United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill from a tanker off its coast on Friday, as numerous vessels in Gulf waters come under attack during the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The authorities "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement, referring to an emirate north of Dubai.
It said "teams immediately began containment, cordoning, clean-up and remediation... to limit environmental impacts", adding that the emirate's beaches had been closed.
Many residents in the north of the country have reported oil smells on social media in recent days, including residents in northern districts of Dubai.
Frequent attacks on ships have been reported in recent weeks near the Strait of Hormuz, at the heart of the conflict between Iran and the United States.
The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on October 9 that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control.
According to the maritime security company Vanguard, the vessel in question was the oil tanker GEM NO.2, sailing under the Panamanian flag.
Saudi Arabia postpones UN data forum, statistical event
Saudi Arabia's General Authority for Statistics has postponed the United Nations World Data Forum and the Second Saudi Statistical Forum, previously scheduled for 9 to 12 November 2026, in Riyadh, to 2027, it said in a statement on Friday.
The move follows Saudi Arabia's decision on Monday to delay its flagship investment conference to 2027, after deadly attacks in recent weeks linked to the widening conflict set off by the US and Israel's attack on Iran disrupted business activity. The Future Investment Initiative had been due to take place from 26 to 29 October.
The authority said it postponed the UN data forum and the Saudi statistical forum to ensure broad international participation by speakers, experts and partners, and the delivery of an event that meets the expectations of the global data and statistics community.
Several other major events in Saudi Arabia, including the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament and the World Rally Championship's Saudi Arabia round, have also been cancelled or postponed amid escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.
Far-right Ben-Gvir calls for ending Palestinian Authority
Israel's far-right national security minister called Friday for the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority after an attack by suspected Palestinian assailants in the West Bank left five Israelis injured days ahead of elections.
"We have to act before it's too late. The Palestinian Authority must be dismantled and demilitarised, and its terror infrastructure wiped out completely," Itamar Ben Gvir said in a statement. There was no immediate indication of any Palestinian Authority involvement in the incident.
How an Israeli spyware is threatening global security
Al Jazeera is the latest target of Israeli spyware weaponising digital ads for surveillance, but the attack is just the tip of the iceberg, warns Silverstein.
Israeli troops on Friday shot dead two suspected Palestinians in the occupied West Bank after a shooting at a military checkpoint in Hebron that left at least six Israeli soldiers wounded, officials said.
The incident comes as tensions soar in the occupied West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters, and days ahead of Israeli elections.
US regulator is probing suspicious Iran oil trading
The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission is probing suspicious oil trading activity around the US war in Iran and scrutinizing prediction market trading around elections, the agency's enforcement director said on Thursday at a conference in New York.
CFTC Enforcement Director David Miller made the remarks in response to a Bloomberg News story last week that said a CFTC political appointee had told market surveillance staff to retract a referral to the agency's enforcement team identifying suspicious trading around President Donald Trump's March decision to back away from strikes on Iran's power plants.
When asked about the story during a panel at the conference, Miller said the agency had "from the beginning" been probing the trading and that the investigation remained open.
The report fueled concerns raised by investor advocates and lawmakers over a decline in enforcement activity at the agency, which is dealing with an exodus of staff as it tries to oversee the growing prediction markets industry. Prediction markets allow people to bet on the outcome of various events, from US elections to sports games.

articles.title: Denmark sends ammo to Ukraine for F-16 guns to down drones
articles.body:
- Denmark delivered more than 50,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition to Ukraine on an expedited basis for the cannons on its F-16 fighters.
- Ukrainian pilots are already using the rounds to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type attack drones, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said.
Denmark has rushed more than 50,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition to Ukraine for the cannons on its F-16 fighter jets, and Ukrainian pilots are already firing them at Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type attack drones, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said on Oct. 23, 2026.
The ministry announced the delivery on X, saying Denmark sent the rounds on an expedited basis in response to a Ukrainian request. It described aviation, and the F-16 in particular, as one of the most effective tools against jet-powered Shaheds, and said destroying them requires sufficient stocks of ammunition.
“We are grateful to Denmark for its quick and effective response to our request for additional ammunition. This speed matters directly for strengthening Ukraine’s air defence and protecting people from Russian air attacks,” said Minister of Defence Evgeniy Khmara.
Every F-16 carries an internal M61A1 Vulcan, a six-barrel rotary cannon that fires about 6,000 rounds per minute. Using the gun against drones lets pilots save their far more expensive guided missiles for cruise missiles and other high-priority targets, and 20 mm rounds are held in much larger quantities around the world than Patriot interceptors or Western air-to-air missiles.
The guns burn through ammunition quickly, with Bloomberg reporting that destroying a single jet-powered drone can take about 150 rounds and that, at the current intensity of Russian attacks, Ukraine could need around 10,000 rounds a day. At that rate, the Danish shipment would cover roughly 330 engagements.
Russia began using jet-powered versions of its Geran drones, the Russian-built derivatives of the Iranian Shahed-136, in significant numbers in early 2026. The newer jet models can carry up to 90 kg (198 pounds) of explosives, fly up to 1,000 km (620 miles) and reach speeds of up to 600 km/h (373 mph), making them much harder to catch than the earlier propeller-driven drones. Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat has said Ukraine shoots down about 60% of the jet-powered drones, compared with roughly 90% to 95% for other types.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said combat aviation, primarily the F-16, accounts for 55% to 60% of all intercepts of jet-powered Shaheds, and that Ukraine has expanded contracts to keep its F-16 squadrons supplied with 20 mm rounds. Germany has delivered its first batch of F-16 ammunition for countering the drones, and Belgium and Spain have also sent urgent shipments.
Denmark has been one of Ukraine’s main F-16 partners, pledging 19 of the jets and hosting early training for Ukrainian pilots. Ukraine is also testing several domestically built interceptor drones designed to catch jet-powered Shaheds, while its F-16 pilots continue to use their cannons against the drones with the new Danish rounds.

articles.title: Russian Geran drone crashes in Moldova near homes and energy facility: Chisinau expels Russian diplomat
articles.body:
Moldova declared a Russian embassy staff member persona non grata on 23 October after a Russian Geran attack drone violated its airspace and crashed near homes and an energy facility, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said.
The incident highlights how Russia’s attacks on Ukraine are increasingly threatening neighboring Moldova, where Russian drones have repeatedly crossed the border or crashed during strikes. Moldova recorded 39 Russian drone incursions in the first eight months of 2026, compared with 17 in all of 2025, Sandu said in September.
Moldova’s Defense Ministry said its Air Operations Center detected an unauthorized drone flight at 13:59 on 23 October. The drone crossed from the direction of Ukraine’s Vinnytsia Oblast toward Frunzeuca in Moldova’s Camenca district, in the Russian-backed breakaway region of Transnistria.
The drone disappeared from monitoring screens near Pepeni in Sîngerei district at 14:10, briefly reappeared, and then disappeared again near Meșeni in Rezina district, the ministry said.
Sandu condemned the incursion, saying Russia’s war continues to put Moldovan lives at risk. She said the drone had fallen near family homes and an energy facility.
Moldovan police reported finding the crashed drone near the village of Chiștelnița in Telenești district, less than 100 meters from a home. No casualties were reported. Police cordoned off the area and sent explosives specialists to examine the wreckage.
Moldova steps up diplomatic response
Sandu said Moldova had condemned the incident and declared a Russian embassy staff member persona non grata. She did not identify the staff member or specify when they must leave the country.
The move follows repeated Russian drone incursions. In September, a Russian drone crossing Moldova’s airspace disrupted seven flights, including one involving Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, prompting temporary airspace restrictions.
Earlier in October, three Russian missiles and two drones crossed into Moldovan airspace and exploded on Moldovan territory during Russian attacks on neighboring Ukraine, prompting Chisinau to condemn the violations. Debris fell across several districts, damaging windows at an agricultural facility and sparking fires in fields. Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatîi said the country was seeking stronger air defenses to counter the growing threat.
80% of Moldovans say country is unprepared for attack as Russian drones flow into its airspace, but few back NATO membership
Moldova has limited air defense capabilities and has been working with European partners to strengthen them. Sandu has said the country’s existing equipment can mainly protect individual sites, while the government seeks broader coverage and faster warning systems. The EU has provided €120 million for Moldova to purchase a medium-range air defense system.
Moldovan authorities urged residents not to approach or touch the crashed drone or any fragments, and to call emergency services if they find suspicious objects.

articles.title: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
articles.body:
Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.
The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.
The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”
Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.
The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.
The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.
The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.
Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”
He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.
“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”
Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

articles.title: Zelensky says ceasefire, security guarantees are conditions for just peace for Ukraine
articles.body:
Zelensky says ceasefire, security guarantees are conditions for just peace for Ukraine
The head of state made the statement on Friday during an online address to the Hudson Institute in Washington, Ukrinform's correspondent reports.
Among the key conditions for a just peace, he cited a strong Ukrainian army, at least ten years of funding to maintain it, stronger air defenses, and a clear mechanism for responding to possible renewed Russian aggression.
According to Zelensky, the possibility of unblocking negotiations was discussed following a recent visit to Moscow by White House Special Envoy Steve Witkoff. He expressed hope that Ukrainian and U.S. teams would meet in Abu Dhabi in early or mid-November for talks at the technical level. Trilateral talks at the leaders' level could follow, he said.
"In my opinion, first and foremost, we need to move toward the right position. Today, that means a ceasefire. This is point number one, and I believe that only after that will we be able to begin genuine diplomacy, while the working groups can work on the plan," he said.
He stressed that Ukraine would need financial support from its partners to maintain a strong army for at least ten years. This would be necessary, among other things, to rebuild the country after large-scale Russian attacks and revive its economy.
Zelensky also noted that after the war ends, Ukraine will continue to need air defense systems and other technologies to protect itself. He identified the presence on Ukrainian territory of representatives of the European Coalition of the Willing, with U.S. support, as another element of security guarantees.
At the same time, Zelensky said there was still no clear answer to the key question: who would respond, and how, if Russia resorted to aggression again, using drones, missiles or ground forces.
"We need more than just peace. Peace must be just and lasting. And that depends on security guarantees," Zelensky said.
Other important elements of ending the war, he said, include Ukraine's reconstruction, the involvement of American and European businesses, and Ukraine's accession to the European Union.
Zelensky clarified that bilateral security guarantees with the United States and possible NATO membership are different arrangements, but both must ensure reliable protection for Ukraine.
Zelensky said earlier that he would attend the G20 summit in Florida if there were an opportunity to hold talks there with U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian dictator Vladimir Putin to reach peace agreements. However, he has not yet received an invitation to the summit.

articles.title: Ukraine troops report ongoing problems with Starlink satellite network
articles.body:
The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive.
In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians.
Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations.
Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.
The White House statement said the ceasefire was brokered by Melania Trump, and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said.
Despite the claim the ceasefire had been brokered by Melania Trump, there had already been protracted efforts to organise a humanitarian ceasefire, with claims by Ukrainian officials that it had been Russia that had rejected previous calls.
Calls for a ceasefire had been issued by Pope Leo XIV – who discussed the issue with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe. As recently as 18 October, Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, had also said he thought agreement was close without any mention of the first lady’s involvement.
Ukraine has for weeks been pushing for a civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, at times using drones to airdrop emergency food and medical supplies into town.
Lubinets told Reuters on Friday that the mission to Oleshky would involve demining roads leading into the town, delivering food and evacuating civilians. “A sufficient quantity of humanitarian aid will be delivered to meet the needs of everyone who requires it. What’s more, we are working to ensure that this is not just a one-off event, and that it is not limited to Oleshky alone,” he said.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network, despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.
The slowdown, which has affected the communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Elon Musk, the founder of Starlink, publicly criticised Zelenskyy over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with Trump and Musk denying responsibility. Asked about the Starlink slowdowns on Friday, Trump said he would speak to Musk if the restrictions remained in place.
“I’ve heard it was fixed, but if it’s not, I’ll speak to him,” he told reporters.
Ukrainian officials said throughout the day on Friday that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.
“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.
“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.
The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.
The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, has plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.
Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel, as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday.
Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement.
Among Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.
Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war. “The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.
The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.

articles.title: Ukraine Loads Up F-16 Vulcans With 50,000 Danish Rounds for Russian Drone Intercepts

Ukraine Loads Up F-16 Vulcans With 50,000 Danish Rounds for Russian Drone Intercepts
Denmark has supplied Ukraine with more than 50,000 rounds of 20mm ammunition for the cannons aboard its F-16 fighters, giving Ukrainian pilots a far cheaper way to destroy Russian drones than using scarce air-to-air missiles, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported on October 23.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian pilots are already using the ammunition during interception missions against both jet-powered and propeller-driven Russian strike UAVs.
The cannon option is particularly valuable against drones because it allows F-16s to engage relatively inexpensive targets without expending guided air-to-air missiles that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars or more and are needed for higher-priority threats.
The F-16’s primary gun is the M61A1 Vulcan, a six-barrel 20mm rotary cannon capable of firing at rates of up to 6,000 rounds per minute.
The weapon uses 20×102mm ammunition, including armor-piercing incendiary and high-explosive rounds. Its effective range against aerial targets is roughly 1,000 to 1,500 meters, requiring pilots to close much nearer to a drone than when engaging it with a missile.
That makes cannon interceptions more demanding, but also far more economical when conditions allow them.
Previously, a Ukrainian Mirage 2000-5F scored a first, shooting down a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile not with an air-to-air missile, but with bursts from its built-in 30mm cannons.

articles.title: Xi’s Military Purges Make US Deterrence More Urgent
articles.body:
China’s top military command has been almost emptied out. Of the seven members chosen for the Central Military Commission in 2022, only Xi Jinping and one general remain active. Days before Xi met U.S. President Donlald Trump in Washington last month, Beijing formally expelled Gen. Zhang Youxia, Xi’s longtime ally and former top military deputy, and Gen. Liu Zhenli, the former chief of the Joint Staff Department.
We do not know why Xi is doing this or what he intends to do next. But the purge has further strengthened his hand over the military. Reuters reported that analysts see Xi’s grip on the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) as strengthened by the removal of senior commanders and their protégés even as the upheaval weakens near-term readiness. If Xi chooses to invade Taiwan, impose a blockade, or undertake another act of military aggression in the region, more of that decision now rests with him. We do not know whether he will. That freer hand adds risk.
The scale of the purge is extraordinary. The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that 41 of the 47 officers who held three-star rank in 2022 or were promoted afterward had been purged or potentially purged. Of the 35 three-star generals and admirals Xi promoted beginning in 2020, 32 had been investigated and 29 had been purged or potentially purged. Across the PLA, roughly 52 percent of senior leadership positions have been affected.
CSIS concluded that vacant posts and less experienced officers would complicate large-scale operations against Taiwan, including a blockade or amphibious assault. But we should not assume those complications will last. Taiwan’s defense ministry has warned of “rising unpredictability” in Chinese decision-making amid the purge. With this much upheaval in Beijing and more authority concentrated in Xi’s hands, steady, credible deterrence from Washington matters even more. Beijing should have no reason to believe an invasion, blockade or other act of aggression against Taiwan could succeed.
That means three things.
First, we should not answer upheaval in Beijing by creating upheaval at the Pentagon. One of America’s greatest military advantages is our professional officer corps, whose duty is to the constitution rather than a ruling party. Yet in 2025, Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. C.Q. Brown along with five other senior generals and admirals. In April, Hegseth abruptly removed Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George with more than a year remaining in his term while American forces were fighting in the Middle East. The Pentagon gave no public reason, and Reuters noted that removing a service chief during wartime is “extremely rare.” Experienced commanders who are prepared to give presidents unwelcome advice make our military stronger.
Second, our military resources have to match our priorities. The Iran war is draining weapons that matter for deterrence in the Indo-Pacific. In September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the war had cost the Defense Department about $38 billion through August 1, with another month costing $2 billion to $3 billion depending on the intensity of fighting. More importantly, CBO found that heavy use of missile-defense interceptors will leave U.S. inventories reduced for several years and warned that the shortfall would be especially problematic in a conflict with China over Taiwan. If we are serious about the CCP as our foremost long-term strategic challenge, we should end the Iran war and rebuild depleted stockpiles, immediately.
Third, deterrence requires communication as well as strength. After air and maritime safety talks in May, U.S. and Chinese military representatives agreed that better communication could reduce miscalculations and the risk of unsafe encounters. With this much turnover at the top of the PLA, those channels matter even more.
We do not know Xi’s objectives. We know he has strengthened his own hand amid the uncertainty created by his purge of the military. Without any meaningful check on his power, Xi has a freer hand to pursue potentially more aggressive military decisions, adding risk to our relationship with the CCP.
Our job is not to guess Xi’s next move. It is to make sure Washington remains steady, with experienced military leadership, the weapons and forces needed to deter aggression, strong alliances, and reliable communication to keep a crisis from becoming a war.
