Missile attack on Russia’s Oryol region may have targeted Proton, a factory producing military electronics, Ukrainian monitors say

Oryol Governor Andrey Klychkov said Ukrainian forces had launched a missile attack on a civilian facility — a business in Oryol’s Sovetsky district. Details on casualties and the extent of the damage remain unclear.

articles.title: France and the United Kingdom held joint nuclear exercises for the first time
articles.body:
France and the United Kingdom held joint nuclear exercises for the first time
Kyiv • UNN
France and the United Kingdom held joint nuclear exercises for the first time, without using weapons. The drills strengthened coordination in the face of the threat posed by russia.
France and the United Kingdom, Europe’s two nuclear powers, participated for the first time in joint exercises involving France’s strategic air forces and its airborne nuclear component. French Minister of the Armed Forces Catherine Vautrin said this on X on October 23, UNN reports.
For the first time, British Air Force "Typhoon" fighter jets joined French "Rafale" fighters in exercises organized by the strategic air forces’ airborne nuclear component. This is a decisive milestone in French defense cooperation, demonstrating the coordination and commitment of the two European nuclear powers to European security and credible deterrence
As Le Monde notes, during the "Rummy" exercises, British Typhoon fighter jets, which took part for the first time on Tuesday evening in exercises involving the French airborne nuclear component, escorted Rafale fighters from Saint-Dizier over the Mediterranean to simulate a nuclear strike. No nuclear weapons were used. The exercises were intended to strengthen coordination and operational interoperability between the armed forces of the two countries. "The existence of independent nuclear forces does not preclude coordination," said French Minister of the Armed Forces Catherine Vautrin.
These exercises reportedly embody the rapprochement initiated by the Northwood Declaration in July 2025. Paris and London decided to strengthen coordination between their nuclear forces in the face of the Russian threat, amid the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine wants partners’ Patriot interceptors now. Europe can hand them over only with US approval, Ukraine’s president says
articles.body:
Ukraine's defense minister raised the urgent need for Patriot interceptors with Sweden on 22 October, the Defense Ministry reported. The same day, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned of more Russian ballistic strikes and blamed US supply cuts.
Patriots are Ukraine's main defense against Russian ballistic missiles, and their deliveries keep shrinking. Figures Zelenskyy released in August showed Patriot interceptor deliveries falling from 675 in 2023 to 364 in 2025, with 264 projected for 2026. Europe holds enough PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors for Ukraine's minimum winter needs, Zelenskyy told journalists on 16 October, but he did not yet know how many Europe would hand over, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
Partners' stocks now, Ukraine's missiles later
Russia fired 21 ballistic missiles at Kyiv overnight on 22 October, Zelenskyy said. Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told his Swedish counterpart, Pål Jonson, that Ukraine must counter ballistic threats as fast as possible, in particular with Patriot interceptors.
1,000 Patriot missiles arrive too late for this winter, so Ukraine asked the Ramstein arms coalition to open its warehouses
The ministry's readout says Ukraine has Patriot missiles under contract. It also says Kyiv asks partners to transfer interceptors from their stocks in exchange for future deliveries allocated to Ukraine.
Khmara made the same request at the Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting on 8 September. He said then that Ukraine was contracting about 1,000 Patriot missiles with partners' help and an EU loan, but they would arrive only in the coming years, LB reported. He asked allies for missiles from their stocks now, in exchange for future upgraded missiles under Ukraine's contracts.
"Only when the American side approves it"
Zelenskyy spoke to journalists before meeting Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, Ukrinform reported. He said the Americans had reduced supplies and Russia would step up ballistic attacks.
"Europeans can provide the missiles only when the American side approves it," Zelenskyy said.
He said the US had sent most of its interceptors to the Middle East.
On 19 October, Zelenskyy told US senators that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was not signing off on Patriot deliveries allies had already paid for. Axios obtained the call transcript from Ukrainian officials. A US government official told the Kyiv Independent that Ukrainian officials' claims that Hegseth was holding up the missiles were "not true."
Washington says nothing has changed. "We have our own needs, too," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on 20 October, but there is "nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine." Hegseth told reporters in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, that the US had not changed its posture toward Ukraine, "but certainly with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well."

articles.title: BBC profiles Russian exile who says his surveillance network tracked General Staff officer Fanil Sarvarov before his assassination in Moscow
articles.body:
BBC profiles Russian exile who says his surveillance network tracked General Staff officer Fanil Sarvarov before his assassination in Moscow
In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Russian Armed Forces General Staff’s Operational Training Directorate, was killed in a car bombing in Moscow. A Russian man who left the country in 2022 and now coordinates a network of volunteers tracking Russian military personnel says he helped prepare the killing. His role is detailed in the BBC documentary ”Traitors, Patriots, Spies: Shadowmen Helping Ukraine Inside Russia.”
The film introduces the man as Foma. His face is hidden — viewers see only his silhouette and hear his voice. The filmmakers say that in early 2022, Foma warned Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, about Russia’s planned invasion. He then fled Russia, and the Ukrainians helped him settle in Warsaw. He now lives in Poland.
Foma says he coordinates a network of about 30 people operating in Russia, Ukraine, and several European countries. He says he also maintains ties with sources in Russia’s intelligence services. According to the film, years of working among Russia’s elite gave him a unique network of contacts and a steady flow of inside information.
Foma says his network gathers intelligence on where storage depots and headquarters are located, where units are stationed, where generals live, where officers working at those headquarters live, where strategic bomber pilots who attack Ukraine live, and who gives the orders.
The HUR confirmed that it had worked with Foma, the investigative outlet iStories reported.
One scene shows Foma training volunteers to conduct surveillance in Moscow. He tells them not to bring a phone. He also warns that if they are caught, they face terrorism charges and 25 years in prison.
In the film, Foma says he wants Russian soldiers and officers who order the shooting of prisoners and the rape and murder of civilians to think long and hard before giving such orders, to be scared, and to stop. Those who turn into animals and those who kill people, he says, need to be punished.
The next segment covers the December 2024 killing of General Igor Kirillov, head of Russia’s Radiation, Chemical, and Biological Protection Troops. Foma told the BBC that he was not involved in that killing but confirmed that his network passes information about Russian military personnel to Ukraine. He insists the people his volunteers follow are war criminals.
Sarvarov was killed a year after Kirillov. When the BBC filmmaker asked Foma about Sarvarov’s killing, he said: “Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule.” Foma stresses, however, that his group does not take part in the killings themselves.
A man using the same pseudonym has appeared as a military expert on The Breakfast Show’s morning broadcasts since mid-September. On September 19, after regular military expert Yuri Fyodorov left the channel, The Breakfast Show founder Alexander Plyushchev wrote that the morning show would have a new military commentator: Foma, co-founder of the Telegram channel Volya, who appears on camera with his face hidden.
The BBC film does not explicitly link Foma to Volya. But Agentstvo journalists noticed that several shots show him sitting in front of a computer monitor displaying Volya’s donation page on Patreon.
Plyushchev told Agentstvo that he contacted Foma while looking for a replacement for Fyodorov. “All I knew about Foma was that he did analysis on Georgian political scientist Gela Vasadze’s show and ran the Telegram channel Volya… We understood the risks of having an anonymous commentator, but we decided to try it, since he was providing commentary rather than serving as a source. Foma is now one of four military commentators who regularly work with The Breakfast Show,” Plyushchev said. Agentstvo received no response from Foma, who had been sent an editor’s contact information.

articles.title: Are Israel's drones signalling a new escalation with Hezbollah?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Are Israel's drones over Beirut signalling a coming escalation with Hezbollah?
Reports of increased Israeli drone activity over Beirut and its southern suburbs have raised questions about whether Israel is preparing for a new escalation against Hezbollah.
But while the flights have become more conspicuous in recent days, analysts told The New Arab that their presence alone does not establish that a wider offensive is imminent.
A report by local Lebanese news outlet Lebanon Files said Israeli reconnaissance flights had "returned" to Beirut and Mount Lebanon’s airspace. However, there is no publicly available evidence establishing that the flights had stopped before recently becoming more noticeable.
Israeli drones have continued to be reported over Beirut and its southern suburbs in recent months, including in reports published in September and footage circulated this week.
The question, therefore, is not simply whether the drones are present, but whether there has been a meaningful change in the frequency, duration or scope of their operations.
Surveillance and pressure on Hezbollah
Elijah J. Magnier, a veteran war correspondent and political analyst, told The New Arab that the activity should be taken seriously, while cautioning against treating visible drone flights as evidence of an imminent attack.
"Local reporting today documented a drone flying at low altitude over the southern suburbs. That establishes a visible presence; it does not, by itself, establish a sustained increase in surveillance or an imminent offensive," he said in comments to The New Arab on 21 October.
Magnier said Israeli drone flights could serve several purposes at once, including gathering intelligence, updating potential targets, monitoring movements and exerting psychological pressure on residents. A conspicuous presence over the capital can also serve as a reminder of Israel’s ability to strike south of Beirut.
If Israel were preparing another operation, surveillance could help it locate commanders, monitor weapons movements and identify suspected military infrastructure. But Magnier stressed that these remained possible objectives rather than evidence of a decision to launch an attack.
"Nor does identifying a target establish that a political decision to strike has been taken," he said. Without comparative flight data or intelligence about operational orders, he added, it was difficult to distinguish routine surveillance from preparations for a particular attack.
Nasser Khdour, an analyst at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), also said Israeli drone activity over Beirut was not new.
"Israel has continued gathering intelligence and identifying possible targets in preparation for another round of fighting," he told The New Arab.
Khdour suggested the more conspicuous drone presence was likely intended to increase pressure on Hezbollah and the Lebanese government during negotiations between Lebanon and Israel, with the Iran-backed militant group’s disarmament remaining a central point of disagreement.
The latest round of US-mediated military talks between Lebanese and Israeli delegations began in Tampa, Florida, on 20 October. The talks came amid continued Israeli attacks and demolitions in southern Lebanon, as well as renewed threats by Israeli officials against Hezbollah.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has warned Hezbollah against joining Iran in an attack on Israel, threatening a "powerful response" against Beirut’s southern suburbs, which would include a forced evacuation of the whole area. He has also threatened to expand the invasion towards Nabatieh and the Litani River in the south.
Hezbollah has refused to disarm as long as Israeli forces remain in Lebanon.
Could tensions with Iran draw Hezbollah into a wider war?
The risk of escalation also extends beyond Lebanon. With Israel’s general election scheduled for 27 October, renewed threats involving Iran have added another layer of uncertainty to the regional picture.
Magnier said electoral considerations were relevant to the analysis, but cautioned against presenting speculation about a war being launched for political reasons as an established plan. He said there was no publicly established evidence that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intended to initiate a war to disrupt an election he expected to lose.
A renewed confrontation between Israel and Iran could, however, create a separate decision point for Hezbollah. Magnier said the group’s involvement would become a more serious possibility in such a scenario, but would remain a choice rather than an automatic consequence.
He also cautioned against assuming that Hezbollah’s weakened deterrence meant it had no remaining military capabilities. The group could seek to preserve its personnel and organisational structure while continuing to impose costs on Israel over time, rather than responding to every attack with a major escalation.
That calculation could change, he added, if civilian casualties mounted, senior leaders were targeted or Israel expanded its ground operations.
The conflict between Hezbollah and Israel began in October 2023 and was dramatically escalated by Israel into a full-scale war in September 2024. Fighting resumed on 2 March this year, alongside the US-Israeli war on Iran. Much of Hezbollah’s senior command structure has been eliminated over the past three years, and thousands of its fighters are believed to have been killed.
The drone flights therefore need to be viewed alongside the wider military and political context, rather than in isolation. Israel’s continued strikes, its threats against Beirut’s southern suburbs and the unresolved dispute over Hezbollah’s weapons all contribute to an already volatile situation.
For Magnier, the distinction remains between sustained pressure and a decision to launch a broader campaign. The visible presence of drones demonstrates Israel’s ability to monitor and threaten Hezbollah and its stronghold in Beirut's southern suburbs, but it does not reveal what Israeli leaders intend to do next.
"The drone flights show exposure and pressure. They do not yet tell us whether the next step will be surveillance, a targeted strike or a wider campaign," he said.

articles.title: Witkoff Meets Putin: the Upshot?
articles.body:
Following the meeting between Vladimir Putin and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg, talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US are set to resume. However, Witkoff describing Putin as a “humanitarian” during the meeting has drawn criticism even from US Republicans. The press looks at who stands to benefit from Trump’s attempts at mediation.
Embarrassing and incompetent
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Der Standard (Austria) takes issue with the American special envoy’s fawning praise of Putin:
“No one has ever called him that before. That’s a first. How will Vladimir Putin react to Donald Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, calling him a ‘humanitarian’? Witkoff is a property developer and Trump’s golfing buddy, and together with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, he keeps meeting up with Russian envoys and Putin himself in a bid to end the war in Ukraine. Two wheeler-dealers with no clue about foreign policy who have achieved absolutely nothing so far.”
Kremlin relying on attrition
The US’s haste risks rewarding Russia for its patient strategy, La Stampa (Italy) warns:
“Putin can already derive political advantages from the negotiations, without having to halt the war. Winter will put this strategy to the test. Moscow will seek to weaken Ukraine while the Ukrainians try to protect their cities and hold the front line. In the meantime, acts of sabotage, cyber-attacks and disinformation aim to undermine European unity and the consensus on aid to Ukraine. Putin is banking on wearing down Ukrainian resistance and the West’s willingness to support Ukraine.”
US Reportedly Plans to ‘Offer’ Ukraine EU Membership for Dropping NATO Bid
Russia’s victory by no means certain
Ukraine is not about to throw in the towel, says Aamulehti (Finland):
“Even if the United States were to side fully with Russia, the war in Ukraine would not end. The massacre in Bucha has shown what happens to Ukrainians at the hands of the Russians, which is why Ukraine will not give up the fight. How long would the war last, and how would it end? Recent history answers that question. France waged war in Indochina for eight years. The US fought the Vietnam War in that region for 20 years, ten of which with its own troops. The Soviet Union waged war in Afghanistan for ten years, and the US for twenty. Each of these wars ended in defeat for the major power waging the war.”
Diabolical old men
Writing on Facebook, author Carina Cockrell-Ferre (Russia) discusses the possibility of a Russian attack on Europe:
“The greatest danger facing Europe is that Putin could form a full alliance with Trump, who then assures him that he will not honour the terms of Article 5 of the Nato Treaty. ... This could indeed lead to a Russian attack on Europe. This is the common ground over which these two diabolical old men have joined forces. ... While Europe may be able to block a bad deal for Ukraine, it is powerless to push through a good one. All it can do is delay a Russian attack on Europe by supporting Ukraine and its armed forces.”
Kremlin giving no sign of being ready to negotiate
Future meetings are also unlikely to yield any tangible results, The Spectator observes (Germany):
“There has been nothing to suggest yet that the Russian president is genuinely ready to make a deal or concede on his war aims. ... Facing the prospect of brutal midterm results for the Republicans in two weeks’ time, Trump is desperate for a win with Russia. Putin can sense this and appears to be using this to play for time ahead of a winter in which he hopes to make substantial progress on subjugating Ukraine. Not for the first time, it is Zelensky who is being forced to jump through hoops and show willing in the hope that doing so will save his country from a stitch-up by an enemy and supposed ally.”
Encouraged to escalate
The US’s policies of recent weeks are having repercussions across the world, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (Germany) points out:
“Putin and his inner circle are convinced that in the war against Ukraine and their struggle against the West as a whole, they will firstly have the greater staying power, and secondly be able to play the Americans and Europeans off against one another. Everything the American leadership has done in recent weeks confirms this belief. Consequently, the prospect of a ceasefire, not to mention peace in Ukraine, has become even more remote. Instead, the Kremlin is likely to feel emboldened to escalate the conflict even further. ‘Restoring justice of Russians’ takes place above all on the battlefield, Putin’s foreign minister has said.”
Moscow can take its time
Unlike Trump, Putin is not in a hurry, notes Corriere della Sera (Italy):
“For five years now, Vladimir Putin seems to have been applying the old Russian proverb ‘The slower you go, the further you’ll get’ to a war that he originally thought would last no more than two weeks. … So Putin is biding his time, waiting to see how events unfold and what happens with the elections in the US and Europe – and taking whatever he can get without making any concessions. He has the chance to achieve in Washington what he is unable to achieve on the front line; but he also knows that this window of opportunity could be closed again by a single social media post in the middle of the night. ... What the Russian president needs to work out now is whether the path available to Trump will be long enough.”
Trump wanted Putin to win all along
The US President’s supposedly new stance on the war in Ukraine is not really new at all, argues Dagens Nyheter (Sweden):
“Some interpret this as the US changing sides with regard to Ukraine, and it’s easy to understand why Zelensky feels betrayed. Yet this development is nothing new. The difference is that Trump is no longer making a secret of what he has wanted all along: for Russia and his friend Vladimir Putin to win the war. ... Trump’s eagerness to help Putin now is particularly good news for the Kremlin. Russia is in a bad way, both on the front line and at home, where all its oil depots are burning. So it’s good that it has an ally in the White House.”
What is going on in his mind?
Experts will continue to puzzle over the US president’s policy on Ukraine, says Ilta-Sanomat (Finland):
“A clear intention can certainly be discerned behind Trump’s confused remarks on Ukraine and Russia. He wants to take credit for bringing about peace. But does anyone still believe he could actually achieve such a thing? After all this, can anyone still trust Trump’s word when it comes, for example, to security guarantees for Ukraine, which are a key safeguard for peace? ... When the war in Ukraine eventually ends and Trump is no longer president, a lot will be written about current events. Perhaps the most important question then will be: what on earth was going through Trump’s mind? It won’t make for pleasant reading.”

articles.title: Austria expels Russian Embassy and OSCE diplomats over suspected spying. Vienna remains a Russian spy hub
articles.body:
Austria has ordered four Russian diplomats to leave the country over suspected espionage, declaring them persona non grata following findings by Austrian security authorities, Austrian media outlet Heute reported on 23 October.
The expulsions come as European countries step up efforts to counter suspected Russian intelligence operations amid Moscow’s war against Ukraine. Three of the diplomats worked at the Russian Embassy in Vienna, while the fourth served in Russia’s delegation to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which is headquartered in Vienna.
Austria’s Foreign Ministry said the four had engaged in “activities incompatible with their diplomatic status,” a term usually used for spying, Reuters reported. It did not disclose details of the alleged activities or the intelligence findings behind the decision.
The three embassy diplomats were declared persona non grata under Article 9 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. The fourth, who worked on military security and arms control at Russia’s OSCE delegation, was also ordered to leave Austria.
Vienna remains a hub for Russian intelligence
The latest expulsions bring the number of Russian diplomats Austria has expelled since 2020 to 18, according to Reuters. In May 2026, Austria expelled three Russian Embassy employees suspected of using antennas on diplomatic buildings to intercept satellite internet data transmitted by international organizations based in Vienna.
Vienna’s concentration of international organizations, including the OSCE and United Nations agencies, has made it a key location for intelligence activity. A 2024 report by The Wall Street Journal, described Vienna as a major Russian spy hub for operations targeting Western countries, including surveillance of arms supplies to Ukraine.
Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister Dmitry Lyubinsky said Moscow’s response to the expulsions was unavoidable, according to Russian state news agency TASS, AP reported.

articles.title: MEP Dan Barna: Bulgaria must clearly name Russia’s aggression in the Black Sea
articles.body:
Author
Irina Nedeva
Interview
MEP Dan Barna: Bulgaria must clearly name Russia’s aggression in the Black Sea
The EU will accelerate the creation of a European Martime Security Center
Friday 23 October 2026 14:58
Friday, 23 October 2026, 14:58
MEP Dan Barna in Radio Studio 2 at the European Parliament in Strasbourg
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
The Black Sea is no longer merely a trade corridor. It has become a test of European security. In a resolution adopted on Thursday, the European Parliament expresses solidarity with Bulgaria and Romania over the escalation of Russian attacks on commercial shipping, while also voicing serious concern about “the unclear and ambiguous response of the Bulgarian authorities to the escalating Russian threat in the Black Sea”.
How does the Romanian government view the response of the Bulgarian government led by Rumen Radev to Russian threats in the region? And how can Europe protect shipping in the Black Sea without waiting for the next attack? Is a common European response possible when national governments are sending different signals to Moscow?
In Strasbourg, BNR's Irina Nedeva spoke to Romanian MEP Dan Barna, a former deputy prime minister of Romania and one of the driving forces behind the resolution on behalf of the Renew Europe group. Their conversation addressed the need for a European Maritime Security Centre, the protection of commercial vessels, and the role of Bulgaria and Romania in defending NATO’s eastern flank.
But there is also a broader question facing the EU: can Europe finance its defence, maintain support for poorer regions and avoid new political crises within the Union at the same time?
You are calling for a European maritime security centre in the Black Sea. What exactly should this centre do, who will fund it, and when could it become operational? Is there not a risk of creating yet another institution while ships continue to come under attack?
“This resolution is also a very swift response by the European Parliament. I am pleased that, on the very day it was debated in the European Parliament, NATO also brought the Black Sea into focus. The resolution has two main objectives. The first is to recognise the need to designate the Black Sea as a priority area on the eastern flank. The second, as you rightly pointed out, concerns the establishment and funding of a European Maritime Security Centre.
The purpose of this structure, this centre, is to enhance the capacity to respond rapidly to attacks and security threats in the Black Sea. War is no longer just a war of tanks and aircraft. It is a drone war, and in this kind of warfare, time is of the essence. That is precisely why this centre must strengthen NATO’s and the eastern flank’s ability to respond appropriately and in a timely manner. What we are talking about is building technical infrastructure capable of addressing the realities of Russian aggression.”
Romania and Bulgaria are directly exposed to these risks, but the Black Sea is also an external border of both the EU and NATO. What concrete action do you expect from European partners: military surveillance, air defence, escorts for commercial vessels or some other form of presence?
“Everything you have mentioned is important. I mean the ability to identify risks and drones in a given area as quickly as possible. It is also important to have the capacity to scramble aircraft to destroy these drones. In this context, I would like to commend the Romanian and Spanish pilots who have managed to shoot down several drones in recent days. In the near future, we may also have to address the need to protect commercial vessels and provide them with escorts if Russian drones continue to operate aggressively in the region.”
Irina Nedeva and MEP Dan Barna in Radio Studio 2 at the European Parliament in Strasbourg
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova, BNR
Romania has clearly identified the aggressor. For the first time, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has mentioned Russia as being logically linked to the attacks, while adding that there is no evidence confirming their origin. From Romania’s perspective, how do you view the Bulgarian government’s response?
“We must be absolutely clear, and this resolution emphasises the point: Russia is the aggressor and is carrying out attacks against NATO’s eastern flank, including against Romania and Bulgaria. The text of the resolution, which we agreed on only yesterday, also refers to the perception that Bulgaria’s position is unclear and insufficiently categorical. I am optimistic that the Bulgarian government, too, will demonstrate solidarity and determination by acknowledging that these attacks originate from Russia and that a coordinated response is needed.This is one of the main problems associated with these attacks.
Commercial shipping is crucial not only for the countries of the Black Sea region. Food and essential goods are transported by sea to Africa, Asia and many other countries that depend, for example, on Ukrainian grain. The key question is how to protect this commercial traffic. If the Black Sea were to become a situation resembling that in the Strait of Hormuz, brought about by the war with Iran, this would put enormous pressure on the gas and hydrocarbon markets. Agricultural products could also be seriously affected.”
You advocate both stronger European defence and continued support for cohesion policy and agricultural subsidies. When resources are limited, who should make the compromise? Can countries such as Romania and Bulgaria expect more funding for security without losing support for their regions?
“Europe is under intense pressure from anti-European, sovereigntist and extremist movements. Weakening cohesion policy is precisely the argument used by sovereigntist and pro-Russian forces. They are trying to convince European citizens that Europe no longer works. That is why cohesion policy acts as a bond holding European values and European solidarity together. For this very reason, I believe it is important, for Romania, Bulgaria and Europe as a whole, that cohesion policy remains in place and continues to be strong.”
Romania is emerging from nearly six months of political deadlock with a minority government. Is this a temporary arrangement, or are there grounds to expect stability?
“The outlook is relatively optimistic in terms of stability, though not necessarily in terms of the quality of governance. Romania is currently facing a similar situation within its government, and I am sure Bulgaria has been through many such situations as well. We are talking about parliaments divided into three roughly equal blocs, none of which is willing to work openly with the other two. Yesterday, parliament approved a new government. So we now have a new cabinet. That is good news for the country’s stability.”
You have criticised the lack of tangible progress on enlargement. Is the EU ready to admit Moldova and other candidate countries before reforming its own decision-making processes? And how would you prevent a scenario in which new members bring unresolved rule-of-law problems into the Union?
“I must express my deep respect for Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, because she has managed to turn enlargement policy into a consistent and effective one. Two weeks ago in Strasbourg, she announced the new enlargement strategy, under which the four most successful and best-prepared countries were given roadmaps. This is a significant step forward. I am referring to Montenegro, Moldova, Albania and Ukraine. They are receiving roadmaps that set out a clear path forward, with specific conditions and reforms to be completed. These have been presented to their governments. This represents considerable progress because, at the very least, there is now a clear prospect.
I fully agree that Europe needs reforms, including to its voting system and the way its decision-making mechanisms operate. These reforms must prevent a repeat of what happened with Hungary and Viktor Orbán, when Russia managed to block one link in the chain and bring the entire mechanism to a standstill. To avoid this negative experience and this vicious practice, it is clear that Europe must move towards qualified majority voting instead of the current requirement for unanimity.
As regards enlargement, one approach under the new strategy is to retain unanimity only for the first and final stages of the process, while applying qualified majority voting to the intermediate stages. We are working in this direction, too. I am also a member of the European Parliament–Moldova Parliamentary Association Committee. We are working to help the country carry out the necessary reforms.”
Bulgaria is already in the eurozone. When will we stop having to convert our currencies as two neighbouring countries?
“For us Romanians, and for me personally, this is a painful issue. I would like to congratulate Bulgarian citizens, politicians and society on managing to adopt the euro, despite changing seven governments in roughly two years. The fact that all these governments managed to maintain the course and meet the convergence criteria, enabling Bulgaria to join the eurozone at the beginning of this year, is a source of pride.
I know that Romania and Bulgaria have a healthy sense of neighbourly competition on various issues. I know many people on both sides who take pride in their country’s achievements, in the areas where Romania excels and those where Bulgaria performs well. But when it comes to the euro, you have done better than we have. You have my admiration.”
Irina Nedeva’s full interview with MEP Dan Barna was aired on the 12+3 programme on BNR's Horizon channel.

articles.title: Iran slams IAEA for silence towards attacks on its sites
articles.body:
The statement criticized the IAEA for applying double standards and discriminatory approaches, emphasizing that the Statute is a binding legal document and must not be used as a political instrument to serve the interests of certain powerful states.
Iran also condemned the unacceptable silence of the Agency’s governing bodies regarding the military attacks by the US and the Zionist regime on its peaceful nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026. Furthermore, it highlighted the IAEA's failure to address the lack of comprehensive safeguards on the Zionist regime’s nuclear activities.
The Islamic Republic also called for the full, balanced, and non-discriminatory implementation of the IAEA Statute for all member states, particularly regarding technical cooperation and access to peaceful nuclear energy.
The full text of statement by the Iranian permanent mission in Vienna is as follows:
Permanent Mission of the Islamic Republic of Iran  
  
to the United Nations and other International Organizations in Vienna 
 
PRESS RELEASE  
   
On the Anniversary of the Approval of the IAEA Statute   
   
23 October 2026  
   
Seventy years after the adoption of the Statute of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) 
 
on 23 October 1956, a fundamental assessment is required as to the level and extent of the 
 
adherence to the principles and objectives of the Agency’s founding document. 
This anniversary must therefore be more than an occasion for commemoration; it must serve as 
 
a moment of critical reflection, institutional accountability and a renewed commitment to the full, 
 
impartial and non-discriminatory implementation of the Statute. 
The Statute: A Binding Mandate, Not a Political Instrument
The continued relevance of the IAEA Statute lies in the objective it establishes and the principles 
 
it enshrines. It implementation over the past seven decades has produced achievements in 
 
important areas. However, the failure to implement it fully, consistently, effectively and without 
 
discrimination, under all circumstances and with respect to all Member States, has caused the 
 
Agency to drift away from its core objective and priorities, undermine the principles governing its 
 
conduct, compromise its professionalism, and tarnish its authority and credibility. 
The undeniable fact is that the Statute is the Agency’s constitution, not a document to be invoked 
 
selectively or interpreted according to the interests of powerful States or a group of States. 
Beyond Safeguards: Upholding the IAEA’s Full Statutory Mandate
Article II establishes the Agency’s fundamental objective: to accelerate and enlarge the 
 
contribution of atomic energy to peace, health and prosperity throughout the world. Article III.A.1 
 
requires the Agency to encourage and assist research, development and the practical application 
 
of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. Article III.B.3 further requires the Agency to allocate its 
 
resources efficiently to achieve the greatest possible general benefit, with due regard to the special 
 
needs of developing countries. 
While safeguards are part of the IAEA’s mandate, the Agency is not merely a “watchdog” 
 
organization, as some Member States, in contravention of the Statute, seek to portray it. Such a 
 
narrow and politically motivated characterization distorts the Agency’s mandate and shifts its 
 
priorities away from its broader statutory objective that is the promotion of peaceful nuclear 
 
applications and international scientific and technical cooperation. Verification must not eclipse 
 
peaceful nuclear cooperation, development and the legitimate rights of Member States. An Agency 
 
that concentrates on scrutiny while failing to advance its key statutory responsibilities cannot claim to be fulfilling its mandate in a balanced manner.
Sovereign Equality Cannot Coexist with Double Standards
Article IV.C expressly establishes that the Agency is based on the sovereign equality of all its 
 
members and requires them to fulfil their statutory obligations in good faith. Article III.C prohibits 
 
the Agency from making assistance subject to any political, economic, military or other conditions 
 
incompatible with the Statute. Article III.B.1 requires the Agency to conduct its activities in 
 
accordance with the purposes and principles of the United Nations, while Article III.D requires 
 
due observance of the sovereign rights of States. 
These provisions are neither optional nor subordinate to geopolitical calculations. Sovereign 
 
equality requires that every State be treated fairly and without discrimination under the legal 
 
instruments applicable to it, free from double standards, selective interpretation and politically 
 
motivated action. 
A clear example is the continuing disparity between the scrutiny applied to Iran and the absence 
 
of comprehensive safeguards covering all nuclear activities of the Israeli regime, which remains 
 
outside the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. This disparity raises 
 
fundamental questions about the credibility and consistency of the international nuclear non-
 
proliferation norms. A credible, comprehensive and non-discriminatory approach to nuclear 
 
verification throughout the Middle East is a legitimate demand and a longstanding objective of 
 
regional countries that are parties to the NPT. Regional security cannot be built on selective 
 
scrutiny and unequal expectations. 
Peaceful Nuclear Cooperation: A Right, Not a Political Privilege
Peaceful nuclear cooperation must not be subject to political pressure. Article III.C of the Statute 
 
is clear: assistance must not be subjected to conditions incompatible with the Agency’s legal 
 
mandate. Political pressure and geopolitical rivalries must not obstruct legitimate scientific 
 
cooperation or turn access to peaceful nuclear technology into a privilege reserved for selected 
 
countries. The Agency is expected to defend the integrity of its technical cooperation mandate 
 
and ensure that its programs serve the development needs of all Member States fairly and without 
 
discrimination. 
Attacks on Nuclear Facilities and Unacceptable Institutional Silence
Attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities demand strong and unequivocal condemnation. The 
 
military attacks by the U.S. and the Israeli regime against Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026 constituted serious and material breaches of peremptory norm of international law on the 
 
prohibition of aggression.  They presented a grave challenge to nuclear safety, nuclear security, 
 
peaceful uses of nuclear energy, the credibility of the IAEA and its safeguards system.  
The Agency’s General Conference and Board of governors has repeatedly adopted resolutions 
 
expressly stating that armed attacks on, or threats against, nuclear facilities devoted to peaceful 
 
purposes violate the principles of the UN Charter, international law and the Agency’s Statute. 
 
Nevertheless, the Agency’s governing bodies and Secretariat failed to issue even a simple statement to condemn clear acts of aggression against Iran’s nuclear facilities – unprecedented in the Agency’s history. This failure represents a serious institutional shortcoming and raises troubling questions about the consistent application of the principles the Agency is mandated to uphold. 
The Agency cannot credibly defend the integrity of safeguards while treating attacks against 
 
facilities subject to those safeguards as a secondary concern. The Agency must therefore 
 
unequivocally reaffirm that attacks against peaceful nuclear installations are unlawful and 
 
unacceptable and must not be tolerated under any pretext.
Safeguarding the IAEA’s Independence, Integrity and Confidentiality Principle
Independence, confidentiality and professional integrity must be protected. Article VII.F of the 
 
Statute prohibits the Director General and Agency staff from seeking or receiving instructions 
 
from external sources. It also requires the protection of confidential information acquired in the 
 
course of their official duties and obliges Member States to respect the international character of 
 
their responsibilities and refrain from seeking to influence them improperly. 
These are concrete institutional safeguards, not ceremonial principles. Reports, assessments and 
 
decisions must be based on verifiable evidence, sound technical analysis and applicable legal 
 
obligations—not political demands, unsupported allegations or selective approaches. Any breach 
 
of confidentiality or attempt to instrumentalise safeguards information undermines cooperation, 
 
erodes trust and may compromise the safety and security of nuclear activities. The Agency must 
 
address credible concerns, protect sensitive information and ensure accountability. 
Restoring the IAEA’s Credibility: From Selective Implementation to Full Compliance
Cooperation must be matched by institutional responsibility. Iran recognises the importance of 
 
credible safeguards and professional verification and remains committed to engagement within 
 
the framework of its applicable legal obligations and its inherent and sovereign rights and interests. 
However, cooperation requires good faith, mutual respect, professional integrity and the 
 
consistent implementation of agreed legal commitments.  
On this anniversary, Iran calls upon Agency, particularly the Board of Governors and the Director 
 
General to end double standards, resist politicisation, protect confidential information, condemn 
 
attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities, and restore the full and balanced implementation of the 
 
Agency’s statutory mandate. Iran also calls for an effective and non-discriminatory technical 
 
cooperation policy that enables all Member States, particularly developing countries, to benefit 
 
from nuclear science and technology. 
The Agency’s credibility cannot rest solely on its authority to inspect. It depends equally on its 
 
adherence to the law, its impartiality, its independence and its willingness to uphold the legitimate 
 
rights of all its members. 
The Statute must be implemented as a whole, equally and in good faith—not selectively, not 
 
conditionally and not according to political convenience. The Agency owes this obligation to every 
 
Member State. On the seventieth anniversary of the Statute’s adoption, the Agency is expected to 
 
honour letter, spirit, object and purpose of the Statute through concrete action, not merely words, 
 
and to uphold its principles without political selectivity, discrimination or exception. 
MNA
Seventy years after the adoption of its Statute, the IAEA’s credibility rests on upholding its Statute 
 
in full, serving all Member States equally, and demonstrating that international law and statutory 
 
principles cannot be sacrificed to political convenience.

articles.title: Belarus Still Hosts Russian Drone Relays, Ukraine’s Border Service Says
articles.body:
Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service (DPSU) said Belarus has continued to allow Russian drones to use relay stations on its territory on Friday, Oct. 23.
DPSU spokesperson Andrii Demchenko, speaking in a televised interview, added that the border agency has not recorded Russian troops being moved into Belarus or Belarusian forces being pulled toward the Ukrainian border.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Demchenko said the threat from Belarus remains, but that border guards have no preliminary information pointing to preparations for an attack near the border, as reported by state media Ukrinform.
He said Russia is not sending additional infantry groups or units to Belarus.
According to Demchenko, Belarus is instead supporting Russia through relays that help guide Russian aerial weapons launched at Ukraine via Belarusian territory. He said he believes Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko wants to avoid committing Belarusian units to the war because they would suffer losses.
On June 19, President Volodymyr Zelensky gave Lukashenko a week to dismantle relays near the border, and said on June 24 that they had stopped working two days prior. Zelensky said it was unclear whether the equipment had been dismantled.
In September, Demchenko said border guards had detected the relays being activated again, amplifying signals for Russia’s Shahed and Gerbera drones heading toward western Ukraine’s Rivne, Volyn and Lviv regions.
Witkoff Meets Putin: the Upshot?
He linked the relays to the Sept. 13 drone attack near the Yahodyn crossing with Poland. Russian independent outlet Meduza said that drones struck a gas station near the crossing and a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw line.
Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said on Sept. 23, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, that she considers a new Russian attack from Belarusian territory a real possibility.
“If Russia at some point again wants to attack Ukraine in any way from the northern border, then Lukashenko will be very happy to provide territory, logistics, and Belarusian infrastructure to help [Russian leader Vladimir] Putin achieve his goals and intentions,” she said.
The Associated Press reported in July that Lukashenko has repeatedly said he has no plans to send troops into the war unless Belarus is attacked.

articles.title: European, Middle East ministers urge US-Iran diplomacy, not new attacks
articles.body:
European, Middle East ministers urge US-Iran diplomacy, not new attacks
An escalation would ‘create nothing but losers’, French foreign minister says as US official warns of possible strike.
Foreign ministers from eight countries are cautioning the United States against further attacks on Iran after meeting in Turkiye to discuss the Strait of Hormuz and other regional developments.
Ministers from the United Kingdom, France and Germany, known as the E3, convened with counterparts from the R4 group of Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt on Friday, along with Italy.
Speaking after the meeting in Istanbul, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that none of the countries participating in the meeting approved of another military intervention or attack on Iran.
Such a move would only exacerbate tensions and further expand the conflict, he said, adding that diplomacy and dialogue were the only way to end the war.
A further escalation between Iran and the US “would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told reporters.
“And so the first thing this group of eight countries … will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region,” he added.
Italy’s Antonio Tajani said the aim was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he said, noting that “we must promote dialogue” in order to reopen Hormuz.
The warnings came as the US Ambassador to Turkiye, Tom Barrack, said Washington could “absolutely” strike Iran this weekend.
Speaking to X podcast host Mario Nawfal, Barrack said that although Trump is “open and available and accessible to a deal … he’s also been very clear about what he wants”.
Barrack claimed that any potential US military action against Iran would not be aimed at regime change, saying Trump is “interested in rebalancing so that there’s no hostages, no threats, and the world can calm down”.
Reporting from Istanbul, Al Jazeera’s Sinem Koseoglu said the eight-nation summit was a “first-of-its-kind” attempt to discuss the parameters of regional conflicts and possible solutions.
Although participating countries “all have different national interests, especially when it comes to the crisis in the Gulf”, the Turkish foreign minister “underlined that what is happening in the Gulf … is affecting the other parts of the world”, Koseoglu added.
The eight ministers discussed Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, escalating fighting in Yemen and prospects for ending the Russia-Ukraine war.
Turkiye’s regional efforts
The meeting at an Istanbul hotel came as Turkiye seeks to bolster its role in the region, including through the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, the trilateral pact launched with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August.
Turkiye has said that the pact is not aimed at any specific country and remains open to others joining, including Egypt.
Fidan told reporters the pact has “several advantages, particularly because it is informal and flexible and focuses specifically on the issues we face.”
“We are not aware of any other platform that brings together countries with such different geographical and political backgrounds,” he said, noting that Ankara “is well placed to play a constructive role in this process”.
Cairo has yet to decide whether to join the agreement. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi recently said that Egypt would “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia.
The Iran-backed Houthis are fighting Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government forces and have launched a series of deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Media reports: Fire breaks out near military airfield in Voronezh after missile alert
articles.body:
Media reports: Fire breaks out near military airfield in Voronezh after missile alert
This was reported by the ASTRA Telegram channel, according to Ukrinform.
Alexander Gusev, governor of the Voronezh region, stated that “dry grass caught fire as a result of falling debris from downed targets.”
“Air defense forces on duty detected and destroyed several aerial targets in the sky over Voronezh. According to preliminary data, there were no casualties. Debris from the downed targets caused a fire in dry grass in the suburbs; the fire has already been extinguished,” he wrote on social media.
Earlier, Gusev had reported a missile threat in the region.
According to publicly available data, the 47th Guards Bomber Aviation Regiment is stationed at the “Baltimore” airfield.
The airfield has been regularly used by the Russian Air Force to launch airstrikes against Ukrainian territory since February 24, 2022.
A fire near the “Baltimore” airfield in Voronezh was previously reported on September 2. Prior to that, the airfield had been attacked on May 27.
As reported by Ukrinform, just last week, the Ukrainian Navy, using the “Neptune” coastal missile system, struck six Su-34M bombers at the “Borisoglebsk” military airfield in the Voronezh region of the Russian Federation.

articles.title: Interview: Stratonex wants to bring Ukraine’s innovation loop to Britain
articles.body:
- British company Stratonex Defence Technologies is developing the VARAN unmanned ground vehicle, which has completed initial mobility and remote-operation testing but is not yet operationally ready.
- Co-founder Ben Everitt told The Defence Blog that Ukrainian feedback pushed Stratonex to prioritize affordable unmanned logistics over autonomy.
British defense technology company Stratonex Defence Technologies is developing a range of unmanned ground vehicles, tactical drones, counter-drone systems and military mobility platforms, with a focus on reducing the exposure of personnel to battlefield threats.
The company’s VARAN unmanned ground vehicle is among its central projects. The platform has undergone initial mobility and remote-control testing, but further engineering and integration work is required before it can be considered ready for operational deployment.
In an interview with The Defence Blog, Stratonex co-founder Ben Everitt discussed the development of VARAN, the company’s relationship with technology partners, its approach to manufacturing and the challenges of moving military hardware from prototypes into serial production.
Everitt also outlined the company’s plans for 2027, including closer cooperation with British manufacturers, universities and military operators. He described lessons drawn from Ukrainian battlefield innovation and explained why Stratonex is placing increasing emphasis on connecting ground vehicles, aerial drones, sensors and other technologies into integrated mission systems.
The following interview is presented in full, with the interviewee’s answers reproduced without editorial changes.
Q: Stratonex Defence Technologies is entering a market where established defense contractors and smaller technology companies are competing to develop autonomous military systems. What specific technological or industrial gaps are you seeking to address, and how does your business model differ from that of traditional defense manufacturers?
A: I think you have to start with what’s actually happening on the battlefield, because it’s changing incredibly quickly.
The traditional idea of a frontline is becoming increasingly meaningless. What you’ve really got is a contested kill zone, potentially 20 kilometres or more either side of the line, where drones, sensors and precision weapons mean that if you can be seen, you can potentially be targeted.
So that’s the problem we’re building Stratonex around. How do you operate in that environment without unnecessarily putting people in it?
That’s where the product set starts to make sense. We’ve got unmanned systems that can move equipment, sensors and other capabilities into that space. Then we’ve got fast, stealthy, relatively inexpensive mobility platforms for those occasions when people do need to go into it and need to get back out again quickly.
The phrase we’ve started using is: keep the humans in the kill chain, but out of the kill zone. I really like it because it sums up what we’re trying to do.
The other thing that’s really struck me is the speed at which all of this is changing. I was recently out in eastern Ukraine, near the frontline, in a car with the manager of a UGV factory. His phone goes and it’s a battalion commander on the frontline who is using his vehicles. He’s basically saying, “This works, this doesn’t, and this is what I want the next batch to do.”
I remember thinking: this is extraordinary. You’re watching the innovation loop happening in real time. The customer is on the battlefield and the factory manager is taking the next requirement directly from him.
Obviously we’re operating in a very different environment in Britain, but that sense of pace and urgency is something we really want to capture at Stratonex. We’re not trying to recreate a traditional defence prime. We want to be agile, work with really good technology partners and get really, really cool technology integrated and into the hands of operators quickly.
Q: Stratonex has presented a portfolio spanning unmanned ground vehicles, tactical aerial systems and counter-UAS technologies. How much of this portfolio is being developed internally, and what role do technology partnerships, licensing arrangements and third-party integration play in bringing these products to market?
A: It’s deliberately a mixture. I don’t think there’s any great virtue in saying that every nut, bolt, sensor and line of code has to have been invented inside the same building.
There are technologies and IP that sit within Stratonex, and then there are areas where we work with partners, licence technology or integrate specialist systems developed by other people.
And that’s exciting, because there is some really, really cool technology being developed by smaller companies in Britain and elsewhere. The problem is often not the technology. It’s getting it integrated, tested, manufactured and ultimately bought.
That’s where I think Stratonex can add a lot of value. We can start with the operational problem and ask: what’s the best combination of platform, sensor, communications, autonomy and payload to solve it?
We’re quite deliberately technology-agnostic about that. If somebody has already invented a brilliant sensor, I don’t want to spend three years and a fortune inventing another one just so we can put our badge on it. I’d rather work with them, integrate it and get the capability out there.
Q: VARAN is presented as a modular unmanned ground vehicle capable of operating in GNSS-denied environments using passive 3D sensing and onboard autonomous navigation. How mature is this technology today, what capabilities have been demonstrated during physical testing, and what engineering challenges remain before the platform can be considered operationally ready?
A: VARAN is a real vehicle. We’ve built it, driven it, tested it and spent quite a lot of time getting it muddy, which is the fun bit.
But we’re also careful not to pretend that having a really good prototype is the same thing as having a fully operationally proven military system. There is still engineering, integration and testing to do.
We’ve demonstrated the fundamental mobility of the platform, remote operation and elements of the sensing and navigation architecture. The next phase is about making all of that increasingly robust across different terrain, payloads, communications environments and operational conditions.
What’s been particularly interesting is the feedback we’ve had from Ukraine. We started out, naturally enough, being really enthusiastic about the autonomy. It’s technically fascinating and there are some really cool things you can do with it.
But the Ukrainians keep bringing us back to something much simpler: the really important thing is that it’s unmanned.
If you can remotely drive ammunition, water, batteries or other equipment those last few kilometres instead of putting people in a vehicle and sending them into the kill zone, you’ve already achieved something incredibly valuable.
So we’re still developing the autonomy, absolutely. But we’re not developing autonomy because autonomy happens to be fashionable. We’re developing the capabilities operators actually want.
Q: Published information describes VARAN as a multi-mission platform capable of carrying reconnaissance, electronic warfare and counter-UAS payloads. How does the vehicle’s modular architecture accommodate different power, communications and payload requirements, and which mission configurations have progressed beyond the design stage?
A: This is one of my favourite things about VARAN because you can get terribly technical about modularity, power, data and payload integration, and I have a tendency to do exactly that.
We took VARAN away for a weekend of testing and filming with a group of former Special Forces guys who our Chairman, Major General John Holmes, knows.
I’m there waving my arms around getting incredibly enthusiastic about all the clever things we can do with it. We can forward-deploy surveillance drones on it. We can remotely recharge them. We can put different sensors and payloads on it. We can use it as part of a much wider unmanned system. All really, really cool stuff.
And the former SAS guys basically looked at it and said: “Yeah, but we can chuck all our kit on that and it’ll carry it for us.”
And they’re absolutely right.
Sometimes the simplest use case is the best one. Logistics is the backbone of successful warfighting. If VARAN can carry the heavy stuff while the operator concentrates on doing his job, that’s incredibly useful.
It also goes back to what the Ukrainians have been telling us. Sometimes we get very excited about the word “autonomy” when the thing the soldier really values is the word “unmanned”.
That’s why modularity matters. VARAN isn’t supposed to be one exquisite vehicle designed around one exquisite mission. The base platform gives you mobility, power and communications and then we can configure it around what the operator actually needs, whether that’s logistics, surveillance, EW, counter-UAS or something we haven’t thought of yet.
Q: VisionWave announced a conditional $20 million purchase order for 200 STRATUM VARAN vehicles in September 2026. What role does Stratonex play in the development, integration and potential production of these vehicles, and what milestones must be achieved before the programme moves into manufacturing and customer deliveries?
A: VisionWave is an important partner of ours and we have a distribution agreement with them, but they are a completely separate company, so I don’t really want to speak for them or get into the detail of their commercial announcements.
What I can talk about is what we’re doing with VARAN.
Our focus is on continuing to develop the platform, testing it, integrating different capabilities and getting it ready for manufacture at scale. And that’s a really exciting challenge in itself.
As I said earlier, the defence technology world is actually pretty good at producing prototypes. The difficult bit is getting from prototype to procurement and then into repeatable, affordable production.
That’s what we’re concentrating on. Making VARAN faster, tougher and more useful, testing it properly, listening to operators and making sure that when demand comes we can actually build the thing at meaningful volume.
Ultimately, I’d much rather be judged on the vehicles we build and deliver than the numbers in a press release.
Q: Moving from prototypes and technology demonstrations to serial production remains a major challenge for emerging defense companies. How is Stratonex addressing manufacturing scalability, supply-chain resilience, unit costs and long-term maintenance, and what production capacity do you realistically expect to achieve?
A: Price really matters to us, particularly with VARAN.
Its three big advantages are its price point, speed and durability. It’s more cost-effective than the heavier platforms in this space, it’s fast and agile, and it’s designed to take punishment.
And you have to be realistic about why the price point matters. These things are going into war zones. At some point some of them are going to get blown up.
One Ukrainian battalion commander put it brilliantly when we were talking about equipment: “If you can make it out of wood, make it out of wood.”
That’s obviously an exaggeration, but there’s a really important philosophy behind it. Don’t add cost and complexity unless they actually give the operator something useful.
There’s a tendency in defence to make everything exquisite. But if making something twice as expensive only makes it ten per cent more capable, and you’re operating in an environment where you’re going to lose platforms anyway, that’s not necessarily a good trade.
So we’re designing around manufacturability, modular components, repairability and supply-chain resilience from the start. We don’t want to build a vast Stratonex factory and manufacture every component ourselves. We’d much rather work with established manufacturing partners and scale production as demand develops.
That’s also why durability and field repair matter. Make it tough. Make it repairable. Make it affordable enough that commanders are actually prepared to use it.
Q: Beyond VARAN, your portfolio includes the D-FLY counter-UAS interceptor and TALON tactical unmanned aircraft. What technical or operational capabilities are you prioritising in these programmes, and can you share any previously undisclosed details concerning prototypes, testing results, new configurations or upcoming product introductions?
A: Again, I think it makes more sense if you look at the portfolio through the kill-zone problem rather than looking at each product individually.
You’ve got this 20-kilometre-plus contested space. So how do I see into it? How do I move equipment through it? How do I operate inside it without unnecessarily exposing people? How do I counter the drones that are creating part of the threat?
VARAN answers part of that. TALON answers another part through tactical aerial capability. D-FLY tackles the counter-UAS problem, including the really important question of cost exchange.
And then you’ve got the mobility platforms, which I think are fascinating. E-bikes and e-scooters might look slightly odd sitting next to drones and UGVs until you think about the operational problem. If somebody does have to enter that kill zone, you want them moving quickly and quietly with as little signature as possible.
That’s the common thread.
What gets me really excited now is joining those things together. A UGV shouldn’t just be a UGV and a drone shouldn’t just be a drone. How do the platforms, sensors, communications and effectors start working together as one mission system?
That’s where I think some of the really, really cool stuff is going to happen.
Q: Looking ahead to 2027, which developments do you expect to define Stratonex’s next phase of growth? Are there any new programmes, industrial partnerships, customer agreements or technological milestones that you are prepared to announce or discuss in greater detail with The Defence Blog readers?
A: There’s loads going on and I’m genuinely really excited about 2027.
Obviously there’s the product side. VARAN will continue developing, we’ve got other products coming through, and we’re increasingly interested in what happens when you connect all these different capabilities together rather than thinking about a UGV, a drone or a sensor in isolation.
But the bigger idea we’re working on is what I’d describe as on-shoring the innovation loop.
That comes directly from what I’ve seen in Ukraine. I keep going back to that phone call in the car between the battalion commander and the factory manager. Operator feedback, engineering, testing and production are happening incredibly close together. That’s one of the reasons they are innovating at such extraordinary speed.
We’re obviously not going to recreate the circumstances that have driven that in Ukraine, but we absolutely can learn from it.
So how do we build our own version of that loop here in Britain? How do we bring operators, engineers, SMEs, manufacturers and academia much closer together, so that an operational problem can become an engineering problem, become a prototype, get tested, generate feedback and go around the loop again quickly?
That’s why we’re looking at academic partnerships as well as product-development partnerships. Universities bring extraordinary engineering expertise, research capability, testing facilities and, importantly, really bright people. Industry brings products, manufacturing and commercial pace. Then you need the operator constantly feeding reality back into the process.
For me, that’s potentially much bigger than any individual product.
Britain doesn’t have an innovation problem. There is some really, really cool technology being developed here. The challenge is connecting it, testing it against real requirements, iterating quickly and then actually manufacturing it.
If we can help build that ecosystem around Stratonex, shorten the distance between the operator saying “I need this” and somebody putting a working solution in their hands, then I think we’ve got something genuinely exciting.
That’s a big part of where I want us to go in 2027: on-shore the innovation loop, build sovereign capability and keep turning really good British technology into things that operators can actually use.
And all of it still comes back to the same mission: keep the humans in the kill chain, but out of the kill zone.

articles.title: Trump Invokes Defense Production Act to Boost Oil Production
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has invoked a Cold War-era law in an effort to boost oil production and lower energy prices.
In a presidential memorandum issued Thursday, Trump determined that petroleum production, refining, and related activities are essential to national defense under the 1950 Defense Production Act. The determination follows Trump’s declaration of a national energy emergency in January 2025.
“Ensuring resilient domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity is central to United States defense readiness,” the memo reads. “Without immediate Federal action, United States defense capabilities will remain vulnerable to disruption.”
The memo comes as the price of gas and diesel has soared across the country amid supply disruptions caused by the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran. Brent crude futures rose 1.2% to $114.47 a barrel early Friday, extending gains after Thursday hit a five-month high. U.S. diesel pump prices averaged $6.32 a gallon, slightly higher than Thursday but below the September record, according to AAA. The high energy prices, and related inflation, have become a defining issue for voters in the coming midterm elections.
Here’s what to know.
What does the memo mean for energy production?
The memo means that energy production shortfalls are seen as a national defense risk.
The memo invokes Section 303 of the Defense Production Act, a law that allows the federal government to intervene in private industry for national defense. Section 303 allows the President to make purchases, purchase commitments, provide financial support and equipment, and expand production through other measures.
The memorandum also removes certain Section 303 requirements through an emergency waiver, including ordinary congressional notification and authorization constraints.
While the memo does not specify which projects could be funded, Vice President J.D. Vance said last week that the Administration would use the Defense Production Act to expand capacity at a Delek U.S. Holdings-owned refinery in Texas.
Without taking action, the memo said, U.S. industry would be unable to provide sufficient energy services in a “timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations.”
Has the Defense Production Act been invoked before?
Enacted during the Korean War, the Defense Production Act was first used to expand domestic industries in critical materials, such as aluminum and titanium, for national defense.
Section 303 of the act was also used during the pandemic to fund domestic production of medicines and vaccines. Former President Joe Biden also invoked the statute to support clean energy manufacturing and supply chains, including minerals used in electric vehicle batteries and the production of of energy-efficient heat pumps and insulation.
In April, more than a month after Iran began disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli Feb. 28 strikes, Trump invoked the act to declare petroleum, natural gas, coal, electricity grid, and other energy infrastructure essential to national defense. Citing April’s natural gas determination, the Department of Energy on Monday committed up to $42 million to advance the proposed Constitution Pipeline linking Pennsylvania and New York. The department also announced up to $50 million last week for transmission upgrades in Virginia and West Virginia, citing April’s grid determination.
Last year, Trump signed legislation providing $1 billion for Defense Production Act activities, including energy projects deemed critical to national security.
Trump’s use of Section 303 of the act for fossil fuel projects has drawn criticisms from environmentalists, with the Center for Biological Diversity calling the April memoranda, which waived congressional notification, “unlawful.” Nevertheless, the statute expressly includes energy production and construction in its definition of national defense.
How else has Trump tried to lower energy prices?
The Trump Administration has pursued a number of other measures aimed at lowering energy prices since the Iran War began. Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order temporarily expanding access to tax-exempt dyed diesel, which is typically reserved for off-road farm and construction vehicles. The Group of 7 countries, including the U.S., also agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil reserves to the world over four months.
In August, the Administration extended the Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and certain other commodities between U.S. ports.
Trump also announced an agreement with Putin earlier this month to import diesel from Russia, alongside temporary sanctions relief. The deal has faced significant backlash from lawmakers.
For many of these measures, industry analysts and stakeholders have said the reduction in energy prices is likely to be limited and possibly short-lived. Analysts estimated that the Jones Act waiver was expected to reduce gasoline prices by only pennies per gallon. Capital Economics economist Hamad Hussain said the reserve release could lower diesel prices temporarily, but would not resolve the underlying supply crunch. And analysts warned that the dyed diesel measure would have a limited effect on most consumers since the tax-exempt fuel isn’t widely available at ordinary commercial pumps. A Council on Foreign Relations analysis also suggested that damaged Russian refining capacity may make a near-term effect of the Russia deal on diesel markets unlikely, although Trump said the agreement would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets immediately.
Meanwhile, oil exports from the Middle East topped prewar levels last week, marking a rebound in regional oil shipments despite continuing security risks. Ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, however, still face attacks from Iran, while the Bab el-Mandeb Strait near Yemen has been threatened by the Houthi rebels. Analysts previously told TIME in June that the risk of further attacks and damage to facilities could delay a full-scale recovery.
Thursday’s memorandum could support investment in fuel capacity, but it’s uncertain how quick or measurable an effect it will have on energy prices. Gas prices still depend heavily on globally traded crude, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, although they can be influenced by domestic refining and distribution conditions. The U.S. was the largest crude producer globally last year, averaging 13.6 million barrels of crude a day.
Analysts warned, after the April memorandum, that federal support would not necessarily translate into immediate price relief.
“Until the pipes are in the ground and the fuel is flowing or transported, it may not be able to be called a true structural shift,” Cyrus Brooks, director of marketing at energy research firm RBAC, wrote in April.
Still, Brooks said of the April action that federal recognition of energy as important to national security could support important infrastructure investment, potentially relieving a bottleneck in domestic fuel production, refining or transportation.
“Energy security seems to be the brightest neon sign flashing,” he wrote. “Not because it’s everything, but because nothing works without it.”

Germany's plan to purchase the powerful BGM-109 Tomahawk missile and the Typhon ground-launch system from US manufacturer Raytheon could be delayed for up to five years.
