articles.title: Iran has plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran has detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes, officials say
Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel attack Iran again, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters.
Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington collapses.
The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections.
"If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one of the officials said.
The official warned Washington not to "play with fire", and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.
Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.
Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency. But the global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography.
The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea.
The US Department of State and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Iranian security officials' remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.
'Stronger response'
The plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran's leadership that a renewed US military campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.
Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centres and AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.
Washington's Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they "should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables," the second Iranian security official said.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and US companies fear for their investments in the region.
"Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (US President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans," said Vatanka.
Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.
Restoring connections during wartime could be difficult, experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.
The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.
The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia, with capacity routed through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic travelling between regions, Mauldin said.
Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with US technology firms.
Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain. The IRGC named US tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the height of the war in March.
Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and US technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.
Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.

articles.title: Ceasefire planned for occupied Oleshky as residents face starvation and blocked escape routes, White House announces
articles.body:
US First Lady Melania Trump has secured an agreement for a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations to begin on 29 October, the White House announced on 23 October.
The proposed truce comes after months of worsening conditions in Oleshky, where Russian restrictions have left residents without reliable access to food, drinking water, medicine, and medical care. Ukrainian officials and international monitors have called for a humanitarian corridor as civilians face hunger, landmines, and regular attacks, with residents unable to leave safely.
Ceasefire aims to open evacuation route
According to the White House, Trump and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to agree on the ceasefire's terms, timing, and procedures. Civilian representatives from both countries are expected to visit residents to assess their needs, while those wishing to leave will receive transportation to their preferred destination.
The White House said an American media organization would accompany the teams to document the process and help ensure families' wishes are respected.
Trump said she initiated discussions after learning about the crisis during a private conversation at an event in New York during the 81st United Nations General Assembly. She said the agreement also involves technical preparations, including demining.
Russian troops seize drone-dropped food in occupied Oleshky, accusing recipients of cooperating with Ukraine. Some people go missing, a local official says
Oleshky residents face hunger and isolation
Oleshky, on the Russian-occupied left bank of the Dnipro River, had around 24,000 residents before Russia's full-scale invasion. Recent estimates put the remaining population at roughly 1,700 to 2,000, including about 50 children.
Residents face severe food and medicine shortages, while Russian forces have restricted movement and attacked vehicles attempting to deliver humanitarian supplies. Ukrainian officials have also said Russian troops have seized food parcels delivered by Ukrainian drones and detained or beaten some residents who received them.
Russian troops enter homes and threaten starving Oleshky residents for food and alcohol, officials say
The crisis has drawn growing international attention. Pope Leo XIV appealed to Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a truce to allow aid deliveries and safe civilian evacuations, while Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, said on 18 October that negotiations over a ceasefire and evacuation had advanced to the stage of agreeing on final details.
The White House announcement sets 29 October as the start date for the localized ceasefire. Its implementation will determine whether aid can reach residents and civilians can leave safely after months of isolation.

articles.title: Trump turns to Cold War-era law to tackle fuel crisis
articles.body:
Trump turns to Cold War-era law to tackle fuel crisis
US President Donald Trump has invoked a Cold War-era national security law to boost domestic oil production and refining, as rising fuel prices threaten the Republicans’ chances in November’s midterm elections.
Speaking on Thursday at a Republican campaign rally in Iowa – an agricultural state where farmers have been hit hard by the oil crisis – Trump announced that his administration would use the Defense Production Act (DPA) to provide up to $150 million to expand American refining capacity and produce diesel and gasoline “at record levels.”
He also predicted that the Iran and Ukraine conflicts would end soon, sending gasoline and oil prices “tumbling down.”
Enacted in 1950, the DPA allows Washington to financially support industries deemed essential to national defense. In a presidential memorandum, Trump designated domestic petroleum production, refineries, pipelines, and storage facilities as critical to national security, arguing that private companies could not expand capacity quickly enough without federal intervention.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright promised the funds would be deployed in cooperation with private companies, while the Department of Energy separately projected the initiative would increase refining output by millions of gallons of gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other products per day.
Vice President J.D. Vance had earlier announced plans to invoke the law to expand a Delek-operated refinery in Tyler, Texas, although such projects typically take months, if not years, to complete.
Trump’s announcement comes as his approval rating has plunged to a record low of 31% – compared with 47% when he began his second term – ahead of the midterm elections on November 3, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published Monday. The survey also found that 68% of Americans disapproved of his handling of the economy.
Fuel prices in America sharply rose after the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February, disrupting global energy supplies. According to the US Energy Information Administration, average gasoline prices have climbed from $2.94 per gallon immediately before the conflict to $4.28 in the week ending October 19, while diesel has jumped from $3.81 to $6.28 over the same period.
The Trump administration has sought to tackle the fuel crisis through several emergency measures, including releasing 172 million barrels from strategic oil reserves, relaxing gasoline-blending requirements, temporarily easing diesel regulations, and announcing additional subsidies for struggling farmers.
In early October, Trump also announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release more than 300,000 tons of Russian diesel onto global markets, with additional supplies expected later. He has also repeatedly pressed Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blamed for rising fuel prices.
The president’s pressure sparked pushback from Zelensky, who called Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow “a weak decision” and “not fair and not honest” while refusing to comply with the refineries ultimatum. In response, Trump suggested that Ukraine should “get a new president” instead of Zelensky, whose term expired more than two years ago, while calling continued Ukrainian strikes a “disgrace.”

articles.title: Putin’s key remarks on peace talks and Europe’s ‘schizophrenia’ (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Putin’s key remarks on peace talks and Europe’s ‘schizophrenia’ (VIDEO)
Russia remains ready to negotiate a lasting settlement in Ukraine but will achieve its objectives regardless, Russian President Vladimir Putin told journalist Pavel Zarubin on Thursday. He also outright rejected “schizophrenic” claims in Western media that Moscow could be seeking a war with Europe.
Putin’s comments followed nearly three hours of talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Witkoff brought new peace talk proposals following his own discussions with Vladimir Zelensky, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s Chief of Staff Bjoern Siebert, and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Oslo.
The new diplomatic engagement comes after Putin’s October 9 agreement with US President Donald Trump on Russian diesel supplies, whereby Washington eased fuel export restrictions while engaging with Moscow on broader economic cooperation.
Lasting peace, rather than a temporary pause
Putin confirmed Russia’s readiness to resume trilateral contacts with the US and Ukraine, focusing on security arrangements for both countries after a final settlement. The goal is to achieve definitive peace agreements, rather than “a suspension of hostilities for some short period,” he stressed.
The Russian leader also stated that he agrees with Witkoff’s argument that such discussions would also need to address Europe’s wider security architecture.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov previously suggested the talks could resume around mid-November, potentially in Abu Dhabi.
Putin said an agreement was possible, but insisted that “all the goals of the special military operation will be achieved” one way or another.
Europe’s ‘political schizophrenia’
European claims that Russia poses a military threat and preparations for confrontation amount to “political schizophrenia,” Putin said, arguing that European populations do not want war with Russia and explicitly rejected suggestions that Moscow is preparing to attack them.
“We do not want, we are not preparing for any war with Europe,” he said.
Putin described inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia as unrealistic, expressing hope that its opponents would recognize that peaceful relations better serve their own populations.
‘Historic Russia’ and the territorial question
Asked about Zelensky’s recent comments to Fox News that he would be willing to give up 25% of his territories in order to freeze the conflict on the current battle lines, Putin rejected the premise.
“It is not their territory, it is the territory of historic Russia,” he said, citing residents’ votes for independence and subsequently for reunification with the Russian Federation.
He acknowledged that the issue remained disputed, but argued that describing these developments as Ukraine losing territory was inappropriate.
Fighting ‘to the last Ukrainian’
Putin called it “incomprehensible” that Kiev expects that “the entire world should pay them, fight for them, supply them with weapons, ammunition, equipment,” and stressed that Russia has no desire to fight Ukraine.
“If Ukraine’s current leadership wants to wage war, let them fight. But why do they think everyone should pay for it and supply them with weapons?” Putin questioned.
He noted that much of this desire for war can be attributed to foreign countries that want to fight against Russia in order to weaken it and have promised support to Kiev.
However, Putin stressed that these foreign entities are prepared to fight until “the last Ukrainian” and questioned whether Ukraine’s leadership similarly treats its citizens as expendable cannon fodder.
Putin accused Ukrainian authorities of rounding up men “like stray dogs” and forcibly sending them to the front, undermining motivation. He also argued that nationalist groups that carry out this so-called “busification” do not always bear the frontline burden themselves.
He recalled that, according to official figures, there have been half a million deserters in Ukraine and over 300,000 criminal cases opened, adding that the actual numbers could be significantly higher.
Shared history and missed opportunities
Putin said Moscow had sought a negotiated resolution with Kiev since 2014, including through the Minsk agreements intended to settle the Donbass conflict. He blamed Ukrainian authorities for repeatedly rejecting opportunities to reach an agreement before Russia’s military operation began in 2022.
He described Ukrainians as a people closely related to Russians, pointing to genetic research that has shown they are “one people.” However, he acknowledged that some wished to identify differently and said Russia accepted that reality.
“We are ready even now to negotiate and seek solutions to this difficult, complicated situation,” Putin said. “Everything can be agreed upon.”

articles.title: Pentagon and Lockheed announce deal for 850 F-35 jets over 10 years
articles.body:
The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin have announced a 10-year agreement for the production of 850 F-35 warplanes, underscoring Washington's long-term commitment to the high-tech stealth aircraft.
The two sides announced the deal on Thursday but did not specify a value for the agreement, which comes as the Pentagon seeks to strike multi-year deals to expand American weapons production and boost the US defence industrial base.
The announcement "cements (the plane's) role as the free world's key frontline fighter for years ahead," Lockheed Chairman, President and CEO Jim Taiclet said on a call with investors.
F-35s — which Washington's forces have used in combat during the US-Israeli war on Iran — come in three versions that can cost more than $100 million per plane.
The "framework agreement," which the Pentagon said would "modernise and expand" the F-35 programme, still requires congressional approval and funding.
"We have fundamentally changed how we stabilise the American defence industrial base to produce at speed and scale," top acquisition official Michael Duffey said in the Pentagon's announcement.
"By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win," Duffey said.
The F-35, a joint project between the United States and a number of allies, is one of the world's most advanced military aircraft. There are more than 1,375 F-35s based around the world, according to Lockheed.
The deal, if approved, would give Washington a "predictable, affordable, and resilient" fighter jet programme, Lockheed said, pointing to billions of dollars in expected savings thanks to "long-term pricing and industry volume discounts."
'Greater certainty'
In exchange for the Pentagon's 10-year commitment, Lockheed Martin will fund $7 billion in projects supporting the F-35s, the Pentagon said.
"With the greater certainty that comes from the US government's transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain," Lockheed's Taiclet said in a statement.
"That's good for the taxpayer, good for our suppliers and, most importantly, good for the United States and its allies," he added.
In addition to the F-35s themselves, the agreement also covers "initial spares, 10 years of modification kits and sustainment, and international customer orders," Lockheed said.
The United States recently announced the approval of a $24.3 billion sale of 48 of the stealth planes to Saudi Arabia last month.
Lockheed said the F-35 programme will support more than 315,000 jobs and generate nearly $80 billion in economic activity in the next 10 years, "strengthening the nation's industrial base and providing long-term stability for suppliers."
The company on Thursday announced better-than-expected earnings for the third quarter, once again benefiting from higher activity levels across all of its segments.
Lockheed shares surged more than seven percent in Thursday trading, closing at $590.2.

articles.title: Russian losses in the war with Ukraine.
articles.body:
This publication is divided into two parts:
Bi-weekly Summary. A text summary, updated every two weeks, in which we report on what we have learned about recent losses and the frontline events that led to the deaths of Russian soldiers.
Interactive Infographics. The second part provides visualisations of the losses since the start of the war, showing, for example, where the dead served or which regions they came from. We update the data for these graphics, while the accompanying text is refreshed but remains largely the same.
A detailed description of our method for estimating total deaths using Probate Registry data can be found at this link.
Last update to the named list: October 23, 2026.
Last update to the Probate Registry estimate: May 9, 2026; estimate as of late December 2025
Full named list and a map of verified losses is available here: 200.zona.media.
This week, we are only releasing updated numbers for Russian losses in the war against Ukraine.
The map below shows the distribution of casualties across Russia’s regions. These are absolute figures and have not been adjusted for population or number of military units.
You can filter the map to show total losses, losses by branch of service, or the home regions of mobilised soldiers who were killed.
In most cases, official reports or visual cues like uniforms and insignia allow us to determine a soldier’s branch of service, or how he came to be in the army (mobilised, volunteer, prisoner, etc.).
The chart below compares these different groups of servicemen.
From early summer and into the mid-fall season of 2022, volunteers bore the brunt of the losses, which is strikingly different from the situation in the initial stage of the war: in winter and early spring, the Airborne Forces suffered the greatest damage, followed by the Motorised Rifle troops.
By the end of 2022 and the beginning of the next year, losses among prisoners recruited into the Wagner PMC increased markedly. They were formed into “assault groups” to overwhelm Ukrainian positions near Bakhmut.
By March 2023, prisoners became the largest category of war losses. After the capture of Bakhmut, there have been no cases of mass use of prisoners so far.
By September 2024, volunteers once again emerged as the largest category among the KIA. This shift reflects a cumulative effect: prison recruitment had significantly waned, no new mobilisation had been announced, yet the stream of volunteers continued unabated.
By October 23, 2026, the death of 7,920 officers of the Russian army and other security agencies had been confirmed.
The proportion of officer deaths among overall casualties has steadily declined since the conflict began. In the early stages, when professional contract soldiers formed the main invasion force, officers accounted for up to 10% of fatalities. By November 2024, this figure had dropped to between 2–3%—a shift that reflects both evolving combat tactics and the intensive recruitment of volunteer infantry, who suffer casualty rates many times higher than their commanding officers.
Officers killed in Ukraine
To date, the deaths of 15 Russian generals have been officially confirmed: five Lieutenant Generals, seven Major Generals, two who had retired from active service, and one Ukrainian SBU general who had fled to Russia.
Lieutenant General Oleg Tsokov, deputy commander of the Southern Military District, was killed in July 2023—the first officer of that rank to die in the war. In December 2024, Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, head of the Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical (NBC) Protection Troops, was killed by a bomb in Moscow. Lieutenant General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior officer in the General Staff’s Main Operational Directorate, was killed by a car bomb in a Moscow suburb in April 2025. In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Operational Training Directorate of the Russian General Staff, was killed in Moscow by a car bomb. On March 31, 2026, Lieutenant General Alexander Otroschenko, commander of the mixed aviation corps of the Northern Fleet, was killed in the crash of an An-26 transport aircraft in Crimea.
Two deputy army commanders, Major General Andrei Sukhovetsky (41st Army) and Major General Vladimir Frolov (8th Army), were killed in the first weeks of the war. In June 2022, Major General Roman Kutuzov was killed in an attack on a troop formation.
Major General Sergei Goryachev, chief of staff of the 35th Combined Arms Army, was killed in June 2023 while commanding forces against the Ukrainian counter-offensive in the Zaporizhzhia region. In November 2023, Major General Vladimir Zavadsky, deputy commander of the 14th Army Corps, was killed near the village of Krynky.
In November 2024, Major General Pavel Klimenko, commander of the 5th Separate Motorised Rifle Brigade (formerly the “Oplot” Brigade of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic), was fatally wounded by an FPV drone.
In July 2025, a strike on the headquarters of the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade killed at least six officers, including the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Navy, Mikhail Gudkov.
The two retired generals on the list are Kanamat Botashev, a pilot who had been dismissed for crashing a fighter jet and was fighting for Wagner PMC when his Su-25 was shot down in May 2022, and Andrei Golovatsky, a former Interior Ministry general serving an 8.5-year prison sentence (but maintained his rank) who was killed in June 2024.
On March 17, 2026, SBU Major General Volodymyr Lyapkin was killed in the Kherson region. Until February 2014, Lyapkin headed a department in the Ukrainian special services, but after the victory of the Maidan revolution, he fled to Russia. After the war began, he served in the occupation administration of Kherson and then transferred to the “Bars-33” unit.
The date of death is known in 266,700 cases. While this data does not capture the full daily reality of the war, it does suggest which periods saw the most intense fighting.
Please note that data for the most recent months is most incomplete and will change significantly in the future.
The age of the deceased is mentioned in 268,100 reports. For the first six months of the war, when the fighting was done by the regular army, the 21-23 age group accounted for the most deaths.
Volunteers and mobilised men are significantly older: people voluntarily go to war over 30, and the mobilised are generally over 25.

articles.title: Finland gives Ukraine 10 diesel locomotives that keep trains running when Russian strikes cut the power
articles.body:
Finland will donate diesel locomotives to Ukraine’s state railway, the Office of Ukraine’s President reported. Helsinki also pledged new winter aid, and the two countries signed deals on drones, housing, and satellite communications during Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s visit to Kyiv. One of them is a first step toward a satellite link Ukraine would control itself.
With Russia replacing its missiles as fast as it fires them, Ukraine heads into winter needing equipment that works without the grid. Russian strikes have damaged or destroyed almost 600 locomotives of Ukraine’s state railway since the full-scale invasion began, more than 300 of them diesels, the infrastructure minister said. The attacks have reached engines even near the Polish border, on the railway that carries Ukraine’s evacuations, grain, and cargo.
Diesels that keep moving when the grid goes down
Finland will hand 10 locomotives and their spare parts to Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway, free of charge. Infrastructure Minister Mykola Kalashnyk announced the deal, signed on 22 October at a Ukrainian-Finnish business forum. The engines need no power from overhead lines, so trains can keep running during blackouts.
The engines are Dv12 diesels that VR, Finland’s state rail company, is taking out of service. A VR shareholders’ meeting moved them into state ownership, and the Finnish state is donating them, Yle reported. VR puts their value, spare parts included, at about €2.1 million. Finland’s government said the gift will not affect VR’s ability to run trains at home.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi and Orpo signed the donation certificate, one of seven documents signed that day. Two others plan Ukrainian-Finnish drone production in Finland, one for military and dual-use systems and one for heavy drones. Another covers a precast concrete plant for industrial housing construction.
The day’s agreements are worth around €300 million in total, Zelenskyy said. Projects worth €200 million are already under way within the two countries’ Drone Deal, he added. Under an earlier plan, most drones made in Finland would go to Ukraine.
Finland backs €28.5 million power plant project as Ukraine braces for Russia’s next winter energy assault
Winter money now, a 36th military package by year’s end
Orpo announced a new €10 million package. Of it, €5 million goes to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund and €2 million to humanitarian aid for winter. The last €3 million goes to the Ukraine Recovery Program, for energy and water supply. Finland will also deliver mobile heating containers by December.
Finland has given Ukraine five defense packages this year, worth more than €500 million combined, Militarnyi reported. A 36th package is being prepared together with Ukraine’s military. “We plan to make a decision by the end of this year,” Orpo said. In September, Finland approved a package worth about €290 million.
A satellite link Ukraine would own
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry signed a letter of intent with Finnish satellite firm ICEYE and telecom company Nokia, Militarnyi reported, citing ICEYE. The parties will explore building a secure satellite communications system under Ukraine’s control. The aim is to reduce Ukraine’s dependence on foreign commercial operators.
In this model, the state customer owns the satellites, ground stations, and user terminals, RBC-Ukraine reported. The network could serve defense, border protection, emergency services, and disaster recovery. The letter sets out no timeline or funding.
“Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security,” Zelenskyy said in the companies’ statement. ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said Ukraine needs “secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls.”
The deal comes after a speed cap on Starlink disrupted Ukrainian drone missions this month. The EU, meanwhile, is pushing three European firms to merge into one SpaceX rival. ICEYE has supplied Ukraine with radar satellite imagery for years.
Days before the signing, tracking firm LeoLabs said a Russian government-owned satellite, Cosmos 2612, had spent weeks shadowing an ICEYE radar satellite, coming within 500 meters. The ICEYE satellite is widely believed to provide imagery to Ukraine.
Neither fix is quick. Ukraine’s big locomotive order arrives from 2027, and the first satellites of the ICEYE-Nokia system are expected to launch only in 2028.

articles.title: Russia vows ‘inevitable’ retaliation over Austrian diplomat expulsions
articles.body:
Russia vows ‘inevitable’ retaliation over Austrian diplomat expulsions
Russia will retaliate against Austria for expelling four of its diplomats over alleged misconduct, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Dmitry Lyubinsky has said.
The warning follows Vienna’s decision to declare four Russian diplomats personae non gratae over alleged violations of diplomatic rules, without publicly presenting evidence of wrongdoing.
“A response will follow inevitably,” Lyubinsky told TASS on Friday. He did not specify what retaliatory measures Moscow could take.
Austria announced the expulsions earlier on Friday, citing findings by its security services. Three of the diplomats were stationed at the Russian Embassy in Vienna, while the fourth worked at Moscow’s delegation to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), dealing with military security and arms control.
The Austrian Foreign Ministry accused the four of engaging in “activities incompatible with their diplomatic status” and ordered them to leave the country. It did not identify the diplomats or provide details of the alleged violations.
The Russian Embassy rejected the accusations as “outrageous” and unfounded. Responding to Friday’s decision, the mission accused Vienna of blindly following Western anti-Russian policies and described the expulsions as another unfriendly move against Moscow.
Austrian media have sought to link the expulsions to alleged Russian espionage, although Vienna has provided no public evidence to substantiate the claims. According to the magazine Profil, the country’s Defense Ministry circulated a warning to military personnel and reservists in August about supposed Russian intelligence operatives, complete with the names and photographs of 21 individuals.
The warning reportedly prompted a wave of reports about suspicious contacts, though their nature and credibility remain unclear. Profil also claimed that disagreements between Austria’s Defense and Foreign Ministries had delayed the expulsions. None of the allegations have been publicly substantiated, and no evidence directly implicating the four Russian diplomats in espionage has been presented.
Austria has expelled 18 Russian diplomats since 2020. Despite its longstanding military neutrality, Vienna has joined EU sanctions against Moscow and provided political and financial assistance to Ukraine.
Moscow has previously responded to Austrian expulsions with reciprocal measures. In September 2025, Russia declared an Austrian diplomat persona non grata after Vienna expelled a Russian envoy over alleged espionage involving an employee of the Austrian energy company OMV. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at the time that Moscow would respond to such moves in kind.
The diplomatic standoff escalated again in May, when Austria expelled three Russian Embassy employees over allegations that antennas installed on diplomatic buildings in Vienna were being used to intercept satellite communications. The Russian Embassy dismissed the accusations as “outrageous,” “unjustified” and politically motivated, warning of a harsh response.

articles.title: 491 days in the grey zone and losing both feet: exclusive details of the first-ever aerial evacuation aboard a Heavy Shot drone
articles.body:
491 days in the grey zone and losing both feet: exclusive details of the first-ever aerial evacuation aboard a Heavy Shot drone
In October, Ukraine's defence forces carried out the first-ever medical evacuation of a wounded soldier using a heavy unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). The soldier, a member of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade who goes by the alias Magura, was airlifted from the grey zone aboard a Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 drone. No evacuation vehicle had been able to get to the area for over a year.
The roads are heavily mined, and FPV drones prowl the skies, destroying anything that moves within tens of kilometres. The brigade spent over six months preparing the daring rescue operation, which brought together heavy and light quadcopters, ground robots, electronic warfare units and even artillery.
"I realised there was a person down there: I wanted to get him to safety as quickly and safely as possible," a drone pilot recalls.
Ukrainska Pravda has interviewed the soldiers behind the operation, the drone's developers and the wounded serviceman. Find out how troops from the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, named after Kostiantyn Ostrozkyi, teamed up with neighbouring units to pull off the evacuation and make history.
The operation was made possible by the coordinated efforts of the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, the 14th and 30th Separate Mechanised Brigades, and the 10th Army Corps.
491 days
Sadly, this story began quite some time ago. On 2 June 2025, Kostiantyn "Magura" Vlasenko, an infantryman with the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, set off from the rear with a fellow soldier for their positions on the Kupiansk front, which were on the left bank of the Oskil River. In the grey zone, Magura initially took shelter in one spot. But when it flooded, he had to move into an abandoned building.
His brother-in-arms was killed while making his way to a fallback position. Then, on 14 February 2026, a Russian drone dropped a munition that wounded Magura in both legs. Faced with a fight for survival and having lost one of his feet, he amputated the other foot himself, leaving him unable to get out of his position on his own.
There was no way to drag him out overland: the Oskil River, dense minefields and relentless Russian drone patrols made the approaches impassable. The battalion tried to use a ground robotic system to evacuate him, but Russian forces spotted and destroyed it while it was still on its way. Infantry groups also failed to reach him. Russian drones filled the skies, and Russian infantry had infiltrated the area around his position, effectively sealing it off.
All this is further evidence that the "golden hour" – the crucial first 60 minutes after an injury, when prompt medical treatment can mean the difference between life and death – is becoming increasingly difficult to meet on the modern battlefield. Evacuating wounded soldiers is a dangerous mission in its own right, and one that becomes harder with every passing year.
Every four to five days, drones brought Kostiantyn food, cigarettes and sweets. He kept in touch with his brothers-in-arms by walkie-talkie. He held out in his position until his evacuation on 4 October.
It was Alex, the reconnaissance chief overseeing UAV operations for the 2nd Mechanised Battalion, who came up with the idea of evacuating the soldier by air. It took around six months to move from the initial concept to the flight itself. The military had conventional Heavy Shot bomber drones, but these were not up to the task. The soldiers instead turned to the newly developed Heavy Shot Ayudag-6, a heavy-lift drone that can carry up to 130 kg and is equipped with a cargo winch.
"We'd been using Heavy Shot bomber drones for a long time and had an established line of communication with Gurzuf Defence," Alex said. "When I found out they were testing the new Ayudag-6 heavy-lift drone, I went to them immediately with this unconventional task. The drone was still a work in progress, but the developers were immediately fired up by the idea."
Gurzuf Defence designed the drone primarily for frontline logistics, as a heavy-lift modular platform. However, the engineers ensured from the very beginning that it had enough thrust to lift a person. The drone underwent two years of testing, during which the company's chief developer, Oleh Hynda, became the first person to fly aboard the test model.
"We never intended this drone to be just for evacuations – it's a heavy-duty logistics platform," Pavlo Feldblium, co-founder of Gurzuf Defence, told Ukrainska Pravda. "But we always knew it might have to be used for a rescue mission in certain circumstances. To prepare for this operation, we brought in units with experience of evacuating people using ground robotic systems. It was their experts who configured the winch and the mounting systems."
The company spent several months fine-tuning the platform at the unit's request. Experts from the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade's unmanned ground systems company then fitted the aircraft with additional equipment, and the 2nd Battalion's headquarters spent two months planning the operation. Around 15 military personnel were involved in preparing and planning the mission.
Pre-flight preparations took seven days. The military personnel worked out the flight routes, planned cover corridors and identified alternative emergency landing sites in case of a technical failure.
The evacuation drone was operated by Chornyi ("Black"), a squad leader in a mortar battery at the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Mechanised Brigade. "I first got to know the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 a week before the mission, when I took part in special training exercises. Until then, I'd only worked with standard Heavy Shot drones," he says.
The most dangerous part was hoisting the soldier, who had to attach himself to the cable on his own. The day before the flight, the drone delivered off-the-shelf mountaineering equipment and a phone loaded with a video explaining how to put on and secure the harness.
According to the plan, the soldier had to attach himself to the drone's winch with carabiners, sitting in a semi-reclined position. Any mistake when securing himself, or losing consciousness during the flight, could have sent him falling to the ground.
16 kilometres
Russian FPV anti-aircraft drones meant the cargo drone could not fly alone. Slow and bulky, with a payload suspended beneath it, it would be immediately spotted by Russian reconnaissance. The headquarters planned a diversionary manoeuvre to draw attention away from it.
Several formations helped provide cover for the operation. Alongside the 2nd Battalion of the 30th Mechanised Brigade, units from the 14th and 43rd Separate Mechanised Brigades took part, as did personnel and equipment from the 10th Army Corps. The day before the flight, the neighbouring units involved suggested putting it off because there was no fog. But the forecast showed no fog was expected any time soon, so the command decided to go ahead.
"We studied enemy drone activity to find the time when it was at its lowest. We decided to fly at first light, as night gave way to day," explains Alex, the battalion's reconnaissance chief.
The main diversion was carried out by Vampire heavy bomber drones, which flew into neighbouring sectors simultaneously to draw the attention of Russian anti-aircraft drone operators. The Russians shot down one Vampire, but the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 carrying out the evacuation went unnoticed.
Alex spent 48 hours studying data on Russian assets around the planned mission area. Experts from the 3rd Army Corps also helped prepare the Ayudag's electronic warfare system for the flight.
An Autel quadcopter operated by the battalion provided visual cover for the Ayudag-6, giving the crew a pair of eyes in the sky. However, it struggled to keep pace with the faster evacuation drone. A Ukrainian Lucky Strike drone waited nearby, ready to ram any Russian reconnaissance or strike UAVs that appeared. As the aircraft carrying Magura returned, artillery from the 10th Army Corps delivered concentrated suppressive fire against the identified launch points used by Russian drone operators.
Headquarters had a backup plan in case the drone malfunctioned or was shot down over the left bank of the Oskil River. Reconnaissance teams and ground robot crews were standing by near the designated emergency landing sites, ready to respond.
The Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 relied on Starlink for communications, which kept Russian electronic warfare systems from jamming it. No interference was detected on the control links. The drone's altitude was adjusted to suit the terrain, and it took a different route back to prevent the Russians from identifying its outbound flight path.
The drone was in the air for less than an hour and a half. The operator spoke to the wounded soldier through the drone's onboard camera and microphone.
The drone could not cover the full 16 km on a single charge: carrying a person drained its batteries too quickly. Two ground support teams were deployed along the route in advance to provide the necessary support.
"On command, I flew to a waypoint, where the team changed the batteries. Then I continued to the evacuation point, picked up the wounded soldier and flew him back," says Chornyi, who piloted the evacuation drone.
At the transfer point, the wounded soldier was detached from the winch. The next leg of the evacuation was carried out by a Peacemaker ground robotic system, as using vehicles would have risked exposing the operation to the enemy.
The troops camouflaged the platform and laid mattresses in its cargo compartment. The remotely controlled Peacemaker then covered another 8 km off-road. Once in a safe area, the team transferred Kostiantyn to a vehicle and took him to a frontline stabilisation point for emergency surgery. The Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 returned to base intact after a battery change at a stop along the route.
Kostiantyn told Ukrainska Pravda: "The flight went smoothly. I spent most of the time looking at the terrain below. When I landed, I felt safe and relieved – I'd finally be able to see my family soon. A special thank you to my unit clerk, Livsha, for keeping me well supplied with treats."
Despite the soldier's calm assessment, the actual flight revealed issues that had been difficult to anticipate during training with a dummy load. He had not been given protective goggles, so the powerful airflow beneath the rotors and the headwind caused discomfort. However, this did not detract from the mission's overall success.
Alex also credited Kostiantyn's calmness during boarding with helping make the mission a success. He had to get onto the drone in an open area while its rotors were spinning above him.
"The soldier was exceptionally quick-thinking and determined to survive," he said. "We had already dropped off his equipment and instructions. When the quadcopter approached, he did everything exactly as instructed, as quickly as possible. There was no panic or hesitation – the whole thing took just seconds and went exactly to plan."
The future of aerial evacuation
One successful operation does not make aerial evacuation a regular option, nor can it replace ground-based evacuation. Missions like this require extensive preparation and coordinated support from multiple units. This operation involved reconnaissance, artillery, decoy-drone crews and ground teams. Without them, the aircraft carrying the wounded soldier would have been shot down by the first Russian interceptor drone on its way.
The drone's developers take a similar view. Gurzuf Defence says the risks to a casualty's life during flight are simply too high for aerial medical evacuation to become standard practice.
"We don't see aerial evacuation becoming routine," says Pavlo Feldblium, co-founder of Gurzuf Defence. "When people talk about thousands of such missions or suggest that drones could help meet the 'golden hour', I think of the science fiction of Ray Bradbury or Stanisław Lem. You can't launch an operation like this on the spur of the moment. Every mission is unique and has to be planned around the specific conditions on that section of the front line. It's important to understand that this is always a last resort."
The experience of rescuing Magura, however, has prompted changes to drone development. Gurzuf Defence has decided to equip its mass-produced Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 logistics drones with the technical modifications and mounting kits needed for emergency evacuations, enabling them to be used for rescue missions when necessary.
The company stresses, however, that the evacuation equipment will not necessarily be used on every flight: the drone remains primarily a logistics platform. The developers are also working on entirely new variants of the platform with a substantially higher payload capacity.
The operation has shown that wounded soldiers can be evacuated by air even if they cannot walk and are stranded in remote positions. Other manufacturers are also exploring this capability. SkyFall recently unveiled its StarGate evacuation drone.
This evacuation, carried out by the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade and the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, has proved the viability of the concept and highlighted the urgent need for an evacuation method that can be used when all other options fail. Magura's rescue has set a precedent for saving lives in situations where conventional evacuation is impossible.
Kostiantyn "Magura" Vlasenko, who held a position on the left bank of the Oskil River for 491 days despite losing both feet, has been nominated for the title of Hero of Ukraine.
After Magura was evacuated to the rear, the commander of the 10th Army Corps visited him in hospital and personally presented him with the Order of Bohdan Khmelnytskyi, 3rd Class. The infantryman had been awarded the order in May, while still holding his position. Soldiers from the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, who planned and carried out the aerial evacuation, have also been nominated for state awards.
Representatives of Gurzuf Defence – the manufacturer of the very Ayudag-6 that flew him out of hell – also visited Magura in hospital.
Yurii Denysiuk
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Susan McDonald

articles.title: Trump's midterm election calculations are complicating US policy on Ukraine – Reuters
articles.body:
Trump's midterm election calculations are complicating US policy on Ukraine – Reuters
The upcoming US midterm elections in November may help explain changes in US President Donald Trump's approach to Russia's war against Ukraine and his displays of support for Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Source: Reuters
Details: Reuters said Trump has shifted his position quite openly on a major political issue over the past month. After criticising Putin, he has begun to show support for him.
Quote from Reuters: "What explains the turnabout? The November midterms may offer a clue."
Details: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Reuters once described as "once Washington's most celebrated wartime ally", has found himself caught in the crossfire of US election politics. Trump is putting increasing pressure on him to reach a peace deal with Putin.
"With US voters increasingly frustrated by high energy prices and the cost of living, Trump has turned renewed attention to the war in Ukraine in recent days, arguing that a negotiated settlement there could help ease economic pressures at home, even though US consumers would be unlikely to feel the effects of any peace deal ahead of the 3 November vote," Reuters said.
Trump has said the war may be closer to ending than ever before and that he wants the death and destruction to stop.
However, Reuters suggested that he may also be calculating that settling the four-year conflict could ease pressure on the US economy, voters' wallets and his own political prospects. Russia is a major oil supplier and has not ruled out a broad economic deal with Washington.
Trump has struck a deal with Putin in the past few weeks, temporarily easing some US sanctions on Russian diesel fuel and lifting others in exchange for Moscow supplying more diesel to global markets.
He is considering meeting Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next month without Zelenskyy's participation.
Meanwhile, Kyiv has complained that the US satellite system operated by SpaceX installed on high-speed drones stopped working, limiting Ukraine's ability to strike Russian targets and defend itself against attacks.
Quote from Reuters: "The moves are a shift from Trump's earlier criticisms of Putin and a return to more prickly relations between the US and Ukrainian leaders. Ukraine and several European allies have expressed alarm at an apparent pivot by Trump."
Details: Trump has accused Ukraine of driving up global diesel prices through its attacks on Russian oil refineries. He has also suggested that Ukraine needs a new leader.
"Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," he said at the White House on 19 October.
Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff later called Putin a "humanitarian" for releasing a retired American teacher who had been detained in Russia since 2022.
Quote from Reuters: "The Ukrainian attacks have contributed to higher diesel prices, although market analysts attribute most of the increase to disruptions in fuel shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. That's a consequence of a different war: the US-led one with Iran."
"Trump wouldn't be the first politician to lay blame for inflation abroad. His Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, pointed to Putin after Russia's invasion of Ukraine caused gasoline prices to surge ahead of congressional elections in 2022."
Details: Reuters noted that voters are not convinced by Trump's arguments. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll, around 78% of Americans believe his policies are at least partly responsible for rising prices. Most Republicans and Democrats alike identified the cost of living as their main concern.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy told visiting US lawmakers on 19 October that the latest "decisions on the American side… are hard to explain".
Background: Zelenskyy said he believed Trump could help end Russia's war against Ukraine if he changed his rhetoric towards Putin.

articles.title: Railcar depot, temporary deployment sites for USV operators hit in Russian strikes
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russian forces continued overnight strikes with unmanned aerial vehicles against railway infrastructure facilities, as well as Ukrainian ports and vessels used to support the Ukrainian armed forces, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has summarized the key details about the targets of the strikes.
Defense Ministry statement
Russian forces continued strikes with unmanned aerial vehicles against railway infrastructure facilities, as well as Ukrainian ports and vessels used in the interests of the Ukrainian armed forces, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
Targets hit
According to the ministry, the Poltava railcar depot in Poltava Region was hit. Its grounds are used by the Ukrainian armed forces to store and repair military equipment.
Russian forces also struck two temporary deployment sites for unmanned surface vessel (USV) operators, a boat mooring area and a USV storage site at the port of Vilkovo in Odessa Region, as well as port infrastructure used to store USVs and prepare them for deployment.
In addition, a cargo ship carrying supplies for the Ukrainian armed forces to the port of Odessa was struck at sea.
Russian troops used Geran drones to strike Norwegian-made mobile NASAMS surface-to-air missile systems in Zaporozhye and Dnepropetrovsk Regions, the Russian Defense Ministry reported, releasing footage of the strikes.
Russian forces also used Geran drones to strike a parked Mi-24 helicopter, a military supplies depot and a production building at one of Ukraine’s industrial enterprises.
Situation in Ukraine
A thermal power plant in Ukraine was damaged in explosions, and electricity generation was halted, Ukrainian energy holding company DTEK said on its Telegram channel.
The company did not disclose the name or location of the thermal power plant.

articles.title: Finland Prepares 36th Military Aid Package for Ukraine, Decision Expected by Year-End
articles.body:

- World
Finland Prepares 36th Military Aid Package for Ukraine, Decision Expected by Year-End
Finland is preparing its 36th military aid package for Ukraine, with a decision on its approval expected before the end of 2026, Militarnyi reported on October 23.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo announced the plans during a joint press conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on October 22.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"We are currently preparing the 36th package in close cooperation with the Ukrainian military. We plan to make a decision by the end of this year," Orpo stated.
The Finnish government is coordinating the contents of the upcoming package directly with Ukraine's military to address its operational requirements. Details of the equipment and weapons under consideration have not yet been disclosed.
Orpo noted that Finland had already provided Ukraine with five military aid packages in 2026. He confirmed that Helsinki would continue supplying military equipment and supporting the training of Ukrainian personnel.
The planned delivery is part of Finland's continued military assistance to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Previous shipments have included artillery ammunition, armored vehicles, and other military equipment.
Among the Finnish weapons already deployed by Ukrainian forces are 120 KRH 85 92 mortars and Crotale air defense systems, designated ItO 90M in Finnish service. The Crotale systems are designed to intercept low-altitude aerial targets, including aircraft, helicopters, and drones.
Finland approved its 35th military assistance package on October 9 in response to an urgent Ukrainian request. That shipment contained a single type of defense equipment from Finnish military stocks, while preparations for a larger follow-up package were already underway.
The upcoming package builds on a sharp increase in the scale of Finnish assistance earlier this autumn.
On September 15, Finland allocated its 34th package, worth approximately $335 million, its second-largest defense allocation to Kyiv since the full-scale invasion began. Part of the equipment was purchased directly from the Finnish defense industry, while the contents and delivery schedule remained confidential for operational security.
That decision raised the total value of Finnish defense aid to roughly $4.15 billion, up from about $3.68 billion after President Alexander Stubb approved the $138.5 million 33rd package on May 29.
