articles.title: Signs point to renewed major US military ops against Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Signs point to renewed major US military ops against Iran
The United States appears to be preparing to resume large-scale strikes against Iran, but there is unlikely to be a military solution for either side in the devastating conflict, experts say.
Washington and Tehran's forces have settled into a pattern of strikes on commercial ships, with the United States seeking to enforce a blockade of Iran's ports and the Islamic republic trying to exert control over the key Strait of Hormuz waterway.
Neither country has engaged in major attacks on land-based targets since early September, but that may soon change.
"I'm banking now on the likelihood of strikes shortly after the midterms," said Suzanne Maloney, director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, referring to November 3 elections in the United States.
She pointed to potential signs including the movement of additional US military assets and troops to the Middle East, warnings issued to Americans in the region, and a high alert status for Israeli forces.
Additionally, President Donald Trump "came out publicly and said that he wouldn't strike before the midterms," and "it wouldn't seem to help him at the polls to do so," Maloney said.
The US-Israeli war against Iran -- launched in late February -- is largely unpopular in the United States, especially because it has sharply driven up fuel prices, and is likely to be a drag on Trump's Republican Party in the key vote.
"Fundamentally, the situation isn't sustainable in its current state," Maloney said, noting that the US blockade is "creating greater pain for the Iranians," while Washington has a large number of naval assets tied up in enforcing it.
"There has to be some kind of a resolution, either through diplomacy or through military action," she said.
Asked about the Iran on Friday, Trump told journalists that "we could end it very quickly," but said the question is "do we want to finish it off, or... do we just want to let it wither?"
Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, meanwhile said Friday that there could "absolutely" be a strike this weekend, ahead of Tuesday's Israeli elections.
'Impossible to predict'
Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said there have "certainly been recent signs that renewed strikes may be in the offing," or that "the US is expecting strikes carried out by Iran" or their Houthi allies in Yemen.
He noted the planned deployment of the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East -- which could at least temporarily bring the number of carrier strike groups there to three -- as well as the decision to dispatch another Marine Expeditionary Unit to the region.
Campbell also said Israeli warplanes recently carried out a "show of force" mimicking previous strikes on Iran, and noted that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel.
However, "timing here is impossible to predict," he said of renewed strikes, while noting that "this is admittedly an expansive set of actions to take if the intent is to simply pressure Iran to the negotiating table."
Campbell said Trump's options are more limited than they were earlier in the conflict, with damage to US bases in the region having made any potential ground operation more difficult.
"At this point, there is no safe place to stage the thousands (in some scenarios tens of thousands) of forces that would be required for such an operation," he said.
Maloney meanwhile said that "most of the conventional military sites (in Iran) have already been heavily degraded" by previous strikes, meaning any new campaign will likely "entail more strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets that impact the Iranian population."
But that -- or any type of military action -- is unlikely to bring about a resolution to the conflict.
"From the start... this has been a war that can't be ended with further escalation on either side," Maloney said.
Campbell agreed, saying: "I do not see how renewed strikes on Iran akin to the first fifty days of the war will move the strategic needle for the Iranian regime."
"They have demonstrated a willingness to absorb a significant amount of physical pain and even some alterations to targeting that includes key mixed or even civilian infrastructure will not significantly change this," he added.

articles.title: Streeting declines to discuss Faslane shelters
articles.body:
The Secretary of State for Defence has declined to discuss reported ballistic shelters at Faslane in open session, telling the Defence Committee there is a difference between what others report and what the department is willing to say.
Wes Streeting was giving evidence to the committee on the work of his department.
Michelle Scrogham, the Labour member for Barrow and Furness, raised air and missile defence, noting the committee had heard that covering what is needed would cost a billion pounds per city. She said: “I am interested to hear it reported that Faslane is getting ballistic shelters. Are you looking at rolling that out in other areas?”
Streeting said: “There is a danger of my being dragged into a level of operational security detail that I would not want to share in this format.”
Scrogham replied: “It is public knowledge. It is in the UK Defence Journal.”
Streeting said: “There is a difference between what others report and what we are willing to say. Given the spirit in which we engage with this Committee, first, I would always be happy to try to share with the Committee in a closed format as much as we can of that which we would not want to share in an open session. Given your constituency interest in this, I can reassure you that the security of our nuclear deterrent and the enterprise that underpins it is obviously of the highest importance to us. I would be very happy to make sure that we properly brief you as the Member of Parliament for Barrow.”
Faslane on the Clyde is the base for the Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines that carry the continuous at-sea deterrent, and for the Astute class attack submarines. Coulport, a few miles away, stores and loads the warheads. Barrow-in-Furness, which Scrogham represents, is where the submarines are built by BAE Systems.
Earlier in the same exchange Streeting addressed homeland air defence more generally, saying the government is putting £790 million into integrated air and missile defence to modernise older systems and that a layered approach is needed. He noted that Luke Pollard had described the idea of an iron dome for Britain as an iron sieve.
Ministers confirmed in Parliament this month that a future requirement for hardened aircraft shelters across Royal Air Force bases in the United Kingdom has been identified, and that hardened shelters may form part of future infrastructure considerations at RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus.
The Defence Committee reported this week that Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and to Britain, including to the nuclear deterrent, and that failure to deter Russia from underwater threats puts subsea data cables and energy pipelines in British waters at particular risk.

articles.title: Sudan: El Fasher civilians suffer unlawful killings, detention and torture one year after city’s capture by the RSF – new testimony
articles.body:
- Surveillance and detentions rife in city
- With limited humanitarian aid, risks of child malnutrition remain high
- “A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today” – Agnès Callamard
Civilians in El Fasher in North Darfur, Sudan, are still suffering detention, torture and limited access to humanitarian aid one year after the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) captured the city and committed brutalities against civilians, Amnesty International said today.
In new testimony, residents who recently escaped the city told Amnesty International how schools had been turned into detention centres, how their movement was strictly controlled, and that unlawful killings were rife.
According to figures gathered by humanitarian organizations working in the city, fewer than 70,000 people are present in El Fasher, compared to its pre-war population of more than one million. Humanitarian access remains limited, and humanitarian workers and other civilians in the city are constantly surveilled or monitored. Arbitrary detention risks, for both civilians and humanitarian workers, remain extremely high.
A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
“The RSF’s claims that El Fasher is safe for civilians to return to after the horrific massacres that took place one year ago could not be further from the truth,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today. Men and women live under constant RSF surveillance, and with the ongoing threat of detention, torture and killing.
“One year since El Fasher fell to the RSF, the international community has failed to take the necessary actions to address the desperate plight civilians face as the conflict rages. There has been little accountability for abuses in North Darfur. The moves towards a ceasefire have been half-hearted, and Amnesty International is not aware of any diplomatic attempts to establish an international force that would meaningfully protect civilians.
“Crucially, the United Arab Emirates has continued to support the RSF, while governments with the required influence have largely failed to name and denounce their role or hold them to account.
“Without a ceasefire, accountability, and a protection force, civilians will continue to suffer in El Fasher and across Sudan. The Sudanese Armed Forces have consistently opposed the extension of an arms embargo and a ceasefire, continuing to believe that a military ‘solution’ to the conflict remains possible, thereby also setting aside the suffering of the Sudanese people.”
In August and September 2026, Amnesty International interviewed 25 civilians, including 19 residents and six humanitarian workers, regarding the situation in El Fasher. Of the residents, 15 left El Fasher between July and August 2026 and one was still in the city; the other three had fled earlier.
On 9 October, Amnesty International wrote to the RSF regarding the findings. At the time of publication, no response had been received.
In July 2026, Amnesty International released a major report that documented how the RSF committed crimes against humanity and ethnic cleansing during its campaign to seize El Fasher, with certain ethnic groups, including the Zaghawa, singled out for abuse. Amnesty International continues to document flagrant abuses committed by both parties to the conflict in Sudan, including in El Obeid, North Kordofan, as well as in South Kordofan and Blue Nile States.
Detention, torture, and unlawful killings in prisons
Of the 19 residents interviewed, 17 were detained by the RSF. Most were arbitrarily detained during the RSF capture of the city, while several were detained when they returned to retrieve belongings from their homes or to search for missing family members. They were all held in captivity for months. Several noted that people of particular ethnic groups, notably Zaghawa and Masalit people, were more likely to be detained and abused.
Most men were held in detention centres or prisons, where they witnessed unlawful killings, suffered torture and other ill-treatment, and were given minimal food or water. All were released only after family members paid ransom, or by escaping.
If you sleep a lot, they don’t like that, they will execute you
Modathir*, a 29-year-old Zaghawa man, who was detained in Shala prison
Modathir*, a 29-year-old Zaghawa man, was detained in Shala prison. He was regularly beaten and witnessed unlawful killings. He told Amnesty International: “Torture is something which is permanent in any [RSF] detention. They executed people who tried to look at them… If you sleep a lot, they don’t like that, they will execute you. They ask, ‘You want to take a rest? We will give you permanent rest’.” In July 2026, Modathir escaped, fleeing from house to house in order to reach safety.
Mamoun*, a 33-year-old Zaghawa man, was also held in Shala prison until July 2026. He said he witnessed the RSF shooting prisoners, and the death of a man with untreated diabetes who the RSF refused to help. Mamoun was regularly beaten, and said: “They take people out [of the cell] randomly, they accuse you of being with the Joint Forces or the military… And they beat you until you faint… Sometimes I was beaten four times a day… It just depends on their mood.” Mamoun was eventually released after his family paid a ransom.
Paying ransom was not always a guarantee of freedom. Musa*, a 23-year-old Zaghawa man, said that he and his father were detained at El Fasher Children’s Hospital in October 2025. They were released more than a month later after they paid a ransom. However, instead of being allowed to leave the city, Musa said the RSF took them to an RSF-guarded house and held there until around May 2026 when they were able to escape.
Musa and his father were forced to work for the RSF including collecting corpses, and were sometimes forced to speak on camera to say that the city was inhabitable, encouraging people to return. He said: “They paraded us inside the city and told us to talk [about how] El Fasher is good and safe.”
Detention in schools
Women, children, and some older or injured men were held in schools that were de facto detention centres. They described high rates of malnutrition, including among their own children.
Amnesty International interviewed nine people who were detained by the RSF in schools. They had extremely limited access to food and medical treatment; some women said that their children became malnourished during their detention there. All of these individuals were released or managed to escape by July or August 2026.
Haram*, a 45-year-old Zaghawa woman, and her young children were detained at a school in the Daraja Oula neighbourhood. She told Amnesty International: “[The RSF] were verbally abusing people… Zaghawa people were beaten, [the RSF] would just select and randomly beat [people]. They called us falangayaat women [a slur that indicates slavery or servitude].”
Hadia*, a 30-year-old Gimir woman whose husband was shot by the RSF during their capture of El Fasher, was detained in a school with her children, along with hundreds of other women and children. The RSF provided them very limited food and water.
Hadia was too malnourished to provide her youngest child, aged 18 months, with sufficient breast milk. When she finally escaped and reached Tawila in August 2026, all three of her children were diagnosed with malnutrition; one was hospitalized. Hadia told Amnesty International: “My children were very skinny and weak.”
Aloya*, a 54-year-old Zaghawa woman, spent several months detained in a school. She was afraid that her Zaghawa identity would be discovered and so never spoke the language while there. She said: “Daily there were four to five people dying… mostly from lack of food.”
Hatim*, a 38-year-old Berti man with a serious shrapnel injury in his jaw, was detained by the RSF when he returned to El Fasher to retrieve personal belongings from his house in spring 2026. He was taken to a school where he was kept for about four months with an estimated 300 people, mostly women. He told Amnesty International: “You could not move freely, you had to stay there… [The RSF] beat me up two times I tried fleeing… including on my wounds.” On his third attempt, Hatim was able to escape.
Amnesty International analysed satellite imagery of school detention sites between October 2025 and September 2026. While several sites indicated signs of human activity in previous months, by September 2026 there was little daily activity, suggesting that these detention sites may have been closed. Shala prison and Mina al-Bari detention centre, another facility where residents were held, still showed significant signs of human activity.
‘Everybody is terrorized’: RSF surveillance and limited humanitarian access
El Fasher residents told Amnesty International that while a small number of humanitarian organizations were operating in the city again as of September 2026, the RSF closely monitored their movements and prevented residents from speaking freely to them.
One resident who had returned to El Fasher in June 2026 told Amnesty International: “The El Fasher I knew is gone, it is a completely destroyed city. The public infrastructure, the schools, government institutions, hospitals, all are destroyed… It seemed like everybody is watched very closely, they don’t give humanitarian workers any private space to talk… Everybody is terrorized.”
Another resident said: “There is no complete blockage of [humanitarian] access, but… when organizations are implementing activities [the RSF] will monitor implementation… There are no pictures, no interviews, no interactions of any kind.”
Humanitarian workers expressed concerns about malnutrition, particularly amid a poor harvest season. According to official assessments, IPC Level 5 famine, the highest threshold possible, is highly likely in North Darfur, including in El Fasher, in the months ahead.
Forced labour
Both men and women were subjected to forced labour, such as collecting dead bodies and rubble from El Fasher’s streets, or cooking and cleaning for the RSF without pay.
Misbah*, a 32-year-old Zaghawa man, was detained by the RSF in October 2025. He was brought to a house in the Daraja Oula neighbourhood, where he was forced to cook and clean for RSF officers. He was tied up and given very little to eat. He said he was beaten every day, and said: “I never thought I would survive.”
The RSF should immediately release all those who have been arbitrary detained, and end torture and unlawful killings in detention and elsewhere. The use of forced labour, which is prohibited by international law, must also end.
Amnesty International is again calling for an immediate ceasefire and for the urgent deployment of an international force to protect civilians. All countries must also immediately stop providing arms and ammunition to all parties to the conflict in Sudan. In particular, all countries must cease arms transfers to the United Arab Emirates until it stops supplying weapons to RSF in violation of the UN embargo on Darfur. The UN Security Council must also expand the existing arms embargo on Darfur to the rest of the country.

articles.title: Starobelsk massacre survivors recount lingering terror to RT (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Starobelsk massacre survivors recount lingering terror to RT (VIDEO)
The survivors of the deadly Ukrainian drone attack on the Starobelsk college in May have spoken to RT about the emotional scars left behind by the tragedy that killed 21 students in their sleep.
Multiple waves of kamikaze UAVs struck the dormitory of the Starobelsk Professional College, located in Russia’s Lugansk People’s Republic (LPR), on May 22. The building partially collapsed as a result of the strikes, killing 21 people and injuring 42 others, mostly teenage girls studying to become teachers. The Ukrainian military subsequently targeted first responders with additional drones, according to investigators.
Twenty students who survived the attack on the dormitory that fateful night came to Moscow on Wednesday at the invitation of Russia’s Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova.
Lantratova and the students discussed their professional aspirations, with the official noting that some of them have already become volunteers in various projects. She also said that the human rights commission’s doors are open to survivors wishing to undertake an internship there. The official gifted a bus to the college as well as tablet computers to its students.
Speaking to RT, one of the survivors recounted how she took cover in the basement on the night of the attack and “ended up getting buried under the debris.” Acting on “autopilot,” she extricated herself from the rubble and ran for her life. The student said that in the wake of the tragic incident, she “started to be afraid of everything, even the slightest rustle.”
“Especially during the first week, it was absolutely terrifying. I was afraid of every single loud noise,” the survivor told RT.
Another student shared a similar experience of lingering trauma, saying that following the attack, “any loud noise, even just something falling was terrifying. My heart would immediately start pounding violently.”
Lantratova said the attack had been funded with Western taxpayers’ money and accused Kiev’s backers of glossing over the atrocity perpetrated by the Ukrainian military. Kiev has denied responsibility for the incident, with various officials providing conflicting accounts of the massacre.
President Vladimir Putin vowed “inevitable punishment” for the Starobelsk massacre, and several days later, Russia launched one of its largest retaliatory drone and missile strikes, targeting Ukrainian military command facilities, air bases, and defense industry enterprises.

articles.title: Exclusive: Ukraine fears Trump could grant Russia long-sought relief for fertilizer industry
articles.body:
Exclusive: The next Russia deal Trump may be weighing after diesel
U.S. President Donald Trump looks on during an event in the Oval Office of the White House on Oct. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump may be considering further sanctions relief for Russia following his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, several Ukrainian and U.S. officials familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent.
The potential move would fit an approach in which the Trump administration offers Russia economic benefits in hopes of persuading Moscow to end its war against Ukraine, one U.S. government official and one Senate official said.
Trump's diesel deal with Putin has drawn bipartisan criticism in Washington and strained relations with Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelensky called the agreement a "weak move," warning that it could pave the way for further sanctions relief.
Now, Ukrainian officials fear the administration could explore a deal involving Russia's fertilizer industry, two people familiar with the matter said.
The U.S. has not directly sanctioned Russia's fertilizer industry or banned imports of Russian fertilizers. But any potential agreement could provide sanctions relief for vessels, companies, banks, and individuals linked to the industry, one senior Ukrainian official said.
Russia has long sought an ease of restrictions affecting its agricultural exports, arguing that banking, insurance, and shipping barriers have limited its access to markets.
Moscow raised the issue repeatedly during negotiations over the Black Sea Grain Initiative (BSGI) back in 2022, but Western governments maintained that Russian food and fertilizer exports were not directly sanctioned.
"The fertilizer story is quite old, and Russians were trying to push it long ago," a Ukrainian intelligence official told the Kyiv Independent.
"Russians always lobbied for fertilizer relief in contacts with Americans and Europeans," the official added. "They actually left BSGI because of no progress on fertilizers."
Russia withdrew from the Black Sea Grain Initiative in July 2023, saying insufficient progress had been made on its demands.
Ukrainian officials now fear Washington could be prepared to offer Moscow concessions on an issue it has pursued for years.
A sanctions-for-peace push
Trump announced the diesel deal on Oct. 9, saying Russia had agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel to the U.S. and international markets.
"Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The announcement raised questions in Washington about the deal's legality.
"We view the Russian diesel deal as illegal as per the 2022 law that had passed both chambers and was signed into law," one Senate official said.
Congress passed the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act in 2022, banning imports of Russian-origin energy products, including diesel.
Several people familiar with the matter said Democratic officials were contacting U.S. industries involved in facilitating the deal to ensure they understood the potential legal and investigative risks.
The deal could face further scrutiny in Congress. But as questions over its legality mount, Ukrainian officials fear Washington could seek other ways to offer Russia economic concessions, with fertilizers emerging as one possible area.
"Well, they clearly have some kind of plan," one official said.
Some Senate officials also believe the Trump administration overestimates the scale of the economic deals Russia could offer Washington in return.
The potential fertilizer deal remains unclear, and the officials who spoke to the Kyiv Independent named no specific sanctions Washington might lift.
The Kyiv Independent has contacted the White House for comment and will update the story when it receives a response.
read also
Kyiv warns against further concessions
The Ukrainian president has publicly warned that the diesel deal could be the start of a broader rollback of sanctions against Russia.
"There's intuition, there's intelligence, and there are various details," Zelensky said Oct. 16. "In my view, we cannot accept these agreements. Because gas deals will follow. And I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, they will lift sanctions on other things as well."
The warning shows Kyiv's concern that Washington is shifting toward economic incentives for Moscow even as Russia continues its war against Ukraine.
Before the diesel announcement, Russian officials had repeatedly argued that Moscow and Washington should expand their business ties. The Trump administration, meanwhile, had maintained that economic deals should follow an end to Russia's war.
Ukrainian officials argue that offering concessions before securing a ceasefire is unlikely to persuade Putin to stop fighting. Instead, they say, such agreements could provide Russia with additional revenue while leaving Moscow's military objectives unchanged.
The concern is especially acute because, according to Ukrainian officials, Russia offered the U.S. nothing meaningful in return for the diesel deal.
"It's clear that this only encourages Putin," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
"He feels that he can go with a war against us, and on top of that, our allies are lifting sanctions against him and striking deals with him."
Speaking to Russian media on Oct. 22, Putin once again made his intentions clear.
Asked whether he would agree to a ceasefire allowing Ukraine to retain the territory it controls, he replied: "It's not their territory; it's the territory of historical Russia."

articles.title: Europe will have to accept dependence on us – US tech giant
articles.body:
Europe will have to accept dependence on us – US tech giant
European governments should stop worrying about their growing dependence on American AI, US tech giant Palantir’s top executive for the UK and Europe has said. Instead, they should focus on the advantages the products offer, particularly against Russia, Palantir UK CEO Louis Mosley believes.
The European Commission is frantically trying to reduce reliance on American tech and the US in general.
“Europe is going to have to accept some dependency,” Mosely told Bloomberg News this week.
The Commission estimates that the bloc relies on foreign providers for over 80% of its digital products, services, infrastructure, and intellectual property. However, many are skeptical that replacement is possible. In a Wire’s 2025 survey cited by the European Parliament, only 16% of regional IT leaders said the bloc could achieve digital sovereignty within five years, with almost 60% citing US dominance as a key obstacle.
Nevertheless, this year several European governments have rejected Palantir products or announced plans to phase them out. France’s domestic intelligence agency, the DGSI, which adopted the company’s analytical software in 2015, has plans to drop it over the coming years in favor of a domestically developed alternative from ChapsVision.
“We cannot depend on the goodwill of certain partners who, as we’ve seen in recent days, are capable of cutting off access to models,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said when announcing the decision in June.
Berlin has reportedly chosen the same French competitor over Palantir for Germany’s domestic intelligence agency BfV.
Similar moves to ostracize the American firm have been reported in Spain and Denmark, as well as the non-EU nations of Switzerland, Norway, and the UK.
Mosley cited Palantir’s extensive use of the Ukraine conflict as a testing ground for its military solutions, saying “the questions around sovereignty are secondary” for Kiev. The company got involved in Ukraine following the escalation of Kiev’s conflict with Russia in 2022, supplying what it calls “targeting packages.”
One of Palantir’s flagship products is Maven, an AI-powered system that processes vast amounts of intelligence data to help identify targets and generate strike recommendations for troops. It accelerates the so-called “kill chain,” allowing the military to consider substantially more potential targets than human personnel previously could.
Originally developed as a Pentagon project, Maven involved Google until 2018, when employee protests prompted the company to withdraw from the initiative. NATO purchased its own version of the system for use at its European headquarters in March 2025.
“I can provide categorical reassurance that where customers have bought our software, they are in full operational control of that software,” Mosley assured in a separate interview with Reuters concerning NATO’s purchase.
There are no kill switches. There’s no ability for Palantir or the US government to reach in and switch it off.
The US government has a track record of restricting foreign access to flagship AI models. The French prime minister’s remark about a lack of goodwill was a reference to Washington’s blockage of Anthropic’s Mythos 5 tool, which lasted for almost three weeks.

articles.title: US offers Russia Nord Stream restart as part of peace deal
articles.body:
US proposes restart of Nord Stream as part of peace deal with Russia
The United States is proposing that Russian gas supplies to Europe and the operation of the Nord Stream pipeline be resumed as an economic incentive for Moscow as part of a potential peace settlement to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
Source: The Economist
Details: The Economist describes the gas proposal as the latest concession Washington is offering Vladimir Putin. Ukrainian officials, meanwhile, do not yet know all the details of the latest US proposals.
The magazine reports that Russia would be offered commercial deals with US companies, sanctions relief and the normalisation of political relations. Ukraine would be offered an investment package and EU membership in exchange for abandoning its bid to join NATO. The proposals also envisage the creation of a demilitarised zone in Donbas.
The Economist stresses that the US cannot unilaterally decide to restore Russian gas supplies to the European market. It assesses that such a proposal would run counter to EU law.
Ukrainian negotiators fear that US representatives could strike lucrative economic deals with Russia even before the war ends.
The Economist itself questions Moscow's willingness to make peace. It assesses that Russia is likely to drag out the negotiations while securing immediate concessions on sanctions.
The renewed diplomatic push comes after US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff visited St Petersburg on 21 October, The Economist notes.
Background: On 18 October, it was reported that the Trump administration had proposed that Europe resume purchases of Russian gas. According to The New York Times, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff raised the idea during talks with Ukrainian and European officials.

articles.title: Israeli airstrikes, artillery shelling hit southern Lebanon amid intensified drone activity
articles.body:
Israeli warplanes carried out airstrikes and artillery shelling in southern Lebanon on Friday, while drones flew intensively at low altitude over the capital Beirut and the southern city of Tyre, Lebanese state media reported, Anadolu reports.
Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency (NNA) said Israeli fighter jets struck the vicinity of Ali al-Taher hill on the outskirts of Nabatieh al-Fawqa in the Nabatieh district.
The agency reported intermittent Israeli artillery shelling near the town of Zawtar al-Sharqiya in the same district before noon.
In Kfar Shouba, in the Hasbaya district, an Israeli drone dropped a stun grenade in the Khallet Zuhair area on the outskirts of the town.
The agency also said Israeli forces carried out a large explosion overnight in an area between Zawtar al-Sharqiya and Kfar Tebnit in the Nabatieh district.
Israeli forces continued setting fire to wooded areas in the town of Qantara toward the Salouqi area in the Marjayoun district, it added.
Meanwhile, Israeli drones were observed flying at low altitude over Beirut, Tyre and surrounding areas in southern Lebanon.
The attacks came after two days of US-sponsored technical military talks between Lebanon and Israel that began Tuesday in the US state of Florida, with no results announced.
On June 26, Beirut and Tel Aviv reached a US-mediated framework agreement providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of armed groups.
The agreement also introduced a pilot-zone approach to implementation, but its provisions have so far been applied in only three southern Lebanese towns: Froun, Srifa and Zawtar al-Gharbiya, while more than 50 towns remain under Israeli occupation.
Despite the agreement, Israeli attacks on Lebanon have continued, killing at least 4,386 people and injuring 12,407 others since March 2, while displacing more than 1 million people.
Israel continues to occupy areas of southern Lebanon, including territory held for decades and other areas seized during previous conflicts.

The attacks came after two days of US-sponsored technical military talks between Lebanon and Israel that began Tuesday in the US state of Florida, with no results announced.
On June 26, Beirut and Tel Aviv reached a US-mediated framework agreement providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of armed groups.
The agreement also introduced a pilot-zone approach to implementation, but its provisions have so far been applied in only three southern Lebanese towns: Froun, Srifa and Zawtar al-Gharbiya, while more than 50 towns remain under Israeli occupation.
Despite the agreement, Israeli attacks on Lebanon have continued, killing at least 4,386 people and injuring 12,407 others since March 2, while displacing more than 1 million people.
Israel continues to occupy areas of southern Lebanon, including territory held for decades and other areas seized during previous conflicts.

articles.title: Oleshky Evacuation: Russia Announces Kherson Frontline ‘Silence Regime’
articles.body:
Chief of the Russian General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced Moscow will halt fire along the Kherson frontline in what it described as a “silence regime” to allow a humanitarian operation in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, starting Oct. 27.
Gerasimov set the announced date two days earlier than the date previously agreed upon with the White House, noting that it would take effect at 4 a.m. Moscow time.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“To ensure the safety of people and the delivery of socially important cargo, engineering reconnaissance will be organized and safe movement of a humanitarian convoy into the settlement of Oleshky in Kherson region will be ensured,” Gerasimov said, according to Interfax-Russia on Friday, Oct. 23.
The operation to last several days
Asked about the duration of the humanitarian operation, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov declined to provide a specific timeline.
However, according to Russian state-owned media TASS, he said that the operation would “naturally” take “at least several days.”
Kyiv confirms the ceasefire
Although Ukraine has confirmed the White House-brokered arrangement, it has yet to comment on Moscow’s earlier start date.
The Kremlin’s decision to declare a ceasefire raises immediate concerns of possible sabotage among Ukrainian media, given Moscow’s pattern of breaking previous ceasefires, particularly those it declares itself.
Ukraine’s human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, who led the talks with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, earlier confirmed that the ceasefire would take place on Oct. 29.
Ukraine Ends Blanket Deferments, Ties Full Exemptions to Military Service
He outlined three key components of the deal. “First, a silence regime will be ensured; second, humanitarian cargo will be delivered to Oleshky; third, free movement of civilians from Oleshky will be ensured,” Lubinets said, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
However, he did not provide additional details on how long each stage would take, nor how much aid would be delivered. No details were given on the evacuation routes either.
Lubinets also urged the public and media to be careful when sharing information about the mission. “The whole world now knows about Oleshky,” he said, promising to keep Ukrainians informed and show the results of the operation.
Davyd Arakhamia, who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, said that the operation to unblock Oleshky and its surroundings would begin soon.
He described the agreement as a result of a long process involving many people at different political levels, singling out Pope Leo XIV and Melania Trump for their roles.
At the time of the report, neither Kyiv nor Washington has explained why Moscow announced a start date earlier than the one agreed upon.
How the negotiations unfolded
Oleshky, located in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region on the left bank of the Dnipro River, about 5 km (3 miles) southeast of the city of Kherson, has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Ukrainian officials and European leaders have long been aware of the crisis in Oleshky and have worked for months to secure a safe evacuation and restore food supplies, which have not reached the city since May 26.
Beyond food, the town’s residents barely have any drinking water or medicine.
According to Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, Oleshky’s only pharmacy has also reportedly run out of essential medications months ago, while overall medical care has been significantly complicated due to power cuts and lack of fuel as the city remains isolated.
“Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, canned goods, and even snails. Residents say that Russian soldiers have threatened them at gunpoint to seize their food,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
In a statement on Sept. 16, Lubinets said that the residents had started escaping on foot independently across mined fields and under threat of constant Russian drone attacks, simply because they saw no other way out. At the time, he also said Russia had failed to uphold previously agreed arrangements for a humanitarian mission.
“They see no other way to escape this hell,” Lubinets said, adding that his office had received 176 appeals regarding the humanitarian situation in Oleshky, and had already verified at least 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.
On Monday, Oct. 19, Lubinets confirmed that Kyiv and Moscow were in daily contact over a possible evacuation, noting that the Russian side had taken up all proposals previously submitted by Ukraine.
“I cannot disclose many details, but I will say this: In my view, we have made significant progress,” he said.
Ukrainian authorities estimate that about 6,000 people, including some 200 children, remain across Oleshky and the surrounding settlements.
According to European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno, who declared a hunger strike on Tuesday, Oct. 20, in protest over the starvation of civilians in Oleshky, roughly 1,700 people remain in the city from a prewar population of 24,000, including 47 children.
However, neither figure could be independently verified, particularly because Russian occupation authorities narrowly restrict access to information from the area.
White House brokers a date
Earlier on Friday, the White House announced that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to temporarily halt military activity in Oleshky to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare civilian evacuations, starting Oct. 29.
It was not specified how long the truce would last or how many people are expected to be evacuated.
According to Washington’s statement, non-military representatives from Ukraine and Russia would visit residents at home to assess their needs.
“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” said US First Lady Melania Trump.
The Associated Press previously reported that neither the Ukrainian nor the Russian government immediately commented.
Vatican reaches out to both countries
Pope Leo XIV held a telephone discussion with Putin on Oct. 16, in what marked the second phone call between the two, following their first conversation on June 4, 2025 that also focused on the war in Ukraine.
The pope had expressed his deep concern about the humanitarian situation in Oleshky, urging the Russian president to agree to an immediate ceasefire and allow the delivery of food and medical assistance to the city.
He also called for a safe evacuation of the civilians.
While the Kremlin backed Vatican’s initiative and agreed to cooperate, it again pinned the blame for the crisis on Ukraine, despite Kyiv’s repeated appeals to Russian authorities and international partners to secure humanitarian access to the town.
The pontiff then spoke to President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday, Oct. 19, reiterating his earlier request for a humanitarian ceasefire. He expressed hope for a cooperation between Kyiv and Moscow which would allow for the desperately needed food and medical supplies to reach trapped civilians.
“We are working to help our people there. We are preparing decisions,” Zelensky said, confirming the conversation.

articles.title: German grocery wholesaler Metro’s Russian operation donates 1 billion rubles to a fund equipping front-line Russian troops, weeks after Putin placed its assets under temporary management
articles.body:
German grocery wholesaler Metro’s Russian operation donates 1 billion rubles to a fund equipping front-line Russian troops, weeks after Putin placed its assets under temporary management
The retail chain Metro, whose Russian assets were placed under temporary management less than a month ago, said it had donated 1 billion rubles to the “People’s Front: Everything for Victory!” fund.
The money will go toward “purchasing equipment needed by the military on the front lines,” the company said in a press release.
The fund said the money would help meet “urgent needs” for vehicles, communications and reconnaissance systems, equipment to counter drones, and “other things needed by troops in the “special military operation.”
“As part of Russia’s economic system, we believe it is important to take part in the state’s strategic initiatives,” said Johannes Tholey, Metro’s chief executive in Russia.
In late September, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree placing the assets of the German retail chain Metro under temporary management. The company had remained in Russia after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The appointed manager was JSC UK Torg Rus, a company registered three weeks earlier. Its listed owner was Johannes Tholey, who has headed Metro Cash & Carry since 2023.
Le Monde later reported that Metro itself had proposed that the Russian authorities place it under temporary management, deciding to “act preemptively” to avoid the worst-case scenario.

articles.title: AP: Trump's administration gives conflicting accounts of restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield access
articles.body:
AP: Trump's administration gives conflicting accounts of restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield access
Recent attempts to restrict Ukraine's access to satellite systems have triggered a blame game among officials in US President Donald Trump's administration and their allies, who have offered conflicting explanations for the sudden restrictions on Kyiv's ability to intercept Russian attacks.
Source: Associated Press, citing sources
Details: Restrictions imposed on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service and a key part of Ukraine's drone operations and communications, alarmed Ukrainian military and government officials last week. Commanders reported lost drones and interrupted missions. After several days of uncertainty, Trump said on Thursday 22 October that the service was operating again at full speed.
However, AP quoted a senior European official familiar with the situation on the ground in Ukraine as saying that nothing had changed in Starshield's operation and that the speed limit remained at around 160 km/h.
Ukraine has received no clear official explanation of who ordered the restrictions or why, according to the official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
The incident and the subsequent lack of accountability have sparked outrage among Ukraine's allies and supporters of a tougher policy towards Russia on Capitol Hill. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal announced a new investigation into how the speed of Ukraine's defence systems had been restricted.
Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the disruption of the satellite internet network created by Elon Musk, which Ukraine has relied on for years to counter attacks by Moscow.
As recently as Thursday, Trump insisted that he had not issued such an order. Vice-President JD Vance hinted at coordination between the White House and Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth denied any involvement by the administration.
Background:
- On 16 October, Trump said that the White House had nothing to do with the restrictions on Ukraine's access to Starlink.
- According to The Telegraph, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk approached Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink and Starshield operations in Ukraine.
- On 17 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a test conducted by Ukraine in EU countries had confirmed that the restrictions on its use of Starlink were imposed as part of a planned operation.
- Rubio said Trump's administration "had nothing to do with" the restriction of Starlink's operation in Ukraine.
- On 18 October, Zelenskyy told NBC that the signal to restrict Starlink and Starshield access for Ukraine had come from the US government.
- Hegseth said the US was not involved in restricting Starshield's operation in Ukraine and had issued no such orders.

articles.title: ‘I killed lots of terrorists, but it didn’t make me feel better’: The trauma haunting Israel's elections
articles.body:
‘I killed lots of terrorists, but it didn’t make me feel better’: The trauma haunting Israel's elections
From our special correspondent in Tel Aviv – After more than three years of war, the number of Israeli soldiers suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder following bloody campaigns in Gaza and Lebanon has risen drastically. In the lead-up to Israel’s crucial legislative elections, FRANCE 24 speaks with soldiers left shell-shocked by the country’s wars.
The group of Israeli army veterans meets in the departures hall of Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport. They’re anywhere from 20 to 50 years old, and glad to be back together. They hold one another, laughing, and slap each other on the back.
For a year now, these 18 men have come together to give them a chance to speak, and be heard, and to support one another. Accompanied by a team of psychologists, they are all living with varying degrees of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). At the invitation of donors who have funded the programme, they are all on their way to spend a week in New York.
Most of them have no interest in speaking to the media. But Lior Tapicer, a burly blond man with a broad grin, steps forward and lowers his voice.
“They’re all crazy, I love them,” he said. “They make me feel less crazy.”
He agrees to tell us his story – that of a young man traumatised by the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, and by months spent fighting alongside his combat unit, looking for revenge in the ruins of the Gaza Strip.
‘I could die at any second’
Twenty-nine years old, Tapicer has been discharged from the Israeli Defence Force (IDF) and is now working as a naturopath, he said. He says that the trauma that had made him unfit to keep going as an army reservist first took root in him during the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks.
As reports of the attacks on southern Israel spread, he joined his unit and rushed off to the kibbutzim near the border with the Gaza Strip, where combat with Hamas militants and other Palestinian fighters was still raging.
“They gave me an old rifle, I didn’t even have a combat helmet – we were driving in an open jeep,” he said. “The smell of burnt bodies was everywhere, there were bodies everywhere. It was scary as shit – I remember the feeling of being in my own country, and being afraid that I could die at any second.”
Read more‘I don't recognise the country I grew up in anymore’: Some Israelis tempted by exile
The nightmare dragged on into the next night.
“We went into a house – there was shooting, but we were staying silent so they didn’t know we were there”, he said in a detached voice. “And I entered one of the rooms and there was a baby bed, and it was all blood. I won’t describe it.”
A few days later, he entered the Palestinian territory with his combat unit. Having served as a soldier in the Israeli-occupied West Bank since he turned 18, he admits that he was burning for vengeance.
“They attacked us, murdered people, raped,” he said. “To be sincere, when I enlisted the first day, my mind and my body was like, ‘I’m going to kill as many as I can. I’m going to get revenge.’ That’s what I felt in the moment – a lot of hate.”
He broke after four months of fighting. One night, his comrades found him shaking uncontrollably, unable to stand. They decided to have him taken away from the front.
‘I didn’t recognise myself in the mirror’
Although Tapicer was back with his unit 10 days later, he slowly began to realise that his body refused to keep going.
After a few more months, he was declared unfit for service and returned to civilian life. But his mind and his body were still at war. He was wracked with guilt for having left his comrades, who were still fighting in the densely populated territory. He stopped his work as a personal trainer, and began avoiding his family and friends.
“I didn't recognise myself in the mirror,” he says. “I was half a man. My family, my girlfriend, my friends – you know what is to see somebody you love, and feel no love? You feel empty.”
While he says his symptoms have improved since he started treatment for PTSD, the trauma hasn’t left him. Loud noises, the smell of burning, fights with his girlfriend – many things can set off panic attacks, even if they are growing shorter and shorter.
Read moreIsrael marks three years since October 7 attacks with strikes on Gaza, political debate
According to Gaza’s health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s onslaught in Gaza since the October 7 attacks. The Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel killed 1,220 people, with more than 970 Israeli soldiers dying in the subsequent wars launched in Gaza and Lebanon.
When asked about the human cost of Israel’s war in Gaza, Tapicer said that vengeance was a dead end.
“Today, I understand that it’s a problem you’re not going to solve like that. I killed a lot of terrorists and it didn’t make me feel better. It actually makes me feel worse.”
A heavy toll
Since October 7, the wars that Israel has carried out across the Middle East have taken a heavy toll on its soldiers. In January, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said that there had been a 40 percent increase in cases of PTSD among the army’s ranks since September 2023.
Of the more than 22,000 people treated for war-related injuries, 60 percent struggle with PTSD – a struggle that drives some to try to kill themselves. Last year, a Knesset report found that some 279 soldiers had tried to take their own lives between January 2024 and July 2025.
Last July, the Israeli parliament officially recognised “combat trauma” as a disability linked to service in the country’s armed forces, allowing impacted soldiers to benefit from state-funded treatment.

In Afula in Israel’s north, the Clalit-HaEmek Medical Centre has been overwhelmed by a non-stop flow of patients suffering from severe psychiatric problems.
Psychiatric services director Alon Reshef said he believed the worst was yet to come.
“When the whole stress comes down, we will see a tsunami of people with all kinds of mental problems – and I think we’re on the verge of it,” he said.
“The waiting list for hospitalisation are getting longer and longer and longer. And not only that, but the cases that we meet are much more complex, much more severe. And it's not only PTSD. If you have a mental health problem, let's say depression or schizophrenia, it's also affected, because all these disorders react to what’s happening in society. The number of forced hospitalisations has risen dramatically. So all the signs show that the mental crisis is not only a problem of the practitioners like me or the patients, but a problem of society – and particularly among those soldiers who fought for a long time in Gaza.”
‘Society in Israel is ill’
Reshef hopes that whatever government emerges from the October 27 elections will take the issue of Israelis’ mental health seriously.
“Society in Israel is ill,” he said. “It has lots of vital powers, but right now it is sick. Too much hate, too many confrontations. And nobody listens to the other … It will take years to heal.”
His colleague, Ronen Sidi, has begun carrying out the experimental treatment of severe forms of PTSD with MDMA, more commonly known as ecstasy. By releasing serotonin and dopamine, this synthetic party drug can help patients work through their trauma, learning to live with the feelings that threaten to overwhelm them.
Sidi, a psychologist specialising in psychedelic treatments, said that the treatments were so far yielding positive results, noting a decrease in the intensity of his patients’ symptoms.
Trauma and resilience
Himself a former member of the special forces, Sidi is all too familiar with the trauma that can follow the savage acts that soldiers are often exposed to. But he said that an army’s cohesion in wartime stemmed first and foremost from the legitimacy of the government that sent it to fight.
“There's a lot of studies about PTSD, but there are also quite a few now about resilience,” he said. “What seems to have a lot to do with resilience is a sense of meaning – if you have a reason to do what you do, you can endure a lot of difficulty.”
For the Israeli reservists who have served for sometimes up to 600 days since the October 7 attacks – up from a baseline of 15 to 20 days a year – this point remains fundamental, he said.
“Three years after the October 7 attacks, and with a government that a lot of people don't agree with what they're doing, a lot more soldiers are saying, ‘I have to fight, it's hard – it might even be less hard than it was two and a half years ago – but what am I doing here? Where is this leading?"
‘I want to get better so I can keep serving my country’
In the port of Jaffa south of the sprawling city of Tel Aviv, Or is enjoying a few days of rest between two stretches of military service. A few months ago, the 32-year-old social worker asked to be treated for PTSD.
Serving as a medic in an infantry unit, he has taken part in several missions in war zones and racked up more than 400 days of military service since October 7. Beer in hand, he says, calmly enough, that he is starting to crack.
“It’s a very long war, every soldier has seen horrible things. Sometimes we feel hate. A few months ago, I asked to be treated for PTSD. Many of my friends are doing the same,” he said. “No one comes through three years of war unscathed. Like a lot of people, I feel in control when I’m in the army, but when I get home, I don’t feel well.”
Read moreHow Netanyahu survived the political fallout from the October 7 attacks
His request for treatment came after an experience that left him badly shaken. Four months ago, his combat unit was on patrol when they were surprised by Hamas fighters near a tunnel entrance. The resulting shootout killed one soldier and left several more wounded.
“It was horrible. People told me after that I was screaming, I had lost my mind,” he said. “The soldier who was killed had his face torn off, and it was me who put his body in a jeep. I did everything like a robot, but I remember images, smells.”
Since then, the young man has continued to undertake stretches of military service, but has been assigned to surveillance rather than frontline combat. He is also seeing a psychotherapist.
“I need to take care of myself. I need to get better so I can keep serving my country,” he said.
‘I don’t want to keep fighting wars’
Like many reservists, Or says that he no longer has confidence in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and its conduct of the war. But as with many Israelis, fear of Hamas rides roughshod over all other considerations.
“I was shocked by the orders that I was given in Gaza, I didn’t think it was the right way to do things. But we had no other choice. We were scared. We knew that Hamas wanted to kill us all, whatever happened, because they hate us. I don’t agree with everything my country has done, especially against civilians, but it’s war,” he said.
“War is bad for Israeli society – it only encourages the extremists,” he added in a resigned tone.
Or doesn’t understand the hostility the rest of the world has towards Israel’s determination to raze the Gaza Strip to the ground, seeing the war in the narrow Palestinian territory as fundamentally defensive in nature. The social worker identifies as a left-wing voter, though he says that the October 7 attacks have shaken his convictions.
He says he hopes that the coming elections will bring about a government that has solutions to the problems facing Israel.
“I don’t want to keep fighting wars,” he said. “I often think that I’ve reached the limits of what I can endure. But they always ask more of me, and I’m able to push those limits back a little further.”

articles.title: Zelenskyy says restrictions on Starlink remain in force

Zelenskyy says restrictions on Starlink remain in force
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.

The answer is simple. We want people to understand us, and I mean people, societies, nations, as many people as possible. And when people understand what is really going on, political leaders can take a stronger path. The one that can really bring peace closer."

articles.title: Ethiopia's Tigray rebels urged to disarm
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Ethiopia's Tigray rebels urged to disarm as commander vows to fight on
An official in Tigray’s new federal-backed administration urged rebel fighters to lay down their weapons Friday, hours after a rebel commander called for continued resistance despite losing the northern Ethiopian region’s capital.
The calls to surrender and fight on came nearly three weeks after rebels lost control of Mekelle. At a hospital in the city, two wounded men said a drone strike killed four civilians as they loaded goats onto a truck earlier this week.
Redae Halefom Woldeselassie, the caretaker administration’s chief executive for political and public mobilisation, said rebel forces were collapsing and urged fighters to enter a disarmament and reintegration program.
“This is not the time for settling scores, I call upon you to return to your homes and continue your civilian lives,” he said in Mekelle.
He dismissed the prospect of the rebels retaking the city and portrayed the conflict as serving a small group of leaders rather than the people of Tigray.
Hours earlier, Lt. Gen. Fisseha Kidanu, identified in a television broadcast as commander of the Tigray army, pledged to reverse recent military setbacks.
“Local militias across the region — alongside all volunteers joining the resistance — are expected to engage the enemy,” he said Thursday night on Tigray Broadcast Media, a new rebel television station. His location was not disclosed.
Fisseha urged attacks on government-held positions despite his opponents’ advantages in drones and heavy weapons. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, has also claimed to have inflicted heavy losses on government forces. The Associated Press could not independently verify those claims.
Government-allied fighters entered Mekelle on Oct. 4 after the TPLF withdrew. Ethiopia’s government subsequently established a six-month caretaker administration promising to restore services, help displaced people return and prepare for elections.
The government’s allies include the Tigray Peace Force, comprising former members of the TPLF’s armed wing — a division within Tigrayan forces that has complicated the renewed conflict.
Redae said Ethiopian troops and allied forces were conducting joint security operations, including measures to prevent looting. He promised preparations for displaced residents to return but gave no timetable.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, speaking Monday to the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation, accused the TPLF of acquiring weapons and forcibly recruiting young people instead of disarming under the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. He said his government had done everything within its capacity to implement the accord.
Wounded men describe drone strike 
At Ayder Hospital in Mekelle, Luel Berhanu, 22, and Samuel Belay, 20, said they were loading goats onto a truck in Finariwa, about 80 kilometers (49 miles) south of the city, when a strike hit around 9:30 p.m. Tuesday.
They said four civilians were killed and about six people wounded. The AP could not independently verify the casualties or establish who carried out the attack.
Luel said the truck’s headlights were on and a drone was hovering overhead shortly before the explosion. He said the blast severely injured his right eye and right arm, leaving him unable to see through that eye.
Samuel said they were working as day laborers loading the animals.
Hospital footage showed Luel with a bloodstained bandage covering his right eye and dressings around his shoulder and arm. Samuel lay on his side with an intravenous line attached to his arm.
A witness interviewed by the AP reported movements earlier that day by fighters identified as Agew Shengo, a militia that has previously fought alongside Tigrayan forces in neighboring Amhara region. Luel said rebel forces had been in the area several hours before the strike but none were present when it occurred.
Losing Mekelle may not end the war 
The renewed fighting has effectively shattered the Pretoria agreement, which ended the devastating 2020-2022 war.
Magnus Taylor, deputy Horn of Africa director at the International Crisis Group, told the AP last week that controlling towns and roads would not necessarily secure rural areas where Tigrayan fighters regrouped during the previous war.
“We shouldn’t imagine that this conflict is completely over just because the TPLF has lost Mekelle,” he said.

articles.title: New exchange: Ukraine brings back 270 more defenders from Russian captivity – photos
articles.body:
New exchange: Ukraine brings back 270 more defenders from Russian captivity – photos
On Friday 23 October, 270 military personnel returned to Ukraine from Russian captivity as part of a new exchange.
Source: Zelenskyy on social media; Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War
Quote from Zelenskyy: "270 of our people are home. A very important result. National Guard members, including Azov warriors, border guards, warriors of the Territorial Defence Forces, the Navy, the Land Forces, the Airborne Assault Forces, and the State Special Transport Service, as well as nine civilians, are returning home. Most of them had been in captivity since 2022."
Details: According to the president, most of those released are warriors who defended Ukraine in Mariupol. People who defended the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, and Chernihiv fronts are also returning.
"Many were illegally convicted in Russia. Among those returning are five people who were believed to have been killed in the Russian terrorist attack in Olenivka in July 2022," Zelenskyy wrote.
Background: Ukraine and Russia held their last prisoner of war exchange in August, when 103 service personnel from the National Guard, the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the Navy, the Territorial Defence Forces and the State Border Guard Service were brought back to Ukraine.

articles.title: Standoff hits Sudanese consumers as Egypt halts cargo trucks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Border standoff hits Sudanese consumers as Egypt halts cargo trucks
Egyptian authorities have suspended cargo truck crossings into Sudan, triggering severe shortages and price hikes that ordinary Sudanese are struggling to absorb.
The decision followed the killing of two Egyptian truck drivers and the injury of a third on 12 October, when a 23-year-old Sudanese gunman opened fire on them in a popular market south of Khartoum.
The incident occurred only a day after scores of artisanal miners, including Sudanese nationals, were killed by Egyptian airstrikes in the border area between Egypt and Sudan.
According to the Egyptian army, the strikes were staged inside Egypt. However, unofficial Sudanese claims to the contrary have caused anger in different parts of Sudan.
Sudanese demonstrators took to the streets, particularly in Nyala—the capital of South Darfur State and a stronghold of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces which battles the Sudanese Armed Forces for control over Sudan.
Activists also called for a boycott of Egyptian goods, planning to blockade the desert road linking Khartoum to border crossings to halt incoming freight.
Cairo framed the suspension as a protective measure to shield Egyptian drivers from targeted violence.
Regardless of Cairo's rationale, the move has dealt an immediate blow to Sudanese consumers, threatening to trigger widespread inflation at an already precarious moment.
A recent viral video captured a Sudanese shopkeeper gesturing to his fully stocked shelves. Most of the goods, he noted, were either imported directly from Egypt or relied on Egyptian raw materials.
"Do you know what the decision to suspend the entry of cargo trucks from Egypt into Sudan means?" the trader asks. "It means that the prices of all these products will shoot up in the coming days."
Lifeline severed
Egypt serves as a vital gateway for Sudan's access to global markets, particularly as international sanctions continue to cripple Sudanese businesses.
Sudan's civil war, which has been grinding on since April 2023, has also put the brakes on a sizeable portion of the country's industrial and agricultural production, making it more dependent on imports for the needs of its people.
In 2025, bilateral trade reached $1.19 billion, with Egyptian exports accounting for $933.3 million.
In the first half of this year, bilateral trade reached $759 million, up from $570 million in the corresponding period of the previous year, according to the Egyptian government. Egyptian exports amounted to $595 million, almost 40% up from the export figure recorded in the first half of 2025, the government says.
Trade between the two countries partly owes its activity to their ability to develop a barter-style system that helps them avoid stringent international sanctions on Sudanese businesses and foreign currency shortages on both sides, specialists said.
However, cutting off Egyptian goods leaves the war-ravaged nation deeply vulnerable, forcing consumers to endure sudden supply bottlenecks alongside skyrocketing prices, Sudanese specialists said.
"This suspension is having far-reaching economic and human consequences," Sudanese political analyst Osman al-Merghani said.
Speaking to The New Arab, he added that the market has been paralyzed in almost all Sudanese states due to the dramatic rise that happened in commodity prices.
"Some commodities, including sugar and rice, have also completely disappeared, which is causing a lot of suffering to ordinary consumers," al-Merghani said.
Online hostility vs. diplomatic containment
The current disruption to bilateral trade comes at a time when a social media war is raging on between the Egyptians and the Sudanese against the background of the 11 October strikes.
Sudanese nationals commenting on the incident slam Egypt for killing what they describe as "innocent" artisanal miners and allegedly infringing on Sudanese territories, throwing light on growing anti-Egypt sentiments in some parts of the southern neighbouring country.
Egyptian social media users counter by defending their national army, and accusing the Sudanese of mining for gold inside Egypt, hence stealing the country's mineral resources.
The surge in anti-Egyptian rhetoric has heightened anxiety among the estimated 1,000 Egyptian nationals still remaining in Sudan.
Before the war erupted in April 2023, between 10,000 and 15,000 Egyptians lived in Sudan, mostly those married to Sudanese, working in Sudan or investing in the country.
An Egyptian national has recently posted a video where he implored Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to help him and others return safely to Egypt.
"The Sudanese are lying in wait for us on the road between Khartoum and the Egyptian border," the man said in the video which appeared on social media on October 14.
Most Egyptian nationals present in Sudan are reportedly concentrated in coastal areas under the control of the Sudanese Armed Force, especially Port Sudan where the Egyptian Consulate operates and business activities remain comparatively stable.
The governments of the two countries keep working, meanwhile, to contain fallout from the 11 October strikes.
On 16 October, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Sudanese Finance Minister Gibril Ibrahim rejected attempts to harm their countries' bilateral relations, noting that those relations are based on shared respect and good neighbourliness.
Meeting the Sudanese minister on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Washington DC, the Egyptian foreign minister reaffirmed Cairo's unwavering support for Sudan's unity and territorial integrity.
This meeting came four days after the foreign ministers of the two countries underscored the importance of respecting each other's country's sovereignty, territorial integrity and borders.
Analysts in Cairo view these diplomatic containment efforts as proof of the high strategic value both nations place on bilateral ties.
They call for managing those relations wisely, especially in the presence of persistent attempts by some parties to sabotage them.
"It is clear that some parties work to widen the gap between the two countries and cause a rupture in their relations," Egyptian political analyst Islam Mansi said.
"These parties do their best to incite the Sudanese people against Egypt, a country bound by historical ties and a shared destiny with Sudan," he told TNA.

articles.title: Putin: Russia has told US it is ready to resume trilateral talks
articles.body:
Putin: Russia has told US it is ready to resume trilateral talks
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has said that Russia has informed the United States of its readiness to resume trilateral negotiations.
Source: Kremlin-aligned Russian news agency TASS, citing Putin's remarks on the evening of 22 October
Details: Putin said the aim of negotiations with the US and Ukraine will be to "achieve lasting peace and ensure Russia's security". He stated that Russia is still "ready to negotiate and seek a way out of the difficult situation in Ukraine".
He claimed that Russia will fulfil its objectives and that "all the goals of the special military operation" (the term used by Russian propaganda to describe the Russia-Ukraine war) will be achieved.
Putin also claimed that Ukrainians are being "rounded up in the streets like stray dogs and forcibly sent to the front".
Quote: "Kyiv chose war itself – 'fine, then'. Russia offered to help Ukraine reach an agreement with Donbas, but Kyiv chose guns, Putin said."
Background:
- On 21 October in Saint Petersburg, a meeting took place between US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and Putin. It lasted for about 3 hours.
- The talks in Russia took place the day after Witkoff met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders of Norway and Finland in Oslo.
- During the meeting on 21 October, Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian".
- In turn, Putin told Witkoff that Moscow is ready to resume trilateral talks in the Ukraine-US-Russia format in mid-November.
- Shortly after the meeting with Witkoff and discussions about peace and negotiations, Russian forces launched 21 missiles towards Kyiv, killing at least two people and injuring more than 30.
